struct.domain: Structures, thermal, power and large space infrastructure

bottlenecks.name: Qualification evidence, margins and model credibility
bottlenecks.description: Proving primary structure will not fail. Practice stacks deterministic factors of safety (ultimate ~1.25 uncrewed, ~1.4 crewed, general), empirical buckling knockdown factors from 1960s lower-bound curves (NASA SP-8007; a universal 0.65 for composites that NASA itself calls possibly unconservative), building-block test pyramids from coupons to full-scale static tests, and model-credibility processes (NASA-STD-7009). Each dedicated qualification article costs months to years.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~25% of structures/thermal engineering effort on a new vehicle or large spacecraft (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High for the math, capped for the payoff. Worst-case imperfection theory and model-form error are genuinely open; reliability-based margins, rare-event estimation and certified error bounds are solved in principle but expert-scarce, which is exactly what on-demand AI supplies. Standards bodies and agencies gate the benefit, so downstream nodes are capped at Medium.

bottlenecks.name: Launch loads and dynamics
bottlenecks.description: Coupled loads analysis (CLA) cycles with the launch provider using Craig-Bampton component models, repeated as designs mature; random vibration, acoustic and shock environments enveloped from flight data plus fixed margins; the mid-frequency band where neither finite elements nor statistical energy analysis is reliable. NASA NESC built Norton-Thevenin Receptance Coupling (2023-2024) precisely because full CLA is slow and costly.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-High. CLA setup and model reduction are expert-scarce routine work that AI agents can run on demand (fast, P1); the mid-frequency problem is open applied math (slower, P6). Forcing-function uncertainty (liftoff acoustics, buffet) and mandatory qualification-by-test remain.

bottlenecks.name: Damage tolerance, fatigue and inspection for reuse
bottlenecks.description: Crack growth and composite damage under the low-cycle, high-amplitude, cryogenic and thermal-cycling spectra of reusable stages; COPV liner cracks; non-destructive inspection turnaround between flights; qualifying structural health monitoring (SHM) with a probability of detection. First stages are ~70% of launch-vehicle cost (ONERA, 2026), so reuse economics hinge on inspection cost.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~15% and rising with reuse (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. Inverse-problem stability, optimal sensor placement and model-assisted POD are solved in principle but expert-scarce (AI helps quickly). Damage physics is data-limited: theory needs coupon-to-subcomponent test campaigns. Catalog families 372, 365, 366 touch this only through confidence (P5) and one ceiling (P3).

bottlenecks.name: Thermal design and heat rejection
bottlenecks.description: Radiator sizing under the Stefan-Boltzmann T^4 law with view factors to Earth, Sun and the spacecraft itself; heat transport (pumped liquid and two-phase loops, heat pipes) whose microgravity behavior is still correlation-based; thermal-model correlation after thermal-vacuum tests; the chip-temperature versus chip-life trade. For compute satellites thermal is now a primary mass term: ~25% of SpaceX AI1's reconstructed 2.1 t (33FG, Jun 2026).
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~20%, much higher on orbital compute programs (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. Radiator and loop design optimization and model correlation are expert-scarce and well-posed (AI helps fast). The physics is fixed (T^4, junction-temperature limits) and the binding gates are manufacturing at Starlink volume and flight data for two-phase models. Family 369 (hot spots) is a nil link.

bottlenecks.name: Large deployables and in-space assembly
bottlenecks.description: Deployment reliability of booms, membranes and panels; the impossibility of representative 1 g ground tests for 100 m to km structures; nonsmooth contact and friction dynamics, membrane wrinkling, thermally induced vibration; robotic assembly. ACS3 (2024) flew an ~80 m2 sail on 7 m booms; follow-on booms target 2,000 m2.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-Low. Better models and scaling laws help, but qualification needs flight data, and formation flying (Google Suncatcher's 81-satellite 1 km cluster; SpaceX Starmind's ~10-satellite clusters) is displacing monolithic km-scale structures.

bottlenecks.name: Power-system integration (fission and very large solar)
bottlenecks.description: For Fission Surface Power: reactor, shield, closed Brayton converter, 500-600 K radiators and lander integration within ~6 t (reactor) on a heavy lander, with radiation transport for shielding (outside the release) and nuclear launch approval. For orbital compute: solar array areal density, which 33FG identifies as AI1's primary mass constraint (ROSA-class 1.8-2 kg/m2 needed).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Low-Medium. Multiphysics trades accelerate, but fuel, licensing, nuclear ground testing, heavy-lander availability and solar-cell/array manufacturing dominate. First-of-a-kind designs freeze before AI design capability matures.

struct.scenario_contrast: S1 (plateau): research-grade applied math reaches outside teams around 2030, so the cognitive tiers (1-4) land 2028 to beyond 2031 and only 7 of 16 are Medium or better by 2031. The early wins are AI agents running routine analysis (2028) and expert confirmation of the elasticity and hot-spots manuscripts; tiers 5-7 are mostly Low or Speculative (4 of 13 Medium or better, two of them hardware anchors that happen without AI math). S2 (exponential, base case): the cognitive clock compresses by about 2 years on average (median tier 1-4 year 2029; all 16 Medium or High by 2031). Worst-case imperfection theory, certified uncertainty margins, SHM detection limits and radiator optimization arrive in 2028; the physics nodes (composite damage, microgravity two-phase flow, deployment dynamics) arrive in 2030 because data, not cognition, binds. The physical tiers move only about 1 year on average (median 2030) because standards revisions, build-and-qualify cycles, sensor qualification, manufacturing ramps and launch cadence bind. By 2031 under S2: lighter buckling rules (Medium), a first flight structure sized with AI-certified margins (Medium, 2030), SHM inspection credit (Medium), 100 kW/t compute satellites (Medium, 2030) and 1 GW of orbital compute (Medium, 2031, with AI math a second-order contributor), while a km-scale monolith stays Speculative and the lunar 100 kWe reactor stays Low in every scenario. S3 (recursive): moves half the cognitive nodes another year (mainly physics nodes through autonomous labs, and verified numerics) but only 4 of 13 physical nodes, by one year each (reusable-stage life management, a 1,000 m2 sail, 1 GW orbital compute, the structural-mass step). It cannot compress orbital exposure, fleet flight hours, heavy-lander schedules, nuclear licensing or standards cycles. Net: in this domain the S1-to-S2 gap is large in analysis labor and design rules, small in flown hardware by 2031; most of the S2 payoff lands in second-generation hardware after 2031.
key_insights: The catalog barely reaches this domain; the capability does. Only five families touch it (372, 365, 366, 368 elasticity and fracture; 369 hot spots), all as confidence (P5) except one possible ceiling: 365's conductivity nonuniqueness (T3) may bound resistance-based damage sensing in carbon-fiber structures. The hot-spots result (369) changes no thermal design.

The largest near-term effect is labor, not theorems: AI agents running and checking stress, loads and thermal analyses (prototypes exist in 2026) compress design cycles severalfold by ~2028 under S2. This is 'solved in principle but expert-scarce' work, and it is the only node that is High by 2031 in every scenario.

The clearest 'lighter primary structure' chain runs through an open applied-math problem, not a famous conjecture: worst-case imperfections in thin shells. Raising a knockdown factor from 0.65 to 0.80 cuts buckling-critical wall mass ~10% (t scales as KDF^-1/2); optimized shells save 14-31% (Wagner et al. 2025). Standards revision and validation tests cap it at Medium, and the vehicle-level payoff is ~1-3% payload.

Uniqueness is not stability. For structural health monitoring, AI-produced problem-specific stability estimates and probability-of-detection curves matter far more than 372-style uniqueness theorems, because inspection credit depends on what damage size N sensors can see at 90/95 confidence.

For orbital data centers, heat rejection is an engineering and manufacturing problem, not a math or physics blocker. Thermal mass per GW falls from ~19,400 t (Starlink-like, 310 K, one-sided) to ~3,400-3,500 t (AI1 or StarThink V2, ~370 K, two-sided) through temperature and architecture choices already made; AI-optimized design adds perhaps a further 10-25% of thermal mass (~350-900 t, or 3-9 Starship flights per GW), i.e. a few percent of launched mass.

First-of-a-kind timing trap: Fission Surface Power (launch-ready target Q1 FY2030) and AI1 (spec published Jun 2026) freeze their designs before S2's AI design-optimization capability (~2029) matures, so AI-math gains land in second-generation units after 2030.

Formation flying is displacing km-scale structures: Google Suncatcher (81 satellites within 1 km) and SpaceX Starmind (~10-satellite tight clusters, Oct 2026) solve the aperture and bandwidth problem with GNC and optical links. A km-scale monolith stays Speculative by 2031 even under S2.

Data, not cognition, gates the physics nodes (composite damage, microgravity two-phase flow, deployment dynamics, mid-frequency vibration). Compute-satellite fleets streaming thermal telemetry from ~2027-28 become the most valuable two-phase dataset in history; whoever owns the fleet will own the models.

Certification by analysis is the biggest prize (each avoided qualification article saves tens of millions of dollars and a year) but sits behind the slowest gate. Verified finite-element numerics (P2) help less here than in flight software because discretization error is rarely the dominant structural uncertainty.

S3 versus S2 barely matters at tiers 5-7 in this domain: S3 moves 4 of 13 physical nodes forward by one year (reusable-stage life management, a 1,000 m2 sail, 1 GW orbital compute, the structural-mass step), mostly because autonomous labs speed damage-model testing, while qualification tests, flight data, manufacturing ramps, nuclear licensing and launch cadence hold the rest. S1 to S2 moves the cognitive tiers about 2 years but the physical tiers only about 1.
nil_effects: Stefan-Boltzmann is not negotiable: radiator area per watt at a given temperature is fixed, and chip junction limits (~85-105 C) cap radiator temperature unless heat pumps spend power to lift it. No theorem changes the ~0.7 km2 of panel per GW at ~1,400 W/m2.
Launch cadence, heavy-lander availability, capital and chip supply set the dates for GW-scale orbital compute and lunar fission power under all three scenarios.
Space nuclear power gates (fuel supply, nuclear launch approval, ground testing, budget) are untouched; radiation transport for shield design is outside the release entirely.
Material strength, stiffness and density limits do not move with mathematics; any gains come from using existing materials closer to their limits (materials domain covers new materials).
Qualification testing of first-of-kind primary structure, thermal-vacuum and vibration tests remains mandatory through 2031; analysis can reduce tests on derivatives, not eliminate them.
Galactic speedups (107 matrix multiplication, 130 FFT) give no speedup to finite-element, vibroacoustic or thermal codes.
Well-posedness theorems (372, 366, 368) change no simulation code; they raise confidence that what the codes approximate exists and is unique.
Family 369 (hot spots) has no effect on radiator or panel thermal design: real hardware is 3D with radiative boundaries and is designed numerically.
Micrometeoroid and debris flux is a property of the environment; mathematics changes only the design response (segmentation, armoring), not the threat to km2-scale radiators.

verif.domain: Flight software, autonomy assurance and certification

bottlenecks.name: Verification and test labor
bottlenecks.description: Requirements-based unit and integration testing, structural coverage (MC/DC at the highest criticality), code reviews and regression re-verification after every change. In DO-178C Level A practice this is the dominant cost: verification can reach 80% of a Level A software budget, effective productivity is under 10 lines per person-day, and cost runs about $25-100 per line. NASA IV&V adds a further 10-15% of development cost.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~40-50% of safety-critical flight-software effort (up to 80% of a DO-178C Level A budget when all verification is counted)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly 'solved in principle but expensive and expert-scarce'. DO-333 already lets formal proof replace most executable-object-code testing except hardware/software integration tests (Airbus replaced unit tests with proofs on A380 software in 2002). Agents that write contracts and proofs, checked by an already-qualified prover, attack this cost directly. This is the largest cost lever in the domain.

bottlenecks.name: Requirements, specifications and environmental assumptions
bottlenecks.description: Writing correct, complete requirements and interface control documents, and stating what the software may assume about sensors, terrain, timing, units and hardware behavior. Most software-caused mission losses trace here: Ariane 501's reused range assumption, Mars Climate Orbiter's units, Schiaparelli's IMU-saturation duration, Hakuto-R M1's terrain, Starliner OFT's timer source.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~15-20% of effort, but the root of all 9 software-related losses in our failure table
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Split. Drafting formal specs from English, unit-typing interfaces, and checking consistency and realizability is expert-scarce work AI does well (cheap unlock). Validating that a spec matches mission intent and physical reality is partly open and data-bound: it needs sensor characterization, terrain data and human sign-off. Once proofs are cheap, this becomes the binding bottleneck (analyst position h).

bottlenecks.name: GNC and numerical algorithm assurance
bottlenecks.description: Showing that guidance, navigation and control code, estimators and onboard optimizers behave as designed: stability margins under saturation and delay, measurement-rejection gates, floating-point round-off and overflow, solver convergence within a timing budget.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~5-10% of effort (concentrated in a few scarce specialists)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly expert-scarce rather than open: round-off proofs (NASA DAIDALUS with PVS, PRECiSA and Frama-C), runtime-error analysis (Astree), Lyapunov and barrier certificates, reachability. Nonlinear hybrid verification at full-vehicle scale and certified onboard optimization are partly open research. Lean coverage of floating point (FloatLib, Sep 2026) and of ODEs and numerics is the formalization gate.

bottlenecks.name: Integration, fault management, configuration and timing
bottlenecks.description: Hardware-in-the-loop and end-to-end testing, fault-combination testing of fault detection, isolation and recovery (FDIR), reboot and timing behavior, parameter tables, command sequences and in-flight patches. Starliner OFT, Beresheet, Hitomi and IM-1 failures sit in this class.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~15-20% of effort; HIL rig time often sets schedule
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Model checking of FDIR and mode logic and verification of configuration data are mature in principle; the cost is building faithful models, which agents can extract from code and ICDs. Physical HIL and hardware characterization (for example, whether restarting one IMU blocks the other's data) stay on the physical clock.

bottlenecks.name: Certification evidence, tool qualification and independent review
bottlenecks.description: Producing and defending evidence for DO-178C/DO-333/DO-330, NASA NPR 7150.2D and NASA-STD-8739.8B, NPR 8705.2C human rating, ECSS-E-ST-40C Rev.1 and ECSS-Q-ST-80C Rev.2, and FAA Part 450 section 450.141; qualifying or accrediting tools; independent verification and validation.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~10-15% of effort; sets the pace of credit, not of engineering
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Little cognitive help needed; the gate is regulatory. The key unlock is architectural: keep the AI outside the trusted base and route proofs through an already-qualified checker, so only the checker needs qualification. Qualifying Lean itself as a TQL-4/5 tool is the slower path (shared node infra-tool-qualification).

bottlenecks.name: Assurance of learned and autonomous components
bottlenecks.description: Neural perception for terrain-relative navigation and hazard detection, learned guidance, and onboard decision-making for landers, rendezvous and constellations. Aviation guidance (SAE ARP6983 / EUROCAE ED-324, EASA NPA 2025-07) relies on data and process assurance, not proof.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Genuinely open for direct verification: exact neural-network verification is NP-hard and 'correct perception' is defined by data, so VNN-COMP-scale tools remain far from flight vision networks. Strong help for the workaround: proving a small runtime-assurance monitor, recoverable set and backup controller (Simplex architecture).

verif.scenario_contrast: S1 (plateau): research-grade math reaches outside teams around 2028. Agents prove ordinary code well, but Lean coverage of numerics and dynamics stays thin to about 2030, so the cheap wins are runtime-error freedom, FDIR and configuration model checking, and AI-drafted specs. First certification credit for AI-generated proofs (through already-qualified checkers) arrives around 2029, with crewed-lander use after 2031. Full Level-A program software costs fall only 20-30%. S2 (exponential, base case): the cognitive clock collapses by 2027-28. Code proofs, specs, round-off bounds, barrier certificates and model building all become compute jobs, and the cost of a fully verified line falls 30-100x. Every remaining gate is physical or institutional: human review of specs, hardware-behavior and terrain data, HIL time, software freezes 12-18 months before flight, a few lander and rendezvous flights a year, and regulator plan acceptance. So uncrewed commercial landers and constellations, which have no certifying regulator for mission software, adopt first (2028-29), while crewed HLS autonomy and Part 450 credit arrive around 2029-30 and stay capped at Medium. S3 (recursive): cognitive work is near-free from 2028 and autonomous labs speed sensor characterization and HIL test automation, pulling environment models and RPO assurance forward by about a year. Launch cadence, lunar truth data, human-rating authority and the open problem of specifying correct perception do not move, so S3 differs from S2 by about a year on the physical nodes, not by a new class of outcome. In every scenario the binding constraint ends up being 'is the spec right?', not 'can we prove it?'.
key_insights: In this domain the catalog barely matters. The relevant evidence is the pipeline: agent-written Lean for the main results of 162 papers in under four weeks (openai/math, T3, unchecked), on top of a public trend from 82% Dafny vericoding (Sep 2025) to 27 of 43 repository-scale verified builds (Vero, Aug 2026). Only family 104 (game solving for synthesis) and, as theory only, family 143 touch verification at all, and neither changes workflows.

Keep the AI outside the trusted base. Under DO-330, a tool whose output is independently checked needs no qualification. If AI writes proofs and an already-qualified checker (SPARK, Frama-C, Astree) verifies them, DO-333 credit for replacing unit tests can flow without qualifying the AI. The regulatory gate becomes a plan-acceptance step (around 2028 in S2), not a new standard. Lean-native pipelines, where AI labs are strongest, must take the slower route of qualifying Lean itself (around 2030 in S2).

Specifications, not proofs, are the bottleneck. Of 12 notable losses and near-losses (Ariane 501 to Athena), 9 were primarily or partly software, logic or configuration errors. In all 9 the missing piece was a wrong or missing assumption, interface spec or process step (Ariane 4 ranges, units, IMU saturation duration, a crater rim, IMU restart bus behavior, the timer source), not proof capacity. Cheap proofs pay off only alongside AI spec drafting and assumption falsification, and those are bound by data and human review.

Uncrewed commercial space adopts fastest because nobody certifies its mission software. Lunar landers and constellations need only internal or customer acceptance, so they lead (S2: 2028-29). Aviation-style DO-178C credit, NASA human rating (NPR 8705.2C) and FAA Part 450 credit all need a regulator, so they are capped at Medium and arrive later.

Cost model: a fully verified line gets 30-100x cheaper (from about $300-600 to about $5-20 under S2), but a certified Level-A program's software gets only about 2.4x cheaper. Hardware/software integration and system testing stay physical, and DO-333 itself keeps integration tests. The bigger change is the assurance level per dollar and re-verification turnaround (weeks to days).

Timing: Artemis IV's 2028 crewed landing software is largely frozen before public research-grade verification arrives, so proofs reach crewed lunar autonomy in 2029-31 block upgrades. Constellations, with more than 355,000 autonomous-dominated avoidance maneuvers a year at Starlink and weekly updates, are where verified autonomy pays first.

Neural-network verification remains genuinely open even in S3, because 'correct perception' is defined by data. The practical route is proven runtime-assurance wrappers (Simplex), which agents make cheap.

Even if it all works, it will be hard to see by 2031. There will be too few landings to show a statistically lower software-caused loss rate, and recent lander losses (Peregrine, Resilience, Athena) were mostly hardware and sensor physics that software proofs do not touch.
nil_effects: Hardware and sensor-physics failures: Peregrine's helium valve (2024), Resilience's degraded rangefinder (2025) and Athena's altimeter interference and low-sun lighting (2025) are untouched by software proofs. That is roughly half of recent lunar-landing losses.

Hardware/software integration testing, HIL time and environmental qualification (thermal vacuum, vibration, radiation) stay on the physical clock. DO-333 explicitly retains hardware/software integration tests.
Multicore timing interference, worst-case execution time on new processors and radiation-induced upsets are measured, not proven. Isolation and timing proofs assume correct hardware.
The number of rendezvous, docking and propellant-transfer flight demonstrations needed for HLS (reportedly around 15-17 Starship flights per landing) does not shrink because software is proven.
Direct verification of flight-scale neural perception stays out of reach through 2031 in every scenario; assurance routes around it with runtime monitors.

Standards revision cycles stay slow: DO-178B (1992) to DO-178C (2011), NPR 7150.2C (2014) to NPR 7150.2D (2022) (general). No DO-178D or regulator-endorsed AI-proof standard is likely before the 2030s, so credit comes through existing alternative-means clauses.
FAA Part 450 license timelines, driven by environmental review, mishap investigations and public-safety analysis, do not shorten because of formal evidence (general).

Catalog results with no verification effect: Unique Games (102), random-SAT thresholds (235), Subset Sum (138) and L=RL=BPL (103) do not change SAT/SMT solver practice on structured verification problems. The galactic speedups for matrix multiplication (107) and the FFT (130) give no onboard or toolchain gain. Learning-theory results (139, 140, 222) do not provide neural-network verification methods.
Command-link cryptography: nothing in the release weakens deployed authentication or encryption. A frontier model pointed at cryptanalysis is a watch item (analyst position f), not a present effect.

signposts.event: The first independent Comparator runs and statement audits of the openai/math Lean files (via Hexagon or Buzzard's group), including the rate of statement gaps.
signposts.what_it_changes: It calibrates how far agent-written formal artifacts can be trusted without human proof review. A low statement-gap rate supports the checker-not-generator path; a high one shifts weight onto spec review and slows verif-checker-not-generator.

signposts.event: Public release of a research-grade math and verification model (OpenAI or a rival) with agentic Lean, Dafny, SPARK or Frama-C workflows.
signposts.what_it_changes: It turns on P1 and P2 for outside space teams and dates the S1-versus-S2 fork for verif-code-proof-agents, verif-closed-loop-guarantees and every node downstream.

signposts.event: A vendor or agency case study of AI-generated proofs over more than 10 KLOC of production embedded code (AdaCore, AbsInt, TrustInSoft, Galois, NASA, ESA), or Vero-class repository benchmarks above 90%.
signposts.what_it_changes: It confirms verif-code-proof-agents and the cost-collapse chain; failure to appear by end-2027 pushes S2 dates back about a year.

signposts.event: An FAA or EASA certification review item, certification-authority paper or software certification plan accepting AI-generated proof artifacts checked by a qualified tool under DO-333.
signposts.what_it_changes: It opens the certified path (verif-checker-not-generator) and makes verif-afss-part450 and verif-hls-autonomy-certification reachable within the horizon.

signposts.event: Publication of SAE ARP6983 / EUROCAE ED-324 and EASA's second NPA under RMT.0742 (2026), and whether they credit runtime assurance or formal robustness proofs.
signposts.what_it_changes: Credit for runtime assurance moves verif-runtime-assurance toward High; silence on formal methods confirms that learned components are assured by process rather than proof.

signposts.event: The root cause of the next commercial lander or rendezvous failure (IM-3, Blue Ghost 2, ispace M3, Griffin, Blue Moon MK1, Starship transfer demos).
signposts.what_it_changes: A spec or assumption root cause supports the thesis that specifications bind; a logic error that a cheap proof would have caught shows adoption lagging capability; a hardware cause supports the nil effects.

signposts.event: NASA guidance on AI-generated code and verification evidence (a revision of NPR 7150.2, the software-engineering handbook, or IV&V practice), or a lander team declaring formally verified descent GNC and fault management at a readiness review.
signposts.what_it_changes: It confirms the uncrewed-first adoption path (verif-lander-verified-gnc-flight) and signals whether NASA's technical authority will accept proofs for human rating.

signposts.event: Maturity of Lean numerics: FloatLib or FloatSpec stable releases, verified ODE and linear-algebra libraries, and a qualification kit for the Lean kernel or Comparator.
signposts.what_it_changes: It sets the dates for infra-verified-numerics, verif-verified-gnc-numerics and the Lean route to infra-tool-qualification.

signposts.event: Starship ship-to-ship propellant transfer demonstration (reported for Q4 2026) and the Artemis III LEO docking test (late 2027).
signposts.what_it_changes: These set the physical clock for verif-rpo-assured-autonomy and verif-hls-autonomy-certification regardless of verification capability.

signposts.event: A mission loss or near-miss traced to an AI-written specification or proof, as opposed to AI-written code.
signposts.what_it_changes: This negative signpost would trigger regulator caution, pull certification-dependent nodes down a band, and strengthen the case for human spec review as the binding gate.

branches.title: The engine: AI math and the launch clock
branches.thesis: If AI's research-grade math reaches outside engineers (2027 in the base case) and its proofs can be checked cheaply, then on-demand analysis spreads through space engineering by 2028, but new programs get schedules only about a quarter to a third shorter (an Amdahl ceiling of ~38%, a 1.6x speedup, in the base case), not 10x, because tests, factories and launches run on their own physical clock, which AI touches mainly through anomaly analysis and through demand for orbital compute rather than through mathematics.
branches.reader_hook: A research-grade result costs about $200-2,000 in tokens (the low figure counts only published successes), so 1,000 hard problems a year cost one to ten engineers before checking, and checking, not generation, sets the price; yet with only about a third of a program's critical path cognitive, Amdahl's law caps base-case schedule compression at about 38%, and realized gains are likelier 20-30%, not 10x.
branches.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Thesis: 'about a third faster' -> 'about a quarter to a third shorter' (auditor: the model computes a shorter schedule, not 1.33x faster; skeptic: 38% is a ceiling); demand coupling added. Hook: cost per result qualified (skeptic + auditor); advocate's '45-50% once the analysis inside test is counted' rejected as double counting. | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Moved from spine to side_chains (still branch members): ['cap-design-optimization', 'physclock-starship-full-reuse', 'physclock-cheap-mass-internal']. The launch clock (Starship reuse to cheap mass) is a separate physical exponential with no hard link to the AI-math chain, so it is a side chain by construction.

branches.title: The famous problems
branches.thesis: If AI settles the headline problems of fluid and kinetic mathematics (Euler blowup, Boltzmann regularity, even unforced Navier-Stokes) and delivers certified error bars on demand, engineers get sharper tools and more confidence from about 2028 in the base case, and math stops being a program bottleneck around 2029. The famous theorems themselves change almost no engine, heat shield or orbit. What reaches engineering codes is the machinery built to prove them (computer-assisted proofs, verified interval numerics) and bespoke guarantees on demand, and it arrives as verification evidence, not performance.
branches.reader_hook: An AI agent formalized a Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau result in 10 days for about $200 with no human-written code (one mathematician, 229 prompts); two of its three failure modes (hypothesis creep, definition-alignment bugs) were in stating the problem, not proving it. Only 16 PDE and 12 dynamics families sit among the release's 372, because that is what was posed.
branches.band_note: For tier-1 math nodes, band_2031 is the judged chance the result is established (T4 Lean check or T2+ expert acceptance) by 2031; the engineering implication is judged separately in why (usually nil to Low, via P5). For tier-2 applied nodes it is the chance the capability is available and used as the signpost describes. Bands are judgments, not computed probabilities.
branches.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [advocate, partly] thesis now dates tools to 2028 and names the computer-assisted-proof spillover; [auditor] reader hook corrected (Ilin: 229 prompts, three failure modes) and band-semantics note added. | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Trunk nodes ['cap-research-math-internal', 'verif-independent-check'] are shown as the chain's entry anchors (also listed in roots); they stay members of the trunk branch only. No spine nodes dropped. The famous-problem nodes end at tier 1 by design: they are pure-math P3 markers with no hardware unlock.

branches.title: Software you can prove
branches.thesis: If AI agents can draft formal specifications and machine-checked proofs for flight code, a verified line of code gets 15-120x cheaper by 2028-29, and constellations, landers, reusable launchers and agent-commanded spacecraft fly proof-checked software from about 2029-30 (S2). Certification credit waits on regulators: plan acceptance about 2030 (Medium, the base-case premise), with engine, entry-guidance, Part 450 and crewed credit at Low by 2031. Fewer lost missions stay hard to see by 2031, because the failures were wrong assumptions, not missing proofs.
branches.reader_hook: A fully verified line of flight code falls from about $300-600 to about $5-20 by 2028-29 in the base case (15-120x), yet a Level-A-rigor program gets only about 2x cheaper (1.8-2.4x), and certified programs bank even that only after certification credit (S2 2030); in all 9 software- or logic-related losses and near-losses among 12 notable cases from Ariane 501 to Athena, the missing piece was a wrong assumption or spec, not proof capacity.

branches.title: Links, spectrum and codes
branches.thesis: If AI can prove optimality gaps for constellation routing and certified interference bounds for shared spectrum, then mega-constellation meshes and direct-to-device service run on certified plans by 2029-30 in the base case (Medium; about a year earlier is possible at a vertically integrated operator that owns its own frontier model, the optimistic case), while the international spectrum regime (no ITU action before WRC-31), quantum links and crypto migration move at regulatory and hardware speed. On security, AI's sharpest effect runs against defenders: cheaper code-breaking resource estimates make crypto-agility urgent.
branches.reader_hook: The FCC's 2026 rules (FCC 24-117 for sharing among non-geostationary systems, FCC 26-26 for sharing with geostationary ones) replace fixed power masks with private coordination backed by simulated performance criteria: 3% throughput loss and 0.1% (GSO) or 0.4% (NGSO) added unavailability. FCC 26-26 also removed the cap on co-frequency beams per location and declined aggregate limits, turning spectrum rights into a math problem. Realistic software gains are perhaps 5-20% of capacity at fixed hardware (judgment), small next to the 10x V3 per-satellite step, but the two multiply: in the urban cells that stay supply-bound even at V3 scale, beam scheduling against proven interference limits sets capacity.
branches.revision_note: C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Trunk nodes ['cap-autoformalization'] are shown as the chain's entry anchors (also listed in roots); they stay members of the trunk branch only. Moved from spine to side_chains (still branch members): ['frontier-approx-ceilings', 'comms-performance-based-sharing-regime', 'comms-ai-cryptanalysis', 'frontier-lattice-crypto-watch']. The post-quantum lane now joins through cap-autoformalization; the cryptanalysis watch item and approximation ceilings are side chains.

branches.title: Fewer tests, faster approvals
branches.thesis: Two tracks. Operators that carry their own risk can count AI analysis as evidence once they trust it: in the base case a commercial operator flies new-design hardware qualified mainly by analysis from about 2029-30 (Medium; High in S3). Government, crewed and national-security hardware waits for a rulebook (a credibility directive or handbook around 2029, Medium) and then for certification by analysis beyond what NASA-STD-5001B already allows (around 2030, Low in the base case). Structures and thermal analysis turnaround runs 2-5x faster from 2029, but qualification campaigns shorten only 10-20% (S2) to 20-30% (S3) by about 2031, because test stands, workmanship screening and real-time endurance tests, not math, bind.
branches.reader_hook: Much of what 'certification by analysis' promises already exists without AI: NASA-STD-5001B lets some metallic structures skip strength tests, and SP-8007-2020 records analysis-based buckling loads already used on the SLS core stage. Avoiding a launch-vehicle primary-structure qualification article saves tens of millions of dollars and up to a year; skipping a spacecraft unit's qualification model saves far less (general). The base case puts the first AI-backed government credit beyond today's allowances around 2030-31, against 2040-2050 in NASA-sponsored studies of aircraft certification by analysis.

branches.title: Engines, fuels and alloys
branches.thesis: If AI can certify combustion and CFD models and put trustworthy error bars on atomistic materials models, then engines could get model-based reuse life from about 2029 and an AI-agent-designed alloy could fly by 2031 (Low in the base case, Medium if AI speeds up its own R&D), but engine development stays test-paced: a fast fleet piles up engine starts, yet every failure mode still costs a redesign and a re-test.
branches.reader_hook: In an illustrative depot model, boil-off costs 1-5 extra tanker flights per lunar-lander refueling campaign, but a validated boil-off model recovers only the margin held against uncertainty: about 0-1 tanker at one tanker every 6 days. And 0.99 engine reliability at 90% confidence takes about 230 zero-failure starts; a high-cadence Starship fleet logs that many in a handful of flights, so what paces engines is finding and fixing failure modes, not counting starts.

branches.title: Getting through the atmosphere
branches.thesis: If AI can run rigorous uncertainty analysis on demand, commercial capsules may fly thinner, model-based heat shields around 2030 (S2, Medium). For the owner of a high-cadence vehicle, its own flight data rather than new theory closes the heating models, so Starship-scale heat-shield reuse arrives around 2030 on the launch curve, with AI adding months. Routine 50-a-year reentry, heavy Mars landings, point-to-point cargo and large fast returns stay paced by demand, launch windows, regulation and shock-tube time.
branches.reader_hook: For NASA's now-cancelled Mars Sample Retrieval Lander, a Monte Carlo at one stressing point found a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness kept the bondline below its limit in ~99% of cases. But it sampled aerothermal error only up to the existing margin factors, while at that 8 km/s entry the baseline radiation model under-predicted shock-tube data by up to 2x.

branches.title: Orbital compute and power
branches.thesis: Orbital AI compute runs on SpaceX's hardware, launch and capital clock, not on AI mathematics: 100-kW-class compute satellites first fly about 2028 and carry paying workloads about 2029 in every scenario, and 1 GW in orbit by 2031 is Low in the base case (S2) and Medium in S3. AI math adds confidence and a few percent: validated radiation-error models and proven fault-tolerance layers right-size mitigation (about 5-20% more useful compute per watt, an assumption), and AI thermal design trims about 2-9% of launched mass. The big mass levers are solar-array specific power and how hot chips and HBM may run, which life tests and flight telemetry, helped by AI applied math, decide.
branches.reader_hook: A gigawatt of orbital compute is about 4,000 Starmind-class satellites, 16,000-18,000 t and 110-180 Starship flights. Temperature and architecture choices already made cut thermal mass per GW from about 19,400 t (Starlink-like) to roughly 3,500-6,500 t; AI-optimized radiator design might save another 10-25% (an assumption), about 350-1,400 t or 4-14 flights, a few percent of launched mass. Qualifying chips and HBM to run about 30 C hotter would save more (about 1,900 t per GW in 33FG's model), and at SpaceX's ~250 kW target inside a filed radiator under 200 m2, thermal design matters as much for chip life as for mass. Solar arrays, at over half the satellite's mass, matter most.

The main chain is hardware on SpaceX's clock, matching the thesis; the AI-math lanes (radiation models, radiator optimization) feed it only softly.

branches.title: Living and working off Earth
branches.thesis: If AI can plan and check robot operations and put honest numbers on life-support and oxygen-plant reliability, lunar and Mars robots do severalfold more work per operator by about 2029 (base case, Medium). A base that runs itself between crew visits waits on heavy cargo landings and Moon Base Phase 2 infrastructure (2029-2032) and stays Low by 2031 in the base case. A tonne-a-year oxygen plant needs only a few kilowatts but is gated by anode endurance, riding a molten bath through lunar dark periods and pilot-plant funding, while Mars logistics stay gated by launch windows.
branches.reader_hook: A 2024 molten-regolith electrolysis rig made 0.07 kg of oxygen an hour and MOXIE made 12 g/h, against about 1.1 kg/h for a 10 t/yr lunar plant and about 65 kg/h for a Starship return. Excavation energy rises 52x (2.74 to 143 J/g) as ice content goes from 1 to 12 wt% in ice-cemented simulant but falls about 3x in pressure-sintered simulant, so the unknown form of polar ice swings excavation cost by two to three orders of magnitude.

branches.title: Seeing farther: space science and Earth observation
branches.thesis: If AI can do the theory, inference and instrument mathematics behind missions, science return per dollar rises from existing archives by 2028 and big-telescope design work gets cheaper. Flight dates do not move: LISA still launches in 2035, BHEX cannot fly before about 2032, and HWO moves at the pace of appropriations (FY2027 request: $5M, down from $150M). The one lane where an observatory can fly sooner is privately funded, such as Schmidt Sciences' 3 m Lazuli (target 2028), and there the physical clock, not AI, sets the date. Warp drives get sharper no-go theorems, not engines. The branch also carries Earth observation, absent before v3: honest error bars on methane and ground-deformation retrievals (S2 2028, Medium), while regulators using satellite methane numbers as compliance evidence is only Low by 2031 in the base case.
branches.reader_hook: Second-order self-force, the waveform physics LISA's extreme-mass-ratio science needs, exists today only for circular orbits around non-spinning black holes; the base case finishes it around 2030, roughly three to five years ahead of the pre-AI path (analyst judgment), yet LISA still launches in 2035.

branches.title: Crowded orbits and space weather
branches.thesis: If AI can make orbit uncertainty, collision risk and space-weather forecasts mathematically honest, then AI-designed trajectories fly from 2029 and certified collision screening that scales to a million objects exists by 2029. The tracking-data gate is loosening on its own track, through the constellations themselves (SpaceX Stargaze: 30,000 star trackers, about 30 million transits a day, free screening, Jan 2026) and existing drag assimilation (the Space Force's HASDM), which narrows the AI-math increment to honest uncertainty and verified software. Keeping LEO safe at 100,000 satellites stays bound through 2031 by sensors that cannot yet track 1-10 cm debris, by regulators and by non-cooperating operators.
branches.reader_hook: Starlink already flies about 355,000 avoidance maneuvers a year at a 3e-7 collision threshold, about 300 times stricter than the 1-in-10,000 norm, while about 1.2 million 1-10 cm fragments go untracked and CME arrival-time error has averaged about 13 hours across all forecasts (about 10 hours for the best ensemble) for 11 years.
branches.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Thesis merges the advocate's two-curves framing (Stargaze) with the skeptic's increment point (HASDM, Stargaze shrink the AI-math share); trajectory flight year 2028 -> 2029 and screening dated 2029 (skeptic). Reader hook: auditor's corrections (about 330x, rounded to 'about 300 times'; 13.2 h is the all-submission average, best ensemble 10.3 h). Spine: astro-small-debris-catalog inserted before LEO safety as its binding gate. | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Trunk nodes ['cap-research-math-public', 'cap-applied-math'] are shown as the chain's entry anchors (also listed in roots); they stay members of the trunk branch only. No spine nodes dropped.

branches.title: Plasma, nuclear and fusion propulsion
branches.thesis: If AI makes whole-device kinetic simulation affordable and turns it, with new diagnostics, into a validated electron-transport closure, electric thrusters can be designed before they are built around 2030 (S2 Low; S3 2029, Medium). AI-optimized thrusters can fly by 2030-31 on generic AI design loops even without that closure. Wear-test clocks, NASA's life-qualification practice, launch politics and fusion hardware keep the rest back: model-based life credit and faster EP programs stay at Low or below, a U.S. space reactor by 2031 is a Low-probability, politically clocked event, and fusion propulsion and megawatt nuclear-electric cargo stay beyond 2031. The kinetic-theory theorems (Landau damping, family 362) add confidence, not performance.
branches.reader_hook: A 23,000-hour thruster life requirement is 2.6 years of continuous firing that no proof shortens; NASA already credits the 50% life margin by analysis, and the open question is whether analysis can replace part of the test itself. D-He3 fusion has never been burned at meaningful power: a gigawatt-class fleet would need ~50 kg of helium-3 a year against a terrestrial supply of a few kilograms, but a megawatt-class demonstrator needs only grams, so fuel is not what keeps fusion rockets out of flight before 2031.
branches.revision_note: B-plasma-nuclear resolver (2026-10-07): Thesis rewritten (skeptic + advocate): the critical path is algorithms, compute and validation data, not proofs; the generic-AI route to a flown thruster added; reactor band now Low. Hook (skeptic + advocate + auditor): life-margin practice added; He-3 framed per GW-year versus grams for demonstrators. Spine: frontier-landau-damping-general and plasma-kinetic-closures removed (now soft, confidence-only links); roots add cap-design-optimization. | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Trunk nodes ['cap-physics-theory'] are shown as the chain's entry anchors (also listed in roots); they stay members of the trunk branch only. Moved from spine to side_chains (still branch members): ['physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai', 'physclock-reactor-in-space']. Nuclear thermal lane (fuel model to crewed Mars stage) added via cap-physics-theory; reactor launch and nuclear safety case are side chains.

astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.title: Formal astrodynamics library
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.description: Machine-checked definitions and core theorems for orbital mechanics (Kepler's equation, Lambert's problem, the circular restricted three-body problem and its Jacobi integral, Clohessy-Wiltshire relative motion, quaternion attitude kinematics, standard probability-of-collision definitions) in Lean or Isabelle, so GNC and traffic properties can be written as formal specifications.
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.status_oct2026: Essentially absent from Mathlib (general). Building blocks appeared in 2026: a Lean 4 Lyapunov-stability library for autonomous ODEs (lyapunov-odes-lean, Zenodo, May 31 2026), Lean integral curves and flows on Banach manifolds (arXiv 2602.13247), and an agent pipeline that brought 84 of 175 statements of a numerical-ODE textbook to proof-complete Lean (arXiv 2606.14000, Jun 2026). No catalog family applies.
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.why: Every verified-GNC and verified-traffic chain below needs agreed formal definitions to state specifications against; today a team that wants to prove a guidance property must first formalize orbital mechanics itself. The openai/math pipeline produced agent-written Lean for 127 families in weeks (manuscripts dated Sep 10-Oct 6, 2026; formalization timing not separately reported); a core astrodynamics library is perhaps 10-30k lines (assumption), i.e. weeks of agent time under S2 rather than person-years. Parts touching numerical-integration error wait on infra-mathlib-applied.
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.strongest_case_small: Libraries are cheap; agreement is not. Definitions must match what flight-dynamics codes compute (reference frames, time systems, ephemerides, units), and the June 2026 audit found kernel-accepted agent formalizations with weakened hypotheses and parameter restrictions, so a library can compile and still misstate the physics.
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.signpost: A public Lean or Isabelle orbital-mechanics library covering Lambert, CR3BP and Clohessy-Wiltshire, adopted or cited by a NASA, ESA or university GNC group, by end-2027.
astro-formal-astrodynamics-library.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Auditor: 'in under four weeks' corrected (it describes manuscript dates); the uncited Lyapunov library now cited (Zenodo, May 31 2026). Years and bands unchanged.

astro-catalog-dynamics-results.title: Catalog chaos results (weak link)
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.description: The openai/math families closest to orbital dynamics: positive metric entropy for the Chirikov standard map (146), counterexamples to strong forms of Arnold's fixed-point conjecture (347), sharp symplectic ball-packing criteria (343), and uniform limit-cycle bounds for planar polynomial vector fields (143). They concern model maps and planar fields, not the n-body problem.
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.status_oct2026: 146 is T1 (manuscript only); 343 is T1. 347 is T3: the agent-written Lean proof covers a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of the complex quadric threefold with exactly three fixed points, while the separate Morse-number construction is not formalized. 143's Lean part covers only quintic Lienard systems x'=y-F(x), y'=-x (at most two limit cycles, sharp); the uniform bound for planar polynomial fields is manuscript-only (T1). No outside Comparator report as of Oct 7, 2026. The release contains nothing on n-body dynamics, KAM theory for the three-body problem, or Arnold-diffusion rates.
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.premise_tier: T1 (146, 343, and 143's uniform-bound headline); T3 (347 three-fixed-point counterexample; 143 only for quintic Lienard systems)
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.why: Band refers to the results becoming established (T4 for the Lean parts, outside endorsement (T2) for the manuscripts); it is Medium in every scenario because 146, 343 and the uniform-bound headline of 143 are T1 (one band down, as for the sibling confirmation nodes). Their astro implication is separately judged nil-to-Low. The standard map is the textbook model of resonance overlap (Chirikov criterion), used heuristically to judge where near-resonant orbits turn chaotic; if 146 holds (conditional, T1), chaos there is measure-theoretically real, not a numerical artefact. 347 limits what periodic-orbit existence theorems can promise for Hamiltonian maps; 343 bounds symplectic phase-space packing (conditional). None yields a stability region, timescale or station-keeping number for a real orbit, so the downstream astro effect is confidence only (P5).
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.strongest_case_small: No mission designer assumed the standard map was integrable; numerical chaos indicators (FLI, MEGNO, Lyapunov exponents) already guide practice, and these results change zero design decisions. Planar polynomial limit cycles (143) do not describe orbital dynamics at all.
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.signpost: Celestial-mechanics groups citing 146 or 347 in a three-body or resonance paper by 2028; if none do, treat the link as nil.
astro-catalog-dynamics-results.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [skeptic+auditor] Bands High -> Medium in every scenario: two of four headline results are T1 and 143 is formalized only for quintic Lienard systems (lean/docs/143.md, checked), so the sibling T1 drop applies. [auditor] premise_tier and status corrected for the 143 and 347 statement gaps (lean/docs/347.md checked). [advocate keep-High-by-scoping rejected: 143 Lean scope does not support it.]

astro-nbody-transport-proofs.title: Proven bounds on how Earth-Moon trajectories drift
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.description: Computer-assisted proofs, with explicit constants, of transport, diffusion and escape-time bounds in realistic restricted and full three- and four-body models (Earth-Moon CR3BP and bicircular models; ephemeris-forced models only over short horizons), for example how long trajectories starting near a DRO or lunar frozen orbit provably stay bounded.
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.status_oct2026: Open frontier; not in the catalog. Capinski and Gidea gave a computer-assisted proof of Arnold diffusion in the planar full three-body problem (arXiv 2504.09273, Apr 2025), with explicit perturbation-parameter ranges and diffusion-time estimates for an astronomical (Neptune-Triton-asteroid) system, not for cislunar operational orbits. Practice relies on Monte Carlo propagation.
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.why: This is the bespoke, hard-but-not-famous problem class that tl-position-4 says the capability absorbs first. A single computer-assisted diffusion proof took a leading group years; at release-level reasoning cost (the openai/math ~3 hours per result applies to posed pure-math problems with roughly 9% yield, ~372 families from ~4,000 problems, not to validated interval computation), a library of system-specific theorems (one per orbit family of operational interest) becomes affordable once outside teams have access. Value: replaces 'we ran 10^4 propagations' with 'no trajectory starting in set A leaves before time T', the form a disposal-orbit or parking-orbit safety case wants.
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.strongest_case_small: Proven bounds in chaotic regimes are usually orders of magnitude looser than observed behaviour (Nekhoroshev-type times are exponentially pessimistic), and solar gravity, radiation pressure and ephemeris perturbations break the clean models proofs need; operators will keep using Monte Carlo and active station-keeping.
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.signpost: An AI-assisted paper by 2028 proving explicit-time confinement or escape bounds for a real DRO, NRHO or lunar frozen-orbit family in a model that includes solar gravity.
astro-nbody-transport-proofs.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Skeptic: ephemeris-forced scope limited to short horizons (wrapping effect), keeping S2 High; the ~3 hours per result applies to posed pure-math problems with ~9% yield (ref-release-anatomy: ~4,000 posed, 372 families), not to validated interval computation. Auditor: Capinski-Gidea do give diffusion-time estimates; the limit is the system covered. S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding). | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'analyst position (a' replaced with the KB position id tl-position-4.

astro-stability-atlas.title: Certified cislunar stability atlas
astro-stability-atlas.description: Validated (interval or Taylor-model) certified regions where lunar frozen orbits, DROs and stable resonant orbits stay bounded for 10-100 years without control, plus, for unstable halo/NRHO families, certified controlled envelopes and station-keeping delta-v budgets for stated navigation and maneuver-execution errors.
astro-stability-atlas.status_oct2026: Practice is numerical (Monte Carlo, chaos indicators). Verified propagation exists but reaches days to weeks in LEO (verified regularized Dromo interval propagation, TU Delft), not decades in chaotic regimes. ESA's Lunar Pathfinder targets a lunar frozen orbit; Moonlight navigation services are planned for end-2028 to 2030.
astro-stability-atlas.why: Long-lived lunar relay and navigation constellations (Moonlight: four navigation and one communication satellite), surface-base support orbits and disposal orbits need decade-scale budgets. A certified atlas turns propellant margins from 'Monte Carlo 99th percentile plus engineering margin' into a proven envelope; illustratively, halving a 20-30% station-keeping margin extends propellant-limited life by roughly 10-15% (about a year on a 10-year relay), less where batteries, eclipses or parts set life, and the saving is P5 confidence rather than a physical delta-v gain. It needs new theory plus verified numerics, so it lands a year after the pure proofs.
astro-stability-atlas.strongest_case_small: Chaos sets a hard horizon: NRHOs are unstable with prediction horizons of days to weeks, so no proof yields ballistic predictions beyond that; certified budgets then depend on controller and navigation-error models that are engineering assumptions. Frozen orbits and DROs are already known numerically to be stable enough for practice.
astro-stability-atlas.signpost: A lunar relay or navigation operator (ESA Moonlight, a CLPS relay provider) citing certified stability or station-keeping bounds in orbit selection or disposal planning.
astro-stability-atlas.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Skeptic: description corrected (halo and NRHO families are linearly unstable with horizons of days to weeks, so only stable families get uncontrolled decade-scale bounds; unstable ones get certified controlled envelopes and station-keeping budgets) and the life gain recomputed (1.25/1.125 = 1.11, 1.30/1.15 = 1.13: about 10-15%, not 'years'). Advocate: S3 band Medium -> High accepted for the narrowed deliverable (purely cognitive plus verified numerics; near-free cognition from 2029 is an S3-only argument). S3 year 2028 -> 2029 (= S2): both prerequisites (transport proofs, verified numerics) are now S3 2028, and the node lands a year after them as in S2.

astro-scp-guarantees.title: Landing-guidance solvers with proven convergence
astro-scp-guarantees.description: Proofs of iteration bounds to stationarity, recursive feasibility and robustness margins for the real-time guidance formulations used in powered descent and proximity operations, lossless convexification for specific extended constraint classes, and robust or chance-constrained variants. Global optimality for general 6-DoF problems (nonconvex attitude coupling) is not included.
astro-scp-guarantees.status_oct2026: Lossless convexification gives global optimality with deterministic convergence for 3-DoF powered descent (general; the Acikmese-Blackmore line of work behind G-FOLD and reusable-booster landing guidance). Successive convexification has convergence-to-stationarity guarantees via the prox-linear framework, extended to continuous-time, passively safe 6-DoF powered descent (Elango, Vinod, Di Cairano, Weiss, MERL TR2025-008, AIAA SciTech Jan 2025). Global optimality and worst-case iteration bounds for 6-DoF nonconvex problems remain open. No catalog family.
astro-scp-guarantees.why: These are 'solved in principle, expert-scarce' problems: perhaps a few dozen groups worldwide write such proofs (general). Under S2, on-demand research math turns each new constraint type (plume impingement, glideslope, sensor pointing, passive abort safety) into an agent-assisted result in weeks rather than a dissertation chapter (conditional on S2 public access in 2027). Proven iteration bounds are what onboard schedulers need to guarantee a solution inside a fixed guidance cycle (roughly 1-10 Hz replanning for landing, general). The benefit is model confidence (P5) and a deterministic iteration budget, not landing accuracy or propellant, unless programs use the proofs to cut divert margins.
astro-scp-guarantees.strongest_case_small: Reusable boosters already land routinely with convex/SCP-style guidance without global guarantees, relying on Monte Carlo campaigns and fallback logic; a proof changes paperwork, not landing accuracy, unless it lets designers cut propellant or divert margins.
astro-scp-guarantees.signpost: AI-assisted proofs of recursive feasibility or iteration bounds for 6-DoF successive convexification published by a leading GNC group by end-2027.
astro-scp-guarantees.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic: scope limited to what High in 2027 supports (global optimality for nonconvex 6-DoF excluded); 'same-week theorem' softened and marked conditional on S2; benefit stated as P5 confidence. Years and bands unchanged.

astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.title: Certified collision-probability math
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.description: Fast methods that propagate orbit uncertainty that has become non-Gaussian (curved, skewed, multimodal) and compute probability of collision (Pc) with rigorous error bounds, replacing the 2D Gaussian Pc shortcut where it fails.
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.status_oct2026: NASA CARA uses 2D Pc as the main risk input and brute-force Monte Carlo where 2D Pc is unreliable, and notes that Gaussian assumptions suppress the true non-Gaussian structure of position uncertainty. Differential-algebra, Gaussian-mixture and equinoctial-sampling methods exist without certified error bounds at catalog scale. Catalog 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, T3) is a weak link: orbit-state posteriors are generally not log-concave.
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.premise_tier: n/a (139 is T3 and not load-bearing)
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.why: Starlink executed 148,696 avoidance maneuvers Jun-Nov 2025 and 207,152 Dec 2025-May 2026 (over 40 per satellite per year) at a Pc threshold of 3e-7 (1 in 3.3 million), about 330x stricter than the 1e-4 industry norm (FOD News on ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report; in 2022 SpaceX's stated threshold was 1e-5, planet4589 Star2207). Certified Pc removes numerical-method error (2D-Pc breakdown, Monte Carlo sampling error) but not input error: a bound computed from an unrealistic covariance certifies nothing about true risk, and in the dilution region a poor covariance lowers Pc (false confidence, Balch, Martin and Ferson, Proc. R. Soc. A 2019). Starlink's 3e-7 threshold is a risk-posture choice made affordable by cheap autonomous electric-propulsion maneuvers. Fewer maneuvers would come from relaxing that threshold, a risk-acceptance decision the math informs (P5) but does not make; under an even-across-decades Pc distribution, 3e-7 -> 1e-5 removes about 1.5-1.8x of maneuvers (illustrative arithmetic: count proportional to log10(Pmax) - log10(threshold), Pmax 1e-2 to 1e-3). The covariance input is a separate problem (see astro-constellation-hosted-ssa). Rigorous Pc error bounds can be statistical (certified-variance importance sampling, large-deviation bounds) or analytic, so verified floating point accelerates this node but is needed as a hard input only downstream, in production screening code. Band High scores the methods existing and entering at least one operational tool (P1->P4).
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.strongest_case_small: Pc error is dominated by input covariance realism (drag, unannounced maneuvers, sensor biases), not by the propagation method; a perfectly computed Pc from a wrong covariance is still wrong. Operators may keep strict thresholds for reputational and regulatory reasons regardless.
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.signpost: CARA, ESA CREAM or a commercial SSA provider adopting a bounded-error non-Gaussian Pc method in operational software by 2028.
astro-nongaussian-uq-certified.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Why rewritten. Skeptic: the 2-5x maneuver claim did not follow from its own even-across-decades assumption (resolver re-derived 3.52/2.0 = 1.76x for Pmax 1e-3 and 4.52/3.0 = 1.51x for Pmax 1e-2), and the reduction comes from threshold policy (P5), not from certifying the arithmetic; certified Pc does not fix covariance realism or dilution (Balch et al. 2019). Auditor: '100x stricter' corrected to about 330x (1e-4/3e-7 = 333) and the 3e-7 source moved from Star2207 (which gives 1e-5 in 2022) to FOD News on ESA 2026. Hard edge from infra-verified-numerics made soft (skeptic: bounds can be statistical or analytic; verified floating point is needed in the screening code, which keeps its own hard edge). S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding).

astro-coordination-protocols.title: Provably safe maneuver-coordination rules
astro-coordination-protocols.description: Coordination protocols for independently operated autonomous fleets (right-of-way rules, maneuver-intent exchange, behaviour under communication loss) with machine-checked proofs that compliant fleets never maneuver into each other, plus game-theoretic analysis of non-cooperating operators.
astro-coordination-protocols.status_oct2026: No standard exists. Starlink is autonomous within its own fleet; on Dec 9, 2025 a payload from a Chinese Kinetica-1 launch passed close to Starlink-6079 (reported about 200 m, unverified) with no coordination or ephemeris sharing. TraCSS screens (52 pilot users plus UK and Australia accounts, about 11,125 satellites, Jun 2026) but does not arbitrate. Catalog 104 (quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games, T3) is a weak, theory-level link to synthesizing strategies for game models of such protocols.
astro-coordination-protocols.premise_tier: n/a (104 is T3 and not load-bearing)
astro-coordination-protocols.why: This is aviation's TCAS problem in orbit, and TCAS logic took years of formal analysis to trust. Multi-agent protocols with timing, message loss and asymmetric information are a natural target for agent-written proofs, which removes the expert-cost barrier. With about 13-14k active satellites today and filings for roughly 200k (China, Dec 2025) and up to 1 million (SpaceX orbital data centers, Jan 2026), pairwise human coordination cannot scale. Band scores the existence of the proofs by 2031 (P1 capability); certified or regulator-credited use follows P2's 2-4 year lag and is scored downstream (astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale).
astro-coordination-protocols.strongest_case_small: The binding problem is political and commercial (US-China data sharing, ITU, liability), not proof; a proven protocol nobody adopts is worthless, and bilateral API coordination between Western operators already works without proofs.
astro-coordination-protocols.signpost: A CCSDS, ISO or CONFERS draft standard for machine-readable maneuver intent that includes a formal-verification annex, by 2028.
astro-coordination-protocols.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Auditor: reason for exceeding the P2 default band stated (band scores existence of the proofs). Kinetica-1 distance marked unverified (auditor could not retrieve the source). S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding).

astro-cislunar-od-uq.title: Tracking objects in chaotic Earth-Moon space
astro-cislunar-od-uq.description: Orbit determination, initial orbit determination, sensor tasking and uncertainty propagation for non-Keplerian cislunar orbits (NRHO, DRO, L1/L2 halos, transfers) from sparse optical data, with proven consistency and custody guarantees.
astro-cislunar-od-uq.status_oct2026: Earth-centric surveillance networks are not designed for cislunar space, and three-body dynamics make uncertainty dominate performance; more than 30 lunar missions are planned 2024-2030. AFRL's Oracle-Prime (Terran Orbital) completed its Preliminary Design Review in Dec 2025 (announced Apr 2026); no delivery or launch date is public. NASA cancelled the Gateway station on Mar 24, 2026, removing the main planned NRHO traffic node.
astro-cislunar-od-uq.why: Method development is cognitive and the expert community is small, so P1 is a large multiplier; but cislunar objects are faint and few sensors see them, so performance is capped by data. The math advance mainly lets a sparse sensor set keep custody with fewer observations.
astro-cislunar-od-uq.strongest_case_small: Cislunar object counts stay in the tens through 2031, so manual analyst attention suffices; with Gateway cancelled, NRHO congestion is no longer a near-term driver.
astro-cislunar-od-uq.signpost: Oracle-Prime launch (date not announced) and published custody performance; a Space Force or commercial cislunar object catalog.
astro-cislunar-od-uq.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Auditor: Oracle-Prime 'delivery in 2026, launch sought for 2027' is not in the cited Terran Orbital release (resolver checked: PDR completed Dec 2025, 'on track toward delivery', no dates); likely fabricated, removed from status and signpost. S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding).

astro-nav-filter-guarantees.title: Navigation filters with proven error bounds
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.description: Estimators for autonomous navigation (optical and terrain-relative, X-ray pulsar, GNSS at lunar distance, crosslink ranging) with machine-checked consistency and integrity bounds (protection levels), including non-Gaussian and sensor-fault cases.
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.status_oct2026: EKF/UKF variants dominate, tuned by experts; integrity frameworks are mature for aviation GNSS but not for lunar PNT. LuGRE tracked GPS and Galileo and obtained a navigation fix on the lunar surface (Mar 3, 2025); NASA's SEXTANT demonstrated real-time X-ray pulsar navigation (general). Catalog 140 (T3) bounds high-dimensional streaming regression; onboard navigation filters carry about 6-20 states, so it does not bind (nil). 139 (T3) helps only where posteriors are log-concave.
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.premise_tier: T3 for the catalog piece (139, weak); n/a for the main chain
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.why: Lunar PNT (Moonlight initial services end-2028, LunaNet interoperability tests 2029) needs integrity guarantees like aviation GNSS has. Proving filter consistency and fault detection under weak-signal geometry is bespoke applied math that on-demand capability makes routine. Band scores the existence of the proofs by 2031 (P1 capability); certified or regulator-credited use follows P2's 2-4 year lag and is scored downstream (astro-autonomous-nav-demo).
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.strongest_case_small: Navigation accuracy is set by sensors and clocks (weak GNSS signals at lunar distance, pulsar photon counts giving kilometre-class XNAV fixes), not by filter proofs; proofs add assurance, not accuracy.
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.signpost: LunaNet or Moonlight integrity requirements specifying formally verified protection-level algorithms.
astro-nav-filter-guarantees.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Skeptic: family 140 removed from catalog_families (memory-sample bounds bind only at high dimension; onboard filters carry ~6-20 states), kept in status as a nil effect. Auditor: hard edge from astro-nongaussian-uq-certified made soft (protection levels do not need certified Pc first) and P2-above-default band reason stated. S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding).

astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.title: Verified docking and capture logic
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.description: Reachability and barrier-certificate proofs for rendezvous, proximity operations, docking and debris capture that cover approach and abort trajectories, keep-out zones, mode switches, sensor dropouts and learned (neural) controllers under runtime assurance. Contact and capture-mechanism dynamics are excluded: they are validated by air-bearing and robotic hardware-in-the-loop tests on the experiment clock.
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.status_oct2026: Neural-network-controlled spacecraft docking under Clohessy-Wiltshire dynamics is a standard verification benchmark (ARCH-COMP), solved with existing reachability tools such as CORA, JuliaReach and NNV (general); scalable branch-and-bound verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems appeared in Sep 2026 (arXiv 2609.16298); AFRL flew neural-network attitude control of a satellite bus with watchdog and guardrail runtime assurance in shadow mode (Jul 28, 2026). NASA's revised Artemis III is a crewed low-Earth-orbit rendezvous and docking test of Orion with HLS pathfinders from both SpaceX and Blue Origin (three launches, two dockings; readiness no earlier than mid-2027).
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.why: Hybrid verification is limited by state explosion and by the scarcity of people who can construct barrier certificates and decompositions; AI-generated certificates checked by a kernel are a near-ideal fit. It is also the route by which learned controllers, already flying under runtime assurance, gain static guarantees. Existing provers and reachability tools (KeYmaera X, sum-of-squares, CORA, JuliaReach) already solve the benchmark cases without Lean, so Lean/Mathlib coverage (infra-mathlib-applied) accelerates rather than gates this node.
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.strongest_case_small: Contact dynamics (friction, compliance, plume impingement, capture-mechanism behaviour) is the uncertain part; a proof over an unvalidated contact model gives false confidence, and air-bearing and robotic hardware-in-the-loop tests remain the qualifying evidence.
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.signpost: A servicing or debris-removal operator (Astroscale, ClearSpace, Starfish) citing formal reachability proofs in a mission safety review.
astro-hybrid-rpo-verification.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic + advocate: infra-mathlib-applied moved from hard to soft (the KeYmaera X and SOS bypass named in the verification domain's shared-upstream table). Skeptic: contact and capture dynamics removed from the achieved scope, so the cognitive gate and High band stand. Auditor: Artemis III status corrected (two landers' pathfinders; NET mid-2027). Years and bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): S3 2027 -> 2028 (S3 equals S2 through 2027; the S2 one-year lag after cap-applied-math 2027 applies equally in S3).

astro-debris-evolution-models.title: Debris-cascade tipping-point models with error bars
astro-debris-evolution-models.description: Long-term debris-environment models (source-sink and Monte Carlo) with proven stability thresholds (when runaway collisional growth starts) and honest uncertainty from fragmentation physics and compliance assumptions.
astro-debris-evolution-models.status_oct2026: MIT MOCAT (source-sink plus Monte Carlo, open-source pySSEM 2025) uses equilibrium stability as a capacity measure. ESA's 2026 report: more than 40,000 catalogued objects, about 54,000 larger than 10 cm and 1.2 million between 1 and 10 cm; LEO collision risk up 20% since 2024. The CRASH Clock (time to a likely collision if all maneuvering stopped) moved from 2.8 days in its Dec 2025 preprint to 5.5 days (vs 164 days in 2018) in the Jan 2026 revision, showing how assumption-sensitive headline metrics are.
astro-debris-evolution-models.why: Regulators face a SpaceX application for up to 1 million satellites (filed Jan 30, 2026) and roughly 200k Chinese ITU filings (Dec 2025); capacity questions need defensible math. Stability thresholds of source-sink ODE systems and their sensitivity are tractable applied math (P1); results reach practice as confidence about where the cliff is (P5). Band refers to the models existing with proofs and quantified uncertainty; the uncertainty band itself stays wide.
astro-debris-evolution-models.strongest_case_small: Outputs are dominated by inputs no theorem fixes: future launch rates, disposal compliance and fragment distributions drawn from a handful of hypervelocity tests. Estimates will span an order of magnitude regardless; Lifson et al.'s risk-based model, as summarized in Mach33's Oct 2025 analysis, puts LEO environmental carrying capacity near 2.9 million objects, far above today's population.
astro-debris-evolution-models.signpost: An IADC-, FCC- or ESA-cited capacity study with proven thresholds and published sensitivity bands by 2028.
astro-debris-evolution-models.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Skeptic: soft edge from frontier-nbody-arnold-diffusion removed (KAM and Arnold-diffusion times play no role in source-sink or Monte Carlo debris models). Auditor: the 2.9 million capacity figure is Lifson et al.'s model as summarized by Mach33 (Mach33's own volumetric figure is 6.3 million). Advocate: soft edge from constellation-hosted tracking (breakup-cloud custody for >10 cm fragments). S3 2027 -> 2028: capability.json defines S3 as S2 until 2028 with the same end-2027 horizon, and the trunk resolver moved infra-verified-numerics and infra-mathlib-applied to S3 2028 (skeptic, systemic finding).
