materials-new-propellant-flight.title: AI-designed propellant flies
materials-new-propellant-flight.description: A propellant molecule or formulation primarily proposed by an AI design system is qualified and flown in a spacecraft or launch-vehicle propulsion system.
materials-new-propellant-flight.status_oct2026: Benchmark: AFRL's AF-M315E (now ASCENT) originated more than 20 years before NASA's Green Propellant Infusion Mission flew it in Jun 2019. No AI-designed propellant has flown (general).
materials-new-propellant-flight.why: After design (S2, 2028), scale-up synthesis, hazard classification, long-duration materials-compatibility tests, catalyst development and thruster qualification set a ~3-5-year floor even for a startup, longer for NASA or ESA. Chain (S2): cap-autonomous-labs (2028) -> materials-energetics-design (2028) -> scale-up, hazard classification, compatibility and thruster qualification (>=3 years) -> flight (2031 at the earliest; P1->P7).
materials-new-propellant-flight.strongest_case_small: A few percent of specific impulse or density rarely justifies requalification, and existing green propellants (ASCENT, LMP-103S) already serve the market.
materials-new-propellant-flight.signpost: A propulsion startup announces a thruster qualification program for an AI-designed propellant, by 2029.
materials-new-propellant-flight.revision_note: B-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic (grounding rule, accepted): tier-5 hardware outcome inside five years now writes out its chain. Years and bands unchanged (customer and hazard-classification qualification genuinely applies here, so the gate stays 'qualification').

materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.title: Commercial AI chips running in orbit at scale
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.description: Operational orbital AI compute (satellites or clusters of 100 kW class or more with paying customers) on commercial accelerators.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.status_oct2026: Starcloud ran an H100 in orbit from Nov 2025; Starcloud-2 (first commercial mission) was planned for late 2026 (company plan, Mar 2026). Google's first Suncatcher prototype (four TPUs per press reports) launched on Transporter-18 on Oct 1 2026. Nvidia announced the Space-1 Vera Rubin module (Mar 2026) with six launch partners (Aetherflux, Axiom Space, Kepler, Planet, Sophia Space, Starcloud). SpaceX targets first Starmind launches in Q4 2027 (250 kW peak / 175 kW average) and 'significant scale' in 2028 (Musk, Aug 25 2026, who cautioned listeners to be skeptical); Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship. The FT reported on Oct 6 2026 that SpaceX is seeking ~$40B of debt to buy Nvidia chips (unconfirmed by SpaceX).
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.pathway: P7 (not AI-math-driven; AI math enters via P1 fault models and P2 proven fault tolerance, both soft)
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.why: Orbital compute happens on SpaceX's and Starcloud's hardware, launch and capital schedules, and operators already fly commercial accelerators without triple redundancy. AI math adds confidence, not the milestone: validated fault models (materials-see-system-models) and proven fault-tolerance layers (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) right-size mitigation, roughly 5-20% more useful compute per watt (assumption), which improves unit economics. Chain (all scenarios): first 100-kW-class Starmind flight 2028 (SpaceX target Q4 2027, slipped per the tree's 1.5-3x calibration) -> commissioning and first paying workloads 2029. Launch, not capital, is the gate for the leader (SpaceX held $100.8B of cash after its 2026 IPO; Mach33 names launch the physical gate). S1 stays Medium because weaker AI demand in a plateau may defer paying service.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.strongest_case_small: This proceeds whatever happens in AI math; Google's measured dose margins suggest radiation is not the binding constraint in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, where 33FG estimates ~100 um coverglass and under 1%/yr PV degradation.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.signpost: Paying-customer service from an orbital compute satellite or cluster of 100 kW or more, with published radiation-error statistics, by 2029.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: hard edge from materials-see-system-models made soft and the AI-math clause removed from the description, so the node is the commercial milestone and AI math no longer appears to gate 1 GW (this also resolves the auditor's cots-ops -> 1 GW finding, so that hard edge, a true physical precursor, is kept). Skeptic: S2/S3 2028 -> 2029 following the 100-kW radiator first-flight slip to 2028. Advocate: gate capital -> launch (capital does not bind the leader); soft edge from materials-verified-fault-tolerance. Auditor + skeptic: pathway relabelled (not AI-math-driven); ~2.5x lever removed; status updated (Starmind Q4 2027 target, Suncatcher launch, Starcloud-3, FT debt report). Bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): soft edge from plasma-radbelt-charging-forecast (B-safe-orbits request: 500-2,000 km SSO fleets gain from charging forecasts).

materials-perovskite-primary-power.title: Perovskite arrays power operational satellites
materials-perovskite-primary-power.description: Perovskite-based (tandem or thin-film) arrays serve as primary power on operational spacecraft, for example lightweight arrays for compute or broadband constellations.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.status_oct2026: Not operational anywhere as of Oct 2026 (general); flight experiments only.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.why: Solar is ~56% of AI1's reconstructed mass at ~127 W/kg array level (33FG, Jun 2026). A perovskite tandem at equal areal density and ~30% higher efficiency would cut satellite mass ~13% (0.56 x (1 - 1/1.3)); doubling array W/kg would cut ~28%, i.e. ~1.4x fewer launches. 33FG's often-quoted ~600 versus ~1,200 Starship launches per 100 GW/yr (thin-film ~1.7 kW/kg versus rigid ~0.8 kW/kg) is an asymptotic plateau for idealized high-Earth-orbit designs, not today's compute satellites, and covers thin film generally, not perovskites. One to two years of on-orbit lifetime evidence gate adoption; risk-tolerant constellation operators with five-year design lives adopt first. Compute satellites may be designed for chip-limited lives of ~3-5 years (33FG models 5.6 -> 3.4 years at higher power), so one to two years of orbit data covers a larger share of design life; their operators self-certify, and Chinese orbital-data-center programs (Orbital Chenguang, reported $8.4B credit lines) sit next to the perovskite supply base.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.strongest_case_small: Thin-film CIGS, thinned III-V cells and better array structures may deliver the specific-power gain without perovskites, and falling launch costs reduce the value of mass savings.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.signpost: A constellation operator announces perovskite-based primary arrays on a production satellite batch, by 2030.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: launch-saving claim corrected (the 600/1,200 figures are 33FG's idealized high-Earth-orbit plateaus, verified in its Nov 2025 post; AI1-era arrays are ~0.13 kW/kg). Advocate: short chip-limited design lives lower the evidence bar (appended; bands unchanged). Auditor: hard edge from materials-perovskite-tandem-flight (the model-qualified version) made soft, since adoption can rest on any flight heritage. Years and bands unchanged.

materials-in-space-mfg-product.title: Products made in orbit sold at recurring volume
materials-in-space-mfg-product.description: In-space-manufactured semiconductor substrates or crystals, or ZBLAN fiber, sold commercially at recurring volume, with quality advantages predicted by validated models.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.status_oct2026: Demonstrations only: 11.9 km of ZBLAN drawn on the ISS (2024; no published attenuation comparison yet), ForgeStar-1 plasma operations (from Dec 31, 2025; deorbit planned 2026), Varda defense and pharmaceutical reentries (W-5 and W-6 in 2026).
materials-in-space-mfg-product.why: Products sell on measured quality (fiber attenuation, defect density), not on a model's prediction, and Flawless Photonics and Varda already fly without validated models. Process models help investors and operators choose which products clear the cost of launch and return, so they accelerate this node without gating it. Recurring volume needs dedicated free-flyers, frequent return capsules and committed buyers, all physical and capital gates that AI cognition does not compress. Chain (S2): demonstrations 2024-26 -> measured quality advantage published -> multi-year offtake 2029-30 -> recurring sales 2031 (Low).
materials-in-space-mfg-product.strongest_case_small: Economics, not physics knowledge, binds, and terrestrial process improvements may close the quality gap.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.signpost: A multi-year offtake contract for orbit-made substrates or fiber with published quality metrics, by 2029.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.revision_note: B-moon-mars: Skeptic (edge): materials-microgravity-process-models moved from hard prerequisite to soft accelerator, because products sell on measured quality and demonstrations already fly without validated models. Auditor: status corrected to 11.9 km, with no attenuation advantage claimed. Years and bands unchanged. The skeptic's suggestion to move both materials nodes to another branch was not applied (out of scope for this resolver).

materials-hot-section-reuse.title: Longer-life reusable engines from new alloys
materials-hot-section-reuse.description: Operational reusable engines whose hot-section parts (preburners, turbines, chambers) use AI-designed alloys and model-backed life prediction, extending refurbishment intervals or allowing higher chamber pressure.
materials-hot-section-reuse.status_oct2026: Not started (general); depends on the first AI-designed alloy flight.
materials-hot-section-reuse.why: Hot-section refurbishment is a major reuse cost driver (general); doubling the life of the most-replaced parts would cut turnaround cost, but proving life needs fleet hours and post-flight tear-downs, a physical clock: reuse learning took 15 months from first landing to first reflight and 3-5 years to mature life, compressing only 0.8-0.9x in S2 (physclock). Chain (S2): materials-ai-alloy-flight (2030 at the earliest, Low) + materials-creep-oxidation-life-models (2029) -> fleet-leader parts run past the prior refurbishment interval and torn down -> operator-attributed interval increase (after 2031). Chain (S3): alloy flight (2030) -> parts flown on a subset of a high-cadence fleet (100+ heavy flights a year from 2029, physclock-heavy-cadence-100 in S3) -> attributed interval increase (2031 at the earliest, Low).
materials-hot-section-reuse.strongest_case_small: Reuse economics are dominated by vehicle-level design and operations, and engine makers already iterate in-house alloys empirically without AI.
materials-hot-section-reuse.signpost: An operator attributes a refurbishment-interval increase to a new hot-section alloy, by 2031.
materials-hot-section-reuse.revision_note: B-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor (timing/band, two lenses): S2 2031 -> >2031, S2 Low -> Speculative; an alloy first flying in 2030 (Low) cannot have a fleet-proven, operator-attributed interval increase within a year (reuse learning: 15 months to first reflight, 3-5 years to mature life, 0.8-0.9x in S2). S3 kept at 2031 Low; advocate's S3 Medium rejected (alloy flight is now S3 2030, leaving one year for fleet hours and attribution; P7 default Speculative). Gate qualification -> data (fleet hours and teardowns bind; first mover self-certifies). Gate convention (advocate, accepted): the first mover is a self-certifying commercial operator; FAA Part 450 regulates public safety, not engine materials or test counts, so the regulator/certification Medium cap does not apply unless the node needs NASA crew, NSSL or other customer certification. The band here rests on physical clocks, not on that cap. Chains written out (grounding rule). Soft edge from physclock-heavy-cadence-100 (advocate: cadence accrues fleet hours). | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): S3 heavy-cadence year in why updated to 2029 (B-trunk). Years and bands unchanged.

materials-qual-cycle-compression.title: Space materials insertion drops below five years
materials-qual-cycle-compression.description: Concept-to-flight insertion of new space materials (alloys, TPS, PV) falls from the historical 10-20+ years to five years or less as an industry pattern, shown by at least three material programs started in 2027 or later that fly by 2031.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.status_oct2026: Historically 10-20 years (Materials Genome Initiative), and more than 20 years and ~$400M for aerospace insertion; GE spent about two decades and over $1B on ceramic-matrix composites; Ferrium M54 (under six years) is the fast exception.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.why: Cognition is perhaps 20-30% of insertion time (Ferrium M54: under one of under six years went to design; assumption generalizing it). The rest is physical evidence: the physical-gate table compresses material qualification only 0.7-0.8x in S2 and 0.5-0.7x in S3 (5-14 years in S3), so three programs started 2027 or later flying by 2031 is at the edge even in S3. Commercial engine builders insert in-house alloys without MMPDS or NASA-STD-6030 gates (SpaceX's SX500 superalloy for Raptor, general), so handbook-accepted allowables and per-part digital-twin certification accelerate rather than gate; real-time creep, fatigue and oxidation tests still bind. Chain (S3): AI alloy design 2027-28 -> in-house allowables 2028 -> first AI-designed alloy flies 2029 -> two more programs fly 2030-31.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.strongest_case_small: Standards bodies and programs change slowly; a few fast commercial examples will not make an industry norm by 2031.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.signpost: A NASA-STD-6030 revision or MMPDS/CMH-17 policy that lets model-based evidence substitute for part of the test matrix, by 2028-29. Or an engine or spacecraft builder discloses a new material flown within five years of program start.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor] Description restricted to programs started 2027 or later (pre-AI fast programs like Ferrium M54 would otherwise satisfy it); S3 2030 -> 2031 and S3 Medium -> Low (physical-gate table S3 0.5-0.7x of 10-20+ years); chain written out. [advocate] materials-am-digital-twin-qual and materials-allowables-stats-framework hard -> soft (commercial in-house insertion needs no handbook acceptance); binding_gate regulatory -> qualification. Advocate's S2 Low -> Medium rejected (S2 material qualification 0.7-0.8x).

materials-specific-power-step.title: A step change in spacecraft power per kilogram
materials-specific-power-step.description: A fleet-level gain of 30% or more in power-system specific power (W/kg of arrays, storage and power electronics) on new spacecraft, attributable to new materials: perovskite or thin-film PV, high-voltage radiation-robust wide-bandgap electronics, higher-energy cells.
materials-specific-power-step.status_oct2026: Gains today come from array architecture (roll-out and flexible blankets) and cell-efficiency increments (general).
materials-specific-power-step.why: Power-system mass sets launch counts for orbital compute (33FG: compute satellites become power- and thermal-limited), so this is the materials outcome with the largest space-economics leverage. But each material leg needs multi-year flight evidence, so even S2 and S3 land after 2031.
materials-specific-power-step.strongest_case_small: Array architecture and launch-cost moves dwarf material gains in this window.
materials-specific-power-step.signpost: Spec sheets of new compute or broadband buses citing new-material arrays, electronics or cells, by 2031.
materials-specific-power-step.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + advocate: wide-bandgap electronics and battery qualification made soft prerequisites; a 30% power-system specific-power step can come from the array leg alone (solar is 56% of AI1's reconstructed mass; the battery is small in dawn-dusk orbit). materials-perovskite-primary-power stays hard. Years and bands unchanged (>2031, Speculative).

physclock-flight-test-cadence.title: Monthly flight testing of a fully reusable heavy launcher
physclock-flight-test-cadence.description: A new fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship V3) flies at least 12 integrated flights in one calendar year, so flight data rather than analysis sets the pace of learning. This is the data generator that reuse, life-prediction and certification-by-analysis nodes downstream need.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.status_oct2026: Starship has flown 14 integrated flights since Apr 2023: five in 2025 (intervals 48-91 days) and three in 2026 (Flight 12 May 22, Flight 13 Jul 24, Flight 14 Sep 28; 63-66 days apart) after a ~7-month gap for the V2-to-V3 change. Flight 14 was the first orbital flight and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The FAA authorized up to 25 Starbase launches a year in 2025 (general); LC-39A's first Starship launch is targeted for around year-end in the best case (Mach33).
physclock-flight-test-cadence.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-flight-test-cadence.why: Cadence is set by vehicle build and pad turnaround: about nine weeks per V3 loop with one active pad. A second Starbase pad, LC-39A and first reflights (expected early 2027) bring the interval to 3-4 weeks, giving 12 or more flights in 2027. AI barely changes this: Flight 12 went from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 2.8 times the stated interval, because of V3 hardware readiness and a Starbase component failure in April, not analysis. Starship has never met a yearly flight plan: 2, 4, 5 and 3 flights (2023 to Oct 2026), 5 against 25 authorized in 2025. Twelve in 2027 needs about 3x the 2026 rate, a debut of LC-39A (not yet launched) and roughly a dozen new ships before ship reuse arrives, which makes 2027 about a coin flip, so the central year is 2028. AI-assisted mishap diagnosis (physclock-ai-mishap-analysis) shortens stand-downs whose cause is not hardware, a marginal accelerator only.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.strongest_case_small: Two of three V3 boosters (Flights 12, 13) failed in landing burns and Flight 14 expended both stages by plan, and a pad-damaging failure (as New Glenn suffered on May 28 2026) costs 3-12 months. Only five of the 25 authorized Starbase flights flew in 2025.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.signpost: Starship flight count in 2027 (12 or more confirms); LC-39A debut by mid-2027; sustained intervals below 30 days. Flight 15 (NET Oct 19 2026 per press) would be a ~21-day interval.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: 2027 -> 2028 in all scenarios (slip-ratio table; 2,4,5,3 flights per year; 12 in 2027 is about a coin flip). Auditor: tier 0 -> 5 (a launch cadence is not an AI capability), stale strongest-case and engine-out wording fixed, interval range 48-91, exogenous P7 label. Advocate kept cadence unchanged without a counter-mechanism. Band unchanged. Cascade: physclock-test-loop-monthly S3 -> 2028. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): soft edge from physclock-ai-mishap-analysis added (B-certification request; carries the content of the removed physclock-test-loop-monthly). 2028 High in all scenarios re-checked against physclock.json (S2 interval 0.6-0.8x of 63-66 days = 38-53 days, short of monthly without new pads and reflight): kept.

physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.title: Regulators review with AI tools
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.description: The FAA's Office of Commercial Space Transportation, the FCC, NASA safety boards and ESA reviewers use AI systems to re-run and check applicants' flight-safety analyses, environmental documents and safety cases, raising reviewer throughput 2-5x without changing the rules.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed electronic license submissions and four burden-reducing Part 450 changes on Oct 5 2026 and on Jul 30 2026 proposed waiving requirements under 13 laws (Federal Register). The FCC voted on a 'Licensing Assembly Line' replacing Part 25 with Part 100 on Jul 22 2026, aiming to cut satellite licensing from years to months. No agency has announced AI-assisted technical review of launch licenses (general). Outside aerospace, FDA deployed a generative-AI assistant (Elsa) to its scientific reviewers agency-wide in Jun 2025, so a federal safety regulator can adopt internal AI tools within months (Axios, Jun 2025).
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.why: Reviewer hours, not statute, set most of the time between a complete application and a decision (statutory limit 180 days, general). A reviewer who can re-run a debris-risk or overpressure analysis with an AI agent in hours instead of weeks moves the queue. Reform supplies the rules regardless of AI; AI capacity decides whether the reformed process is staffed at 300+ U.S. launches a year.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.strongest_case_small: Agencies adopt slowly under procurement, FedRAMP, ITAR and liability constraints; much review time is interagency consultation, public comment and policy judgment that AI does not compress.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.signpost: FAA or FCC announcing AI-assisted review tooling; published median license evaluation times below 120 days.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.calibration_note: A3: Regulator cap: regulators changing how they review is regulator behaviour, which the same domain caps at Medium for physclock-licensing-in-weeks. S2/S3 High -> Medium.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor] S3 2027 -> 2028 (S3 equals S2 through 2028; agency procurement runs at ~1.0x); status wording fixed to 'requirements under 13 laws' (FR 2026-15415). [advocate] FDA Elsa precedent added to status; advocate's S2 2027 and S2/S3 High rejected: the node's event includes 2-5x reviewer throughput and published review times, which is regulator behavior under the A3 cap (see debates).

physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.title: Tests chosen for information, not habit
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.description: AI designs development test campaigns, the tests operators control, with Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential testing, choosing which tests, levels, sensors and replicates buy the most margin knowledge. Development test matrices shrink 10-30% (assumption) and re-tests fall. Formal qualification matrices stay set by GEVS, SMC-S-016 and ECSS-E-ST-10-03; cutting them needs customer acceptance and is modeled in physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.status_oct2026: The methods exist (Bayesian experimental design, design of experiments, sequential probability-ratio tests) but are expert-scarce; space qualification follows enveloped levels and fixed matrices (GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, general). NASA's certification-by-analysis UQ discussion group published calibration and validation challenge problems (Jul 2025). Design of experiments is not new to aerospace testing: NASA Langley has applied Modern Design of Experiments to wind-tunnel testing since the late 1990s, and DOT&E has required design of experiments in operational test plans since Oct 2010, while space qualification matrices did not shrink.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 139 is T3 but not load-bearing
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.why: A 'solved in principle, expert-scarce' problem: on-demand applied math puts an experimental-design specialist on every development campaign. Design of experiments has been available or mandated for decades, so AI removes the remaining per-campaign expert scarcity rather than inventing a method. If test campaigns are ~25-35% of the critical path and AI trims 10-30% of development test count, schedule gains are ~3-10% before any certification credit. Family 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, T3) concerns the posterior sampling these designs use, but practical posteriors are already sampled adequately; it changes theory, not campaigns.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.strongest_case_small: Test count is driven by standards, customer requirements and workmanship screening, not information value; dropping a test that would have caught a workmanship error is a mission loss, so mission assurance will resist.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.signpost: An operator or prime reports a development test matrix cut by 15% or more through information-optimal design, by 2028.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Re-scoped to development tests operators control (qualification matrices are standards- and customer-set, capped at Medium, and modeled in physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit); signpost changed to match; S2 High kept only with this narrowing. [skeptic] matrix shrink 20-40% -> 10-30% (assumption); DOE precedents (NASA Langley MDOE, DOT&E 2010) added. Advocate's S2 2028 -> 2027 and capability-engineering-adoption hard -> soft rejected: 'typical' matrices are an industry outcome (see debates). | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): soft edge from frontier-rare-event-certified (B-math-frontier request 4). S3 2027 -> 2028 by autofix accepted (capability-engineering-adoption S3 2028).

physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.title: Launch range and airspace scheduled by optimizer
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.description: Range (Eastern, Western, Starbase) and national-airspace scheduling for hundreds to thousands of launches and reentries a year is done by optimization tools that minimize hazard-area closures and conflicts, so range time stops being a cadence limit.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.status_oct2026: U.S. orbital launches: 198 in 2025 and 140 by Oct 7 2026 (Wikipedia). Musk projects Starship launching 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026). Range and FAA airspace integration are coordinated largely by human schedulers (general).
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.premise_tier: n/a; 124 is T1 per the KB catalog, conditional and not load-bearing (the repo's lean/docs/124.md lists a Lean main result with a Comparator challenge, 'Optimal three-machine unit-job scheduling', checked Oct 7 2026; T3 once the catalog is reconciled)
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.why: Launch windows, hazard areas and range assets form a precedence-constrained scheduling problem that mixed-integer programming and heuristics already solve at today's scale; the gap is expert time and integration with FAA air-traffic systems. At 1,000+ flights a year from one coast it becomes a real constraint. Family 124 (polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines, T1 per KB catalog, conditional) is a theory result; its algorithm will not be what schedules ranges. The outcome is FAA and Space Force adoption inside airspace automation, on federal acquisition cycles, so the regulator-behavior cap used for physclock-regulator-ai-capacity applies.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.strongest_case_small: Range capacity is limited by physical assets, safety buffers and airline-disruption politics, not schedule optimization; at 2026-2028 cadence the range is not the binding gate.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.signpost: FAA or Space Force announcing automated hazard-area and airspace scheduling; FAA-reported airspace delay minutes per launch falling.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] S2/S3 High -> Medium (agency adoption; same A3 regulator cap as physclock-regulator-ai-capacity). [skeptic] S2/S3 2027 -> 2028 (FAA acquisition cycles; S3 equals S2 through 2028). [auditor] premise_tier notes the uncatalogued Lean result for 124 (lean/docs/124.md checked by resolver). No dependents.

physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.title: A rulebook for trusting AI-made analysis
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.description: NASA-STD-7009, ECSS and Space Force test standards, or a faster NASA handbook, interim or engineering directive, or ECSS handbook, gain a defined way to count AI-generated analyses (with independently checked derivations, quantified model error and, where available, certified numerics) as verification evidence, graded by credibility level. How much test credit each level earns stays with programs and their Technical Authorities, as under NASA-STD-7009B.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009B (Mar 2024) sets model credibility and leaves acceptance criteria for results to programs (general). A NASA-sponsored aircraft certification-by-analysis guide (contractor report, May 2021) sets a vision for a notional 2040, and a NASA-led UQ position paper (Jan 2024) places widespread certification by analysis in 2040-2050 and calls tool credibility the open challenge; the NASA-FAA CM4QC strategy (Mar 2026) is aviation-focused, for additively manufactured metals. No space standard addresses AI-generated analysis (general). Outside aerospace, FDA issued final guidance on the credibility of computational modeling in medical-device submissions (Nov 2023, built on ASME V&V 40) and a draft risk-based, seven-step credibility framework for AI models used in drug and biologic regulatory decisions (Jan 2025).
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.why: Every test-substitution chain needs a rule saying what analysis evidence is worth. The named base standards revise every 8-10 years (NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024; GSFC-STD-7000 2013 and 2021; ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, about 19 months from draft to publication), so the next base revision of 7009 falls around 2030-32. The faster route is a NASA handbook, interim or engineering directive, or an ECSS handbook. S2's independent checks (2026-27) and automated statement audits (capability-cheap-trust, 2028 after B-trunk) supply the evidence, so a first directive or handbook naming AI-generated analysis lands around 2029. Verified numerics (2028) strengthen the case but do not gate it: NASA-STD-7009B is already risk-based, and FDA wrote AI-credibility rules without machine-checked numerics. Capped at Medium because it is regulator acceptance.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.strongest_case_small: NASA-sponsored aircraft studies put widespread certification by analysis at 2040-2050; base standards revise only every 8-10 years and follow experience and accidents, not capability; a single failure traced to AI analysis would freeze adoption.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.signpost: A NASA-STD-7009 revision, NASA engineering directive or ECSS handbook naming AI-generated analysis; a CM4QC pilot granting qualification credit.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] why: revision cycles corrected from '3-6 years (general)' to the named standards' 8-10 years (7009 2008/2016/2024; GSFC-STD-7000 2013/2021; ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012/2022); the 2029 date now rests explicitly on the directive/handbook route. [skeptic] description no longer maps credibility levels to allowed test reductions (programs set acceptance). [advocate] infra-verified-numerics hard -> soft (a risk-based credibility rule does not need the toolchain to exist); description names directive and handbook routes; FDA precedents added to status. [auditor] status: the 2021 CbA guide is a contractor report with a 2040 vision, 2040-2050 is from the 2024 UQ paper, CM4QC is aviation-focused. Years kept: skeptic's S2 2030/S3 2029/S1 >2031 and advocate's S2 2028 both rejected (see debates). Bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): cheap-trust year in why updated to 2028 (B-trunk moved it from 2027); the S2 2029 date still holds (trunk follow-up 5).

physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.title: Anomaly diagnosis 3-10x faster
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.description: AI agents do the cognitive part of anomaly investigations (telemetry forensics, fault-tree pruning, physics re-simulation of candidate causes, corrective-action analysis), so return to flight is set by hardware fixes and verification tests rather than diagnosis. Root-cause confirmation often still needs hardware reproduction tests.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.status_oct2026: The FAA authorized Falcon 9's return to flight 5 days after the Feb 1 2026 upper-stage deorbit-burn anomaly, with the FAA accepting SpaceX's findings (33FG). Starship loops in 2025 stretched to 82-91 days after the Flight 8 and 9 losses. New Glenn was grounded after an Apr 2026 upper-stage failure, and a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion destroyed a vehicle and damaged its pad (Wikipedia). The FAA accepts operator-led investigations (general).
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.why: Diagnosis is cognitive and sits on the critical path: when the cause is clear, return to flight takes days (Falcon 9, Feb 2026); when it is ambiguous, weeks to months. Searching the cause space 5-10x faster cuts the diagnosis share (illustratively 30-60% of a 60-90 day investigation, general) to days; redesign, requalification tests and FAA acceptance remain. No new regulator acceptance is needed: the FAA reviews findings, not the tools used to reach them. The physical-gate table gives diagnosis 3-10x faster but total return to flight only 0.5-0.8x, and only for non-hardware causes. One operator suffices: SpaceX, which owns a frontier lab and flies most often, generates the anomalies and data.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.strongest_case_small: The slow investigations are slow because hardware must be redesigned, rebuilt and retested or a pad rebuilt (New Glenn), none of which AI compresses; SpaceX already closes clear anomalies in under a week.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.signpost: An operator stating that AI tooling found a root cause; falling median time from mishap to FAA return-to-flight determination.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Title 'Root cause in days, not months' -> 'Anomaly diagnosis 3-10x faster'; description notes hardware reproduction tests. [auditor] facts: FAA authorized return to flight 5 days after the anomaly; Starship 2025 gaps 82-91 days. [advocate] capability-engineering-adoption hard -> soft, cap-applied-math added as hard prerequisite, S2 2028 -> 2027 (single-operator event; S3 2027 equals S2 through 2028). Its former dependent physclock-test-loop-monthly was removed as a duplicate. Bands unchanged.

physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.title: License analyses drafted and checked by AI
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.description: AI agents produce and cross-check the Part 450 flight-safety analysis (debris, far-field overpressure, toxic release, expected casualty), the ground-safety analysis and the NEPA environmental documents that operators submit, turning months of specialist effort into days.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed (Oct 5 2026) consolidating flight-safety-analysis information requirements, dropping overpressure analysis for hypothetical public locations and simplifying containment; a revised draft AC 413.13-1A (Part 450 application guidance) was released for public comment on Jul 20 2026 (FR 2026-14576), alongside a draft AC 413.5-1 on pre-application consultation. Specialist consultancies and in-house teams prepare these analyses today (general).
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.why: These analyses use established methods (Monte Carlo debris dispersion, blast propagation, plume dispersion): expert-scarce, not research-hard. An AI running FAA-accepted methods needs no new acceptance; the FAA evaluates the outputs as it does today. Payoff: license modifications for new trajectories or cadence (for example New Glenn's 12-to-50-per-year review) are prepared in weeks. One operator or consultancy suffices for the signpost, and vertically integrated operators with in-house frontier models need not wait for industry-wide adoption.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.strongest_case_small: Preparation is rarely the long pole for an experienced operator; the long poles are environmental consultations, public comment and interagency review.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.signpost: An operator or consultancy publicly using AI-generated Part 450 analyses; shorter time from application to license modification.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.calibration_note: A3: Gate relabel, no band change: the why states the FAA evaluates outputs of already-accepted methods and no new acceptance is needed, so the binding gate is operator adoption, not regulation. With a regulatory gate the High band would breach the Medium cap.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor] Fact fix: AC 413.13-1A is a comment-stage draft (FR 2026-14576, Jul 20 2026), not an issued revision. [advocate] capability-engineering-adoption hard -> soft and S2 2028 -> 2027: the event needs one adopter using established methods, and S3 (2027) equals S2 through 2028. Bands unchanged.

physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.title: Analysis replaces some environmental qualification tests
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.description: NASA, Space Force and ESA mission-assurance practice grants formal test credit to validated, AI-produced analysis for derivative hardware in structures and thermal: reduced or deleted vibration, acoustic or thermal qualification tests (or levels) on derivative units, beyond what qualification by similarity and protoflight practice already allow. Avionics and propulsion qualification, driven by workmanship, parts and life, stay outside.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.status_oct2026: Protoflight and qualification by similarity are already standard for derivative and heritage hardware (GSFC-STD-7000B GEVS; NASA-STD-5001B Table 1 and Sec. 4.1.2.3). NASA-sponsored aircraft certification-by-analysis studies place wide adoption in 2040-2050; NASA-FAA CM4QC (Mar 2026) addresses additively manufactured metals for aviation; the structures domain places structural certification by analysis at 2030 in S2.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.why: A full qualification campaign for a major subsystem costs months and often tens of millions of dollars (general), but derivatives already use protoflight and similarity, so the counterfactual saving of AI-backed credit is roughly 1-6 months per derivative unit beyond today's practice (assumption). Chain (S2): credibility directive 2029 -> first structural analysis credit 2030 -> extension to environmental qualification of derivative units 2031. First credit comes on risk-tolerant government buys (SDA tranches, NASA Class C/D missions). Information-optimal test design complements analysis credit but is not a precondition. Capped at Medium; S2 Low because it follows a Low structural precedent with one year of window.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.strongest_case_small: Tests find workmanship and integration errors that analysis cannot; first-of-kind and crewed hardware will keep full programs; commercial operators already skip tests where they own the risk, so the gain is mainly on government programs.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.signpost: A NASA, Space Force or ESA program formally deletes or reduces a planned environmental qualification test on derivative hardware on the strength of AI-produced analysis, first on a risk-tolerant buy (an SDA tranche or a NASA Class C/D mission).
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Scope narrowed to structures and thermal environmental qualification; 'protoflight instead of dedicated qualification units' removed (already standard per GEVS and 5001B); saving '6-12 months' -> '1-6 months beyond today's practice (assumption)'; physclock-optimal-test-campaigns hard -> soft; S2 2030 -> 2031, S3 2029 -> 2030 (one year after the structural precedent), S2 Medium -> Low. [advocate] signpost adds risk-tolerant government buys first (SDA, Class C/D); advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 rejected (depended on a 2028 rulebook). Title changed to match the narrowed scope.

physclock-ai-run-test-stands.title: Test stands that run themselves
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.description: Engine stands, thermal-vacuum chambers, vibration tables and materials rigs run around the clock under AI control with adaptive test sequences and automatic data reduction, cutting test-to-insight time from weeks to hours and raising utilization where scheduling, not demand or article supply, limits it (from roughly 30-50% to 70% or more, assumption).
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.status_oct2026: Autonomous laboratories exist for materials chemistry (DOE Genesis Mission first awards Jul 2026, per the capability domain); large aerospace test facilities run human-scheduled campaigns (general). The scarcest facilities are arc jets, large thermal-vacuum chambers and nuclear test infrastructure (general).
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.why: Test facilities are the scarcest physical asset; doubling utilization is worth a second facility (2-4 years and tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to build, general). Adaptive sequencing (stop when the information is in) and instant data reduction compress campaign calendar time 10-25%, in line with the experiment-gate multiplier of 1.1-1.3x in S2 (1.3-1.5x in S3). The scarcest facilities (large thermal-vacuum chambers, arc jets, engine stands) stay paced by test-article build, setup, propellant and liquid-nitrogen logistics and hazardous-operations approvals, which is why S2 is Medium and only S3 is High.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.strongest_case_small: Utilization is limited by article build, setup, safety and consumables (propellant, liquid nitrogen), not scheduling; thermal soaks and life tests run in physical time.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.signpost: A propulsion or test-services company reporting autonomous around-the-clock test operations with utilization figures.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] why: calendar compression 20-40% -> 10-25% (20-40% exceeds the S2 experiment multiplier 1.1-1.3x in research/physclock.json); S2 High -> Medium (S3 High kept); physclock-optimal-test-campaigns hard -> soft (around-the-clock autonomy does not need Bayesian experimental design). [skeptic+auditor] utilization figure marked (assumption). [auditor] pathway P1->P7 -> P1 (an operations change, not a flown-system outcome).

physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.title: Nuclear launch safety cases in months
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.description: AI produces the reactor design analyses (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, accident criticality) and the launch-accident nuclear safety analysis needed for NSPM-20 launch authorization of a space fission reactor, cutting a multi-year analysis cycle to months. LEU/HALEU fuel below 20% U-235 puts a launch in Tier II: the sponsoring agency head authorizes it after an Interagency Nuclear Safety Review Board (INSRB) review. Presidential authorization applies only to Tier III (non-LEU fuel).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.status_oct2026: DRACO (nuclear thermal demo, Lockheed-BWXT contract Jul 2023 for a 2027 flight) was put on hold in Jan 2025 and cancelled in 2025, with DARPA citing falling launch costs. NASA unveiled Space Reactor-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, nuclear-electric, two Mars flybys) in Mar 2026 for a Dec 2028 launch. Its estimate reached $2.1B by Sep 2026, while the House Appropriations Committee recommended $10M for it, within $50M for nuclear-electric propulsion, in May 2026 (Wikipedia). SR-1 uses HALEU uranium dioxide fuel, so its launch falls in NSPM-20 Tier II (NSPM-20, 2019).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.why: Nuclear safety analysis is labor-dominated and export-controlled; on-demand applied math inside controlled networks compresses it from years to months. A fresh-fuel HALEU reactor has a low radiological inventory at launch, so its safety case centers on accidental criticality and the cycle is shorter than for Pu-238 RTG missions (general). The INSRB review, agency-head authorization and appropriations remain, so the node is capped at Medium. An AI-made safety case accelerates a reactor launch but is not a precondition for it (physclock-reactor-in-space).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.strongest_case_small: Space reactor programs die of funding and politics (SP-100, Prometheus, DRACO), not analysis; HALEU fuel and fabrication bind.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.signpost: NASA or DOE states that AI-generated neutronics and accident-criticality analyses were accepted in the SR-1 (Tier II) launch safety review, with review time under 6 months.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.revision_note: B-plasma-nuclear resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + advocate + auditor (verified against NSPM-20 text): HALEU/LEU fission launches are Tier II, authorized by the sponsoring agency head after INSRB review, not presidential. Auditor (verified): the $10M was a House Appropriations Committee recommendation, not a congressional direction. Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027 -> 2028 (S3 equals S2 through 2027; trunk moved capability-controlled-data-access to 2028). Skeptic: signpost now measures the AI contribution. Medium cap kept.

physclock-starship-full-reuse.title: Both Starship stages caught and reflown
physclock-starship-full-reuse.description: A Starship V3 booster and ship are each recovered and flown again, the threshold that turns a $200-250M expendable stack into an amortizable fleet.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.status_oct2026: Boosters were caught on Flights 5, 7 and 8 (Oct 2024-Mar 2025, pre-V3), and B14 and B15 reflew on Flights 9 and 11 (May and Oct 2025); B14's reflight followed inspection and replacement of 4 of its 33 engines. The open items are V3 landing-burn reliability, ship catch and ship reflight: the V3 boosters on Flights 12 and 13 failed in landing burns, and Flight 14 expended both stages by plan. Musk: Flight 15 attempts the first ship catch with odds of 'at least 50 or 60 percent', and ship and booster refly 'at the end of this year or more likely early next' (Mach33, Sep 2026).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-starship-full-reuse.why: Reuse is a flight-test result. Falcon 9 took 15 months from first landing (Dec 2015) to first reflight (Mar 2017). AI shortens failure analysis between attempts but does not change the number of attempts needed. Starship's booster went from catch to reflight in about 4.3 months (B14, Jan-May 2025), far faster than Falcon 9. For the ship, Falcon's 15-month landing-to-reflight lag applied to a first ship catch around late 2026 would give early 2028, so ship reflight in 2027 is roughly 50-60% (judgment); 2027 stays the earliest year. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.strongest_case_small: Ship catch and heat-shield refurbishment are unproven; repeated failures could push ship reflight into 2028 (Mach33 bear case).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.signpost: First ship-catch attempt (Flight 15, NET Oct 19 2026 per press, or a later flight); first reflight of a caught V3 booster and ship by mid-2027.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: status corrected (boosters already caught three times and reflown twice; the open item is the ship); Flight 15 date updated (stale "about Dec 2026"); exogenous P7 label; Mach33 source-weight caveat. Year and band unchanged.

physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.title: Reflight cleared by data, not teardown
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.description: Reusable stages are cleared for reflight from flight sensor data and a probabilistic life model (a digital twin) instead of detailed inspection, enabling booster turnaround under a week and ship turnaround under two weeks.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 in 2025: 95% of launches on reused boosters, median booster on its 14th flight, 38-day median turnaround, 162 missions from 25 airframes; cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 8.0 (2019) and 24 (2020) (Mach33). No V3 stage and no ship has reflown; two pre-V3 Super Heavy boosters were caught and reflown (B14: caught on Flight 7, Jan 16 2025, reflown on Flight 9, May 27 2025, after 4 of 33 engines were replaced; B15: caught on Flight 8, Mar 6 2025, reflown on Flight 11, Oct 13 2025).
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.why: Mach33's base case has flights per stack at 3.3 (2027), 4.8 (2028), 8.9 (2029, about a 40-day average cycle) and 18 (2030, about 20 days), so record turnarounds under 7 days (booster) and 14 days (ship) fit 2030 in S2; Falcon 9 took 8 years from first reflight (Mar 2017) to a 9-day record (Mar 2025), and its 2025 median was still 38 days. Mach33's 2028 base-to-bull cost spread ($1.6B) covers every reuse driver; data-based clearance is one contributor and its share is not quantified, and because this node lands in 2029-30 it affects the 2029-31 manifests, not 2028. Chain (S2): first V3 reflights 2027 -> life twin 2028 -> rapidly reusable heat shield 2029 -> data-cleared turnaround on both stages 2030; S3 one year earlier (reuse learning 0.7-0.8x); S1: heat shield and life twin 2030 -> 2031, Low because both Medium prerequisites must land first. Life data still accrue one flight at a time. Family 372 (Lame moduli uniquely determined from boundary data, smooth isotropic case, T1) supports identifiability for inverse inspection in principle; damaged composites and welds lie outside its hypotheses. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.strongest_case_small: SpaceX scaled Falcon reuse through fleet-leader experience and inspection without formal twins; the limit is wear mechanisms (heat-shield tiles, engines) that only flights reveal.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.signpost: Starship booster turnaround under 7 days; SpaceX disclosing sensor-based reflight clearance.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.calibration_note: A3: Cross-domain consistency. Ship turnaround under two weeks requires a rapidly reusable heat shield, so this node cannot come earlier or be more likely than hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield (S2 2029, Medium in all scenarios). It also sat in the same year as its prerequisite prop-life-twin (S2 2028). Chain (S2): first Starship reflights 2027 -> life twin 2028 -> data-cleared turnaround on both stages 2029. S2 2028 -> 2029; S2/S3 High -> Medium. B-trunk: A3's heat-shield dependency is now a hard edge (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield).
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor: flat factual error fixed ("No Starship stage has reflown"). Skeptic + auditor: S1 2030 -> 2031, S3 2028 -> 2029; skeptic: S2 2029 -> 2030 (Falcon precedent, Mach33 flights per stack, reuse learning only 0.8-0.9x in S2), S1 Medium -> Low, hard edge from hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield, $1-2B-on-2028 claim removed (wrong lever share and wrong year). Chain written into why. Cascade: critical-payload acceptance.

physclock-reactor-in-space.title: A U.S. fission reactor launched
physclock-reactor-in-space.description: The first U.S. space fission reactor since SNAP-10A (1965) is launched: Space Reactor-1 Freedom (nuclear-electric, over 20 kWe) or a Fission Surface Power / Lunar Reactor-1 unit.
physclock-reactor-in-space.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom targets Dec 2028 at a $2.1B estimate (Sep 2026), with $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee (May 2026). NASA centralized space nuclear work under a Space Reactor Office (May 2026) and announced a streamlined management approach (Jun 2, 2026). SR-1 uses HALEU UO2 fuel and reuses the Gateway Power and Propulsion Element bus (three 12 kW AEPS and four 6 kW Hall thrusters); NASA paused Gateway in its current form on Mar 24, 2026. Fission Surface Power had three Phase 1 teams from 2022 (Lockheed Martin, Westinghouse, IX), a 2025 executive order prioritizing a lunar reactor, and a directive targeting launch readiness around 2030. NASA said in Mar 2026 that SR-1 data will inform Lunar Reactor-1 (Wikipedia).
physclock-reactor-in-space.why: HALEU fuel supply, reactor fabrication, zero-power criticality testing and integration take roughly 4-6 years from a funded start (general). The physclock lag ladder applies 0.9x in S2 and 0.8-0.9x in S3, while appropriations and politics compress 1.0x in every scenario. SR-1 is underfunded for Dec 2028; a 2030-31 launch needs FY2027-28 appropriations of several hundred million dollars a year. A conventionally prepared Tier II safety analysis is sufficient, so the AI safety case (physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai) is an accelerator worth perhaps 6-12 months. That shows up in the earlier S2/S3 years, not in the band. Chain (S2): funded start FY2027 -> fuel, fabrication, criticality tests, safety analysis and INSRB review -> launch 2030 at the earliest. Band Low in all scenarios because the binding gates do not depend on the scenario and every U.S. space-reactor program since SNAP-10A has been cancelled.
physclock-reactor-in-space.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled; cheap launch removed DRACO's rationale; the 2026 pause of Gateway in its current form and cancellation of Mars Sample Return show how fast NASA priorities shift.
physclock-reactor-in-space.signpost: FY2027 appropriation for SR-1; DOE fuel delivery; a reactor criticality test.
physclock-reactor-in-space.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder: a space reactor takes 4-6 years from a funded start (0.9x in S2, 0.8-0.9x in S3; appropriations 1.0x). SR-1 has $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee against a $2.1B estimate and Fission Surface Power had no confirmed Phase 2 award, so the earliest funded start is 2026-27. Chain (S2): funded start 2026-27 -> fuel, fabrication, criticality tests and AI-shortened safety case -> launch 2030 at the earliest. S1 2030 -> 2031 (Low kept), S2 2029 -> 2030, S3 2029 -> 2030; S2/S3 bands unchanged. B: S2/S3 bands Medium -> Low (gates scenario-invariant).
physclock-reactor-in-space.revision_note: B-plasma-nuclear resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + advocate + auditor: hard edge from physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai -> soft (a conventionally prepared Tier II safety analysis suffices; SR-1's target predates AI safety cases). Skeptic: S2/S3 Medium -> Low (capital, politics and HALEU bind at 1.0x in every scenario; the S1-to-S2 band jump rested only on AI analysis that is off the critical path; aligns with struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe). Auditor (verified): $10M was a House committee recommendation; Gateway paused, not cancelled; PPE reuse added. Advocate: Space Reactor Office and streamlined-management facts added. Years unchanged.

physclock-pad-propellant-infra.title: Pads and propellant plants for hundreds of heavy flights
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.description: At least four Starship-capable pads operate (Starbase pads 1 and 2, LC-39A, SLC-37 or equivalent) with on-site or pipeline propellant supply, removing pad count and cryogen trucking as cadence limits.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.status_oct2026: Starbase has two pads; LC-39A's Starship debut is targeted around year-end at best (Mach33). A Starbase methane pipeline ('Starpipe') targets Jan 2027 service; SpaceX filed for a 32.4-mile Florida gas pipeline (Oct 2026); a $100B Louisiana campus (five complexes, two pads each) plans construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029. Merchant supply needs about 389 tanker deliveries per flight (Mach33).
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.why: Pad construction (2-4 years per heavy pad, general) and air-separation and liquefaction plants run on the physical clock. On-site propellant costs about $0.2M per flight against $1.7-2.7M merchant, and trucking becomes physically implausible above about 100 flights a year (106 deliveries a day) (Mach33). AI barely touches this; it bounds every high-cadence node. LC-39A has not launched Starship as of Oct 2026, against a late-2025 plan (Spectrum News 13, Mar 2025) and an H2-2026 target (Mach33, Apr 2026); SLC-37 was approved in Dec 2025 and is under construction; at 2-4 years per pad and 1-3 years for the Florida pipeline (filed Oct 2026), four pads with pipeline or on-site supply is a 2029 central year. The node is AI-independent, so all scenarios move together. Environmental caps: Starbase 25 a year (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (FAA, Jan 2026, per NASASpaceflight) and SLC-37 76 (Department of the Air Force, Dec 2025).
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.strongest_case_small: Environmental reviews, litigation or a pad-destroying failure can delay a site by a year or more; SpaceX may run fewer pads harder.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.signpost: LC-39A's first Starship launch; Starpipe in service; Florida Public Service Commission approval of the pipeline.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: 2028 -> 2029 in all scenarios (every element on its best-case schedule; LC-39A a year behind plan; table compresses pads only 0.9-1.0x). Auditor: exogenous P7 label. Bands unchanged.

physclock-heavy-cadence-100.title: 100+ fully reusable heavy launches a year
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers fly 100 or more orbital missions in one calendar year.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.status_oct2026: 2025: 330 orbital launches worldwide, 165 by Falcon 9 (no failures), 5 by Starship; 2026 to Oct 7: 237 launches, 113 by Falcon 9, plus 3 Starship flights (Flights 12-14; only Flight 14 was orbital) (Wikipedia). Mach33's reference case has about 90 Starship flights carrying 10,100 t of Starlink in 2028; Musk says 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026).
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.pathway: P7 (mostly exogenous; AI adds 0-0.5 year in S2 through anomaly closure)
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.why: At Mach33's 2028 base of 4.8 flights per stack, 100 flights need about 21 new stacks (roughly $3B at $143M each, Mach33's 2028 learned-stack estimate against about $250M today) and four or more pads; at 2030's 18 flights per stack, about 6 stacks. Production, reuse reliability and propellant bind. Launch cadence follows its own curve: AI moves it 0-0.5 year in S2 (anomaly closure only) and 0.5-1 year in S3 (AI-run factories from about 2029). Environmental caps also bind: Starbase 25 a year (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (Jan 2026) and SLC-37 76 (Dec 2025), so 100 flights needs both Florida sites running above half their caps. Chain (S2): first V3 reflights 2027 -> four pads with pipeline or on-site propellant 2029 -> 100+ flights 2030; S3 2029 only if the four-pad set is ready early that year; S1 about 2030 on SpaceX's own trajectory. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.strongest_case_small: Falcon 9 took from 2010 to 2022 to exceed 60 launches a year (general); each Starship failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.signpost: Starship flights in 2027 and 2028 (30 or more in 2028 keeps S2 on track); disclosed flights per stack.; SLC-37 first Starship launch; 40 or more Starship flights in 2028.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S2 2029 -> 2030 and S3 2028 -> 2029 (physclock table allows 0-0.5 year in S2 and 0.5-1 year in S3; pads now 2029). Environmental caps, chain and $143M label added; status fixed (only Flight 14 of 2026 was orbital). Advocate: soft edges from physclock-ai-mishap-analysis (the AI channel the why names) and the new compute-demand node; the soft edge from test-loop-monthly was not added (it is a consequence, not a cause). Bands unchanged.

physclock-reusable-competition.title: A second reusable heavy-lift fleet at scale
physclock-reusable-competition.description: A non-SpaceX reusable medium or heavy launcher fleet (New Glenn, Neutron, Terran R, Long March 10B, Zhuque-3 or another) flies 20 or more missions with reflown boosters in one calendar year.
physclock-reusable-competition.status_oct2026: New Glenn: announced 2016 for 2020, first flight Jan 16 2025, first booster landing Nov 13 2025, upper-stage failure Apr 19 2026, vehicle destroyed and pad damaged in a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion; the FAA's draft assessment would raise its cap from 12 to 50 a year (Sep 2026). Neutron: announced Mar 2021 for 2024-25, now NET Q4 2026. Terran R NET 2026. China recovered a Long March 10B booster after orbital flight on Jul 10 2026 (Wikipedia; 33FG). LandSpace's stainless-steel methalox Zhuque-3 reached orbit on Dec 3 2025 and landed its first stage on its second flight, Aug 18 2026, though the stage caught fire and tipped over after landing (Wikipedia).
physclock-reusable-competition.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-reusable-competition.why: Mach33 modeled 15-36 New Glenn launches over 2026-27 and found cadence gated by BE-4 and upper-stage production, not reuse; every competitor slipped 1-5 years against announced first flights. AI helps new entrants most (no legacy process) but cannot shorten engine qualification or pad rebuilds. New Glenn, Neutron, Terran R and LM-10B were designed before 2027, so AI helps them mainly through anomaly closure (0-0.5 year in S2, physclock table); clean-sheet compression applies only to programs started in 2028 or later. Blue Origin has flown one New Glenn in 2026 against a goal of 24.
physclock-reusable-competition.strongest_case_small: For U.S. customer prices only Western competition counts (export control, national-security rules); Chinese fleets do not lower U.S. prices.
physclock-reusable-competition.signpost: New Glenn return to flight and reflown-booster count; Neutron's first flight; Chinese reusable cadence in 2027.
physclock-reusable-competition.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: S2 2029 -> 2030 (existing programs get 0-0.5 year of AI help, not a full year). Advocate: Zhuque-3 landing added to status (verified on Wikipedia, with the post-landing tip-over). Auditor: exogenous P7 label. S1, S3 and bands unchanged. Its hard edge into physclock-cheap-mass-customer is now soft.

physclock-licensing-in-weeks.title: Launch licensing in weeks
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.description: Routine license modifications (new trajectory, cadence or payload class) clear in under 30 days, new vehicle operator licenses in under 90 days from a complete application (against the 180-day statutory maximum), and FCC satellite approvals in months.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.status_oct2026: EO 14335 (Aug 2025) ordered Part 450 reform and NEPA streamlining; FAA proposed rules on Jul 30 2026 (waiving requirements under 13 laws) and Oct 5 2026 (cutting Part 450 analysis burdens); the FCC adopted a Part 100 'Licensing Assembly Line' (vote Jul 22 2026). The statutory review clock for a complete application is 180 days (general).
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.why: Chain (S2): FAA final rules on the Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026 proposals 2027-28 -> AI-assisted FAA review (physclock-regulator-ai-capacity) 2028, fed by AI-drafted Part 450 analyses (physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis) -> published median modification times under 30 days 2028-29. Reform alone gives about 1.2x (physical-gate table, S1); halving the statutory clock needs reviewer capacity, so regulator AI capacity stays a hard prerequisite, while operator-side drafting mostly shortens the time before the clock starts and is an accelerator. One route is a license that covers a whole analyzed flight envelope, so routine changes need no modification (Part 450 already lets one license cover multiple launches of a vehicle or family, 14 CFR 450.3, general). Capped at Medium because it is regulator behavior.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.strongest_case_small: Licensing was not the binding gate for SpaceX in 2025-26 (hardware was); NEPA litigation and environmental consultations remain; a public-safety incident would reverse reform.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.signpost: FAA final rules on the 2026 proposals; published license evaluation times; Starship license modifications approved without delaying flights.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Criterion 'under six months from a complete application' (the 180-day statutory maximum, i.e. the status quo) -> 'under 90 days'. [auditor] pathway P1->P2 -> 'P1 (with policy reform)' (P2 is not on the hard path); chain written out. [skeptic] physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis hard -> soft; skeptic's proposal to also soften physclock-regulator-ai-capacity rejected (the physical-gate table credits reform alone with only 1.2x). [advocate] envelope-licensing idea folded into the why instead of a new node. Years and bands unchanged. [auditor] status wording: the Jul 30 proposal waives requirements under 13 laws.

physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.title: Crew and defense payloads fly on data-cleared reused rockets
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.description: NASA crew or NASA Category 3 payloads, or NSSL Phase 3 Lane 2 missions, fly on reflown Starship-class hardware whose reflight clearance rests largely on flight data and life models rather than teardown inspection. NSSL Lane 1 task orders, which need only a completed launch or a credible plan, do not count.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 analog: first booster reflight Mar 2017; NASA crew on a reused booster with Crew-2 in Apr 2021, about four years later (general). HLS was not human-rated as of Apr 2026; Artemis III became a low-Earth-orbit test (NET Jun 2027) and the first landing moved to Artemis IV in early 2028 (Wikipedia).
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.why: Falcon's lag (first reflight Mar 2017; NASA crew on a reused booster with Crew-2, Apr 2021; first NSSL mission on a reused booster, GPS III SV05, Jun 2021) came from accumulated flight history; AI evidence cannot create flight cycles and saves about a year at most, conditional on the credibility standard (S2 2029). Chain (S2): data-cleared reflight 2030 -> acceptance on flight history plus AI evidence 2031; S3 one year earlier. Capped at Medium because it is customer certification.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.strongest_case_small: NASA crew safety posture will require flight history, not models; HLS and national-security missions may use new vehicles anyway, making the question moot before 2031.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.signpost: NASA or Space Force accepting a reflown Starship for a mission; a NASA certification baseline for Starship reuse.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S2 2030 -> 2031, S3 2029 -> 2030 (follows the revised twin timing). Skeptic: scope limited to NASA crew, Category 3 and NSSL Lane 2 (a Lane 1 mission could fly with no AI evidence and break the causal chain); why rewritten around flight history. Bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): soft edge from physclock-reliability-priors-credit (B-certification request 2).

physclock-cheap-mass-internal.title: Starship internal cost under $300 per kg
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $300/kg, against about $1,500/kg on an optimized Falcon 9 Starlink flight and about $4,915/kg on expended Flight 14.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (Sep 2026): Flight 14 about $4,915/kg ($250M stack, 52 t); base $656/kg in 2027 and about $300/kg in 2028 (bear about $560, bull $141); $13/kg by 2035. Falcon 9 optimized Starlink flight about $1,499/kg at a $25M internal cost.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.why: Mach33 splits the 2026-27 decline (log basis) into reuse 56%, payload 32% and production learning 12%. None is a mathematics lever. This is the independent physical exponential in this tree: it would happen at the same pace with no AI math at all. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.strongest_case_small: Internal cost matters only to SpaceX's own payloads (Starlink, orbital compute); outside customers see prices, not costs (see physclock-cheap-mass-customer). Mach33's base is about $300/kg in 2028, so under $300 in 2028 is roughly 50/50 by construction; it assumes 3.3 flights per stack in 2027 and 4.8 in 2028, which needs a ship reflight in early 2027, and its bear case (ship reflight 2028) gives about $560/kg. Applying the tree's 1.5-3x slip ratio to Musk-anchored milestones puts the central year at 2029; S3 cannot pull it back because it diverges from S2 only during 2028.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.signpost: Flights per stack in 2027; payload per flight approaching 100 t. (internal cost is modeled, not published)
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: 2028 -> 2029 in all scenarios (2028 is Mach33's base-case median, not a likely year; slip ratio applied). Auditor: exogenous P7 label and Mach33 source-weight caveat. Advocate: soft edge to program-cycle-compression (cheap mass can buy schedule). Bands unchanged.

physclock-cheap-mass-customer.title: Customers buy orbit under $1,000 per kg
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.description: Third-party customers can routinely buy dedicated heavy-lift launch below $1,000 per kilogram of customer payload delivered (not per kilogram of vehicle capacity), against a Falcon 9 dedicated median of about $5,300/kg and a rideshare floor of about $7,000/kg today.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Unlock model (Aug 2026): Starship third-party ticket enters at about $3,975/kg in 2027 and fades toward cost with a 2033 midpoint (2030-36 range) as competitors reach cadence; Voyager's $90M Starlab contract is about $900/kg of capacity on a 100 t vehicle for a launch NET 2028-29 (Mach33); on Starlab's delivered mass, which is not published, the price per kilogram is higher. SpaceX flew 83% of 2025 mass to orbit.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.pathway: P7 (exogenous price; AI enters only through competitors' engineering)
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.why: Price follows competition and SpaceX's capacity-release decisions, not cost: Falcon 9 list prices were stable for a decade, and Mach33 finds a one-year delay in credible competitor cadence delays external crossover by about a year. AI math reaches this node only by speeding competitors' engineering. Mach33's 2035 simulations vary when SpaceX releases Starship's spare capacity to customers (2029-2033) as a main price driver, so competition accelerates this node rather than gating it, and SpaceX can price below $1,000/kg without a rival; internal orbital-compute demand can delay that release. Band S2 Low: Mach33's fade midpoint is 2033 (range 2030-36), so crossing by 2031 is roughly 20-30% (judgment), and AI moves it 0-1 year. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.strongest_case_small: Anchor deals like Voyager's already price near $900/kg, so 'routine' is a soft threshold; the markets most sensitive to $/kg (Starlink, orbital compute) are SpaceX's own and see internal cost.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.signpost: Published Starship rideshare or dedicated pricing; a second Starship-class customer contract below $1,500/kg.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + advocate: reusable-competition hard -> soft (not logically necessary; Chinese fleets can satisfy it without lowering U.S. prices). Skeptic: S2 Medium -> Low (2033 fade midpoint; S2 earliest year 2031) and $900/kg relabelled as capacity price; advocate wanted bands unchanged (debate recorded). Advocate's capacity-release mechanism added to why. Auditor: Mach33 caveat.

physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.title: Qualification campaigns 15-30% shorter
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.description: Typical qualification campaigns for derivative spacecraft and launch-vehicle subsystems on programs started in 2028 or later run at least 15% shorter than the pre-2027 baseline of roughly 12-24 months (about 10-20% in S2 and 20-30% in S3, per the physical-gate table; derivatives more, first-of-kind less), through fewer re-tests, analysis credit and faster facilities.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.status_oct2026: Qualification remains test-driven; NASA-STD-6030 requires per-machine qualification for additive parts; new space materials take 10-20+ years to insert (Materials Genome Initiative: 20 or more years from discovery to market).
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.why: Chain (S2): information-optimal development tests 2028 -> credibility directive 2029 -> structural analysis credit 2030 -> environmental-qualification credit on derivatives 2031 -> programs started 2028 or later finish qualification and report 2031 or later. The physical-gate table gives spacecraft environmental qualification campaigns 0.8-0.9x in S2 and 0.7-0.8x in S3, and the capability Amdahl table uses 1.2x for qualification and reviews in S2, so the former 30-50% exceeded even the S3 figure. The incompressible core is thermal-vacuum time constants, real-time life and creep tests (a 10,000-hour creep test takes about 14 months), workmanship screening and statistical replicates. Commercial operators that skip tests on their own risk (physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual), accepted reliability priors (physclock-reliability-priors-credit), autonomous stands and printed-part certification accelerate it but are not preconditions. Capped at Medium; S2 Low because evidence on programs started 2028+ cannot report before about 2031.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.strongest_case_small: Organizations spend saved time on more testing; first-of-kind hardware keeps full programs; the cut lands mostly on derivatives.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.signpost: GAO, ESA or company schedule data showing shorter qualification phases on programs started in 2028 or later (such data cannot appear before about 2031).
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Title and description changed from 30-50% (contradicted by research/physclock.json: qualification campaign 0.8-0.9x S2, 0.7-0.8x S3; capability Amdahl 1.2x) to 15-30% with a 15% threshold. [auditor] tier-7 chain written out. [skeptic] S2 2030 -> 2031, S3 2029 -> 2030, S2 Medium -> Low (signpost cannot report before ~2031; also forced by physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit S2 2031/S3 2030). [skeptic+advocate] materials-am-digital-twin-qual hard -> soft; [skeptic] physclock-ai-run-test-stands hard -> soft. Advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028/S3 High and making qual-by-analysis-credit soft rejected (see debates); advocate's commercial node added as a soft accelerator instead.

physclock-dev-capital-cut.title: AI cuts development cost of new space hardware by about 10-20%
physclock-dev-capital-cut.description: Non-recurring development cost for new spacecraft and launch vehicles falls about 10-20% under S2 as engineering labor for analysis, design, software and verification shrinks; hardware, test articles and facilities do not shrink.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.status_oct2026: Starship program spend exceeded $15B by 2026, against roughly $400M for Falcon 9 development, and SpaceX directed all $3B of its 2025 space-segment R&D to Starship (Reuters via 33FG). SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after an $85.7B IPO in June 2026.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.why: If engineering labor is 40-60% of development cost and analysis, design, software and verification are about half of it (general), S2's 5-10x cognitive speedup removes roughly 16-27% of total cost gross (merely halving that content removes 10-15%). physclock.json's capital row gives a 15-30% fall in development labor cost, which is about 6-18% of total cost, and an effective capital multiplier of 1.15-1.3x (13-23%). Scope growth takes some back, so the realized cut is about 10-20%. A second channel could add to it: standing-army costs scale with schedule, so shorter programs also trim time-proportional overhead. Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> programs started 2028 or later estimated with AI-reduced labor -> first program estimates showing 10-20% lower non-recurring cost 2029 -> completed-program evidence 2031 or later. S3: adoption 2028 with near-free cognition from 2029 -> 2029. S1: 2031. It matters most for capital-gated new entrants; for SpaceX capital is not binding through 2031. What binds is organizations changing practice, not capital.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.strongest_case_small: Labor savings get spent on scope; hardware-rich programs like Starship spend mainly on hardware; government cost growth comes from requirements and funding instability.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.signpost: Startup raises and program estimates citing AI-reduced engineering headcount; NASA cost-estimating relationships revised for AI.
