science-coronal-heating-theory.title: Coronal heating: an AI-built model passes a blind test
science-coronal-heating-theory.description: A predictive model of coronal heating and solar-wind acceleration, built by AI from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter and PUNCH data, makes a discriminating quantitative prediction (one on which the leading mechanisms, waves and turbulence versus small-scale reconnection and switchbacks, disagree) that a later encounter confirms. This is the measurable step; community consensus that the problem is settled would come later.
science-coronal-heating-theory.status_oct2026: Open for about 80 years (general); Parker Solar Probe has made perihelia near 9.9 solar radii since Dec 2024 (general); large data volumes are under-analyzed (general).
science-coronal-heating-theory.why: One of the few open physics problems where the data largely exist and theory-building is the bottleneck, so S2/S3 physics-theory capability could matter, and several perihelia a year give repeated chances to test. The band can be no better than its hard prerequisite (cap-physics-theory, S2 Medium), and a model must be built and then tested against a later encounter, so S2 is Low and S3 Medium; S1 Speculative. Heliospheric tomography helps but is not required: global white-light density barely constrains kinetic-scale heating. A confirmed mechanism would shape what the next heliophysics missions measure (high-cadence spectroscopy versus in-situ kinetic plasma). Bands are judgments.
science-coronal-heating-theory.strongest_case_small: Several mechanisms probably operate; 'settled' may mean an energy budget, not one answer; consensus forms slowly and decisive tests may need new in-situ data.
science-coronal-heating-theory.signpost: An AI-built heating model makes a quantitative prediction confirmed at a later Parker Solar Probe or Solar Orbiter encounter.
science-coronal-heating-theory.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Advocate: retitled and redefined to the measurable outcome its own signpost names (a discriminating blind prediction confirmed), since 'settled' is a consensus gate the node never named. Advocate's S2 Low->Medium rejected (the node needs cap-physics-theory, S2 Medium, then a model and a later encounter); skeptic's S3 Medium->Low not applied because the redefinition removes consensus, the reason for the cut. Skeptic: hard edge from science-helio-tomography made soft (global density tomography barely constrains kinetic-scale heating).

science-quantum-sensor-design.title: Quantum sensors designed against full error budgets
science-quantum-sensor-design.description: AI-derived systematic-error models (relativistic time transfer, magnetic and gravity-gradient effects, wavefront aberrations) and provably robust quantum-control sequences for space clocks and atom interferometers.
science-quantum-sensor-design.status_oct2026: ESA's ACES clock ensemble on the ISS since 2025 (ACES payload paper, 2025; relativistic geodesy study using ACES links, arXiv 2609.21786, Sep 2026); differential atom-interferometer magnetometry in NASA's Cold Atom Lab (Nature Communications, Jul 2026); a quantum gravity gradiometer pathfinder is reported funded (EPJ Quantum Technology, Mar 2025; unverified).
science-quantum-sensor-design.why: Error budgets and robust control are bespoke applied math done by small teams; on-demand AI makes them cheap and complete (P1). Validation needs ground and ISS experiments. S3 equals S2 through 2027, so 2028.
science-quantum-sensor-design.strongest_case_small: Performance is limited by lasers, vacuum, vibration and atom-source hardware in orbit; error budgets are already well understood by the expert teams.
science-quantum-sensor-design.signpost: A flight-instrument design review citing AI-derived systematic-error models; ACES or Cold Atom Lab results matching AI-predicted systematics.
science-quantum-sensor-design.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027->2028. Auditor: pathway P1->P6 -> P1 (designs and error models, default High). Auditor: gradiometer pathfinder funding claim could not be verified (publisher login), marked (unverified).

science-quantum-sensor-flight.title: AI-co-designed quantum sensor flies
science-quantum-sensor-flight.description: A space atom-interferometer gravity gradiometer or next-generation clock whose design and control were materially derived with AI demonstrates its predicted sensitivity in orbit.
science-quantum-sensor-flight.status_oct2026: A quantum gravity gradiometer pathfinder is reported funded (EPJ Quantum Technology, Mar 2025; unverified); ACES flies on the ISS and Cold Atom Lab runs atom interferometry in orbit; no AI-co-designed quantum sensor known to be in flight development (general).
science-quantum-sensor-flight.why: Chain (S2): quantum-sensor-design 2028 -> a next-generation clock payload on a smallsat or hosted slot, a new instrument rather than a derivative, takes about 18-24 months to build (physclock lag ladder: 12-18 months for derivative smallsat payloads) -> rideshare launch around 2030 -> months of in-orbit characterization -> predicted sensitivity demonstrated in 2031. Atom-interferometer gravity gradiometers follow flagship-class cycles of 4-7 years and fly after 2031. S3 equals S2 through 2028 and qualification compresses only 1.3-1.7x after 2028-29, so S3 is also 2031. Low in S2 and S3 because in-orbit performance is hardware-limited (lasers, vacuum, atom sources) and no funded flight able to take AI-derived control late is named. Bands are judgments.
science-quantum-sensor-flight.strongest_case_small: Even S3's faster cognition does not shorten vacuum, vibration and radiation qualification.
science-quantum-sensor-flight.signpost: Quantum gravity gradiometer pathfinder launch date and design methods.
science-quantum-sensor-flight.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S3 2030->2031 (design lands 2028 in S2 and S3). Auditor: stated '4-7 year cycle' arithmetic contradicted the 2031 year; advocate: smallsat or hosted clock payloads follow the physclock lag ladder, not flagship cycles. Resolution: why rewritten with the full smallsat chain (new instrument, 18-24 months), S2 kept at 2031 and Low; auditor's S2 Speculative and advocate's S2/S3 Medium (and S2 2030, S3 2029) both rejected.

science-archival-discovery-engine.title: AI mines the space-science archive at scale
science-archival-discovery-engine.description: AI systems that pose and answer research questions against archival mission data (JWST, Hubble, Gaia, TESS, Fermi, Parker Solar Probe, SDO), building models, running analyses and drafting results, with humans choosing problems and auditing.
science-archival-discovery-engine.status_oct2026: GPT-5 case studies documented new research steps in physics and astronomy (arXiv 2511.16072, Nov 2025); physicists call for AI verification frameworks before discovery claims (VERaiPHY review, arXiv 2607.10039, Jul 2026).
science-archival-discovery-engine.why: The capability channel (tl-position-4) with no physical gate: the data are already paid for and public. Most analysis-limited questions in archives are easier than the catalog's problems, so today's public agentic models (GPT-6 Astra public since Sep 2026) suffice; the Oct-2026 internal mathematics level reaching outside teams (cap-research-math-public) accelerates it but is not required, so S1 is also 2027.
science-archival-discovery-engine.strongest_case_small: Human verification and refereeing bandwidth (tr-position-5) caps how many results become knowledge, and archival low-hanging fruit is finite.
science-archival-discovery-engine.signpost: First AI-led discovery in a mission archive confirmed by a follow-up observation; archive-use statistics.
science-archival-discovery-engine.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Advocate: archival analysis needs today's public agentic models (GPT-6 Astra public since Sep 2026, research/capability.json), not the Oct-2026 internal mathematics level, so the hard edge from cap-research-math-public became soft and S1 2028->2027. Bands unchanged.

science-claims-audit.title: Extraordinary claims audited in weeks
science-claims-audit.description: Independent AI re-analyses and certified checks of extraordinary claims (biosignatures, dark-energy anomalies, new-physics hints, exotic-propulsion metrics) published within weeks, with interval-certified or Lean-checked components where possible.
science-claims-audit.status_oct2026: Observer-robust energy-condition tests for warp metrics with interval-arithmetic certificates exist (Warpax, arXiv 2602.18023, Feb 2026). First rebuttals already come fast: the 2020-21 positive-energy warp claims drew a generic null-energy rebuttal within months (arXiv 2105.03079, May 2021), although a direct recomputation of Lentz's metric came only in Nov 2025 (arXiv 2511.18251); the K2-18 b DMS claim (ApJL, mid-Apr 2025) drew a model-space rebuttal on Apr 30 2025 (arXiv 2504.21788), and the debate then ran for many months.
science-claims-audit.why: Ceilings and counterexamples act fastest (tl-position-3). First rebuttals already arrive in weeks to months (K2-18 b DMS: about 2 weeks; positive-energy warp claims: about 2 months), but full re-derivations have taken one to five years (Lentz, 2020 to 2025). AI adds certified components and closes the gap to a full re-derivation within weeks once outside teams can pose the question; the novelty is certification, not first-response speed. Warp no-go theorems and quantum energy inequalities accelerate only the exotic-propulsion slice. Formal (Lean) checking of GR claims waits on Lorentzian geometry in Mathlib (infra-mathlib-applied).
science-claims-audit.strongest_case_small: Contested claims are usually limited by data quality, not analysis speed; faster audits do not settle data-starved questions.
science-claims-audit.signpost: A journal or agency formally requiring AI-run independent re-analysis for extraordinary claims.
science-claims-audit.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: hard edge from science-energy-condition-nogo made soft (auditing biosignature or dark-energy claims needs no warp theorem). Skeptic + auditor (contradicted fact): the Lentz claim drew a generic rebuttal in May 2021 (arXiv 2105.03079), and the K2-18 b DMS claim drew a rebuttal within about two weeks (arXiv 2504.21788, verified), so 'a five-year refutation lag shrinks to weeks' was replaced. Auditor: soft edge from science-qei-curved. Years and bands unchanged.

science-lightsail-stability.title: Lightsails proven to ride the beam
science-lightsail-stability.description: Sail shapes and metasurface designs with proven passive stability under laser propulsion (no tumbling or sliding off the beam) plus thermal and structural margins: the math-and-design half of beamed interstellar-precursor propulsion, the physics-allowed alternative to warp concepts.
science-lightsail-stability.status_oct2026: Beam-riding stability shown in models (general); Caltech measured radiation pressure on a tethered 40-micron, 50 nm silicon-nitride membrane (Nature Photonics, Jan 2025; AFOSR and Breakthrough Starshot funding) and plans nanostructured surfaces to impart a restoring force or torque; a cm-scale self-stabilizing diffractive sail prototype was shown at RIT (general). No path yet to the ~100 GW-class phased laser arrays a fast interstellar probe needs (general).
science-lightsail-stability.why: Contrast case: here AI mathematics enables (stability proofs, optimized designs) rather than only bounding. The design is cognitive and lands early; laboratory force and torque tests on small membranes validate it, and everything after that (gram-scale propulsion, laser arrays) is capital and hardware. S3 equals S2 through 2027, so 2028.
science-lightsail-stability.strongest_case_small: The binding constraints are the laser array (capital, power, phasing) and sail materials, not stability theory.
science-lightsail-stability.signpost: Published sail designs with proven passive-stability margins, and a laboratory measurement of the restoring force or torque they predict on a nanostructured membrane (the Caltech group's stated next step).
science-lightsail-stability.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027->2028. Auditor: pathway P1->P6 -> P1->P4 (the node delivers designs and analyses). Auditor + skeptic boundary fix: laboratory force and torque tests count here; gram-scale propulsion belongs to science-lightsail-demo. Status adds the Caltech 2025 measurement (verified) cited by the advocate.

science-lightsail-demo.title: Laser-propelled gram-scale sail demonstrated
science-lightsail-demo.description: Demonstration of stable laser-driven propulsion of a gram-scale sail over meters or more, in a ground vacuum facility or in free (suborbital or orbital) flight. Force or torque measurements on smaller membranes count toward science-lightsail-stability, not here.
science-lightsail-demo.why: By F = 2P/c, accelerating 1 g at 1 m/s^2 takes about 150 kW of reflected laser power (a 10 kW-class laser gives about 0.07 m/s^2), plus a sail that survives the absorbed heat and stays on the beam. Chain: stability designs 2028 (S2) -> laboratory force and torque validation 2029-30 -> a sponsor funds a high-power propulsion facility and gram-scale sails -> demonstration. No sponsor or facility is named as of Oct 2026, and capital compresses at most 1.3-1.5x even in S3, so the demonstration is after 2031 in every scenario (Speculative; judgment).
science-lightsail-demo.strongest_case_small: No sponsor, no demo, whatever the mathematics.
science-lightsail-demo.signpost: A funded program for a high-power laser propulsion demonstration.
science-lightsail-demo.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: the node is propulsion of a gram-scale sail, not a force measurement ('or smaller' removed; lab force/torque tests moved to science-lightsail-stability). Auditor: S3 2031->>2031 and Low->Speculative because no sponsor or facility can be named and the tier-5 chain must be written out. Advocate's lab-scale redefinition (S2 2030 Medium, S3 2029 Medium) rejected: it relabels the stability node's validation step as the demonstration.

science-propulsion-funding-redirect.title: No-go theorems redirect breakthrough-propulsion money
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.description: Sharp, audited no-go results move the small pool of breakthrough-propulsion funding and attention away from warp and reactionless concepts toward physics-allowed frontiers (fusion, beamed sails).
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.status_oct2026: NASA's Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project (1996-2002) reported six of 14 tasks reaching null conclusions (NTRS 20060000022) and about a third of 16 tasks not viable (NTRS 20040070788); warp research continues to be published (e.g., atmospheric-signature study of zero-ADM-mass warp bubbles, arXiv 2608.10800, Aug 2026).
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.premise_tier: T5 for the core no-go theorems
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.why: Ceilings change what people stop doing (fc-position-1 exception), but the record is weak: the null-energy theorem (2021) and the positive mass theorem (1979-81) produced no observable redirect, and warp papers kept appearing in Aug 2026. The current research front is positive-energy subluminal shells, which the theorems allow (they need only large positive mass), so funders get no 'violates energy conditions' criterion to exclude them. Program managers could cite an audited theorem instead of a debate, but the gate is human belief (adoption), so Low in every scenario (judgment); S3 equals S2 through 2028.
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.strongest_case_small: The dollars at stake are tiny (single-digit millions per year, general) and the most committed proponents rarely respond to theorems; the ceilings were mostly known by 2021.
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.signpost: Funding calls (NIAC, private institutes) explicitly excluding concepts that require energy-condition violation.
science-propulsion-funding-redirect.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027->2028. Skeptic: Medium->Low in all scenarios and S1 2028->2029 (no observable redirect after the 2021 null-energy theorem; positive-energy subluminal shells are allowed by the theorems, so funders get no exclusion criterion; adoption at zero lag in S1 was inconsistent).

science-return-per-dollar.title: More science per mission dollar
science-return-per-dollar.description: With analysis, theory and modeling nearly free, the science extracted from each flown observatory rises sharply; photons, downlink and mission count become the bottleneck of space science. Measurable test: refereed papers and confirmed results from archival JWST, Hubble, TESS, Gaia and heliophysics data per mission dollar at least double relative to 2025.
science-return-per-dollar.status_oct2026: Archives of JWST, Hubble, Gaia, TESS and heliophysics missions are public and under-analyzed (general); budget pressure is rising (NASA FY2027 request $18.8B vs $24.4B FY2026).
science-return-per-dollar.why: The main 2031 outcome in this domain. The cognitive clock compresses analysis of data already paid for; nothing physical gates it until the archives are exhausted, so the binding gate is adoption (referee bandwidth and absorption), after which new photons bind. S2 Medium: a doubling needs referees and journals to absorb it, and the FY2027 request cuts the Science Mission Directorate 47%, including the research and analysis grants that fund archival work. S3 High because AI-assisted refereeing and near-free cognition from 2029 relieve absorption. S3 equals S2 through 2027, so 2028. Bands are judgments.
science-return-per-dollar.strongest_case_small: Paper counts are not discoveries; referee bandwidth limits absorption; budget cuts may remove missions faster than AI raises yield per mission.
science-return-per-dollar.signpost: Discoveries from archival data per year; agency reports on archive science yield.
science-return-per-dollar.calibration_note: A3: Tier-7 rule: "science per mission dollar rises sharply" is a field-wide strategic outcome and comparable to frontier-math-unbinds (S2 Medium). S2 High -> Medium; S3 High kept.
science-return-per-dollar.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027->2028. Skeptic: binding gate data->adoption (the node's own text says nothing physical binds before 2031; referee bandwidth does). Advocate: measurable test added (at least a doubling of archival papers and confirmed results per mission dollar versus 2025) and soft edges from the two new nodes; advocate's S2 Medium->High rejected, keeping the A3 calibration and the auditor's view, because absorption and the FY2027 cut to research and analysis bind in the base case.

science-portfolio-shift.title: Space science shifts money from analysis to photons
science-portfolio-shift.description: Agencies and decadal surveys rebalance toward more data-collecting missions (small satellites, rideshares, probes) and laboratory data, because AI makes analysis and theory cheap.
science-portfolio-shift.status_oct2026: Priorities set by decadal surveys (Astro2020 reported in late 2021; the next astrophysics survey is expected around 2031-32, general). FY2027 request: NASA -23%, Science Mission Directorate -47%.
science-portfolio-shift.why: If cognition is near-free, the marginal dollar buys more science as data than as analysis. Agencies act through budget cycles and decadal surveys, which compress 1.0x, so the effect appears at the next survey (around 2031-32) at the earliest, and S3 cannot run ahead of S2. The FY2027 request cuts the Science Mission Directorate 47%, which confounds attribution: budget-driven cuts to research and analysis would look like the predicted shift without being caused by AI. Cheaper development (physclock-dev-capital-cut), customer launch under $1,000/kg and privately funded observatories can rebalance the field's portfolio without an appropriation, but by 2031 they are soft influences. Low in every scenario (judgment).
science-portfolio-shift.strongest_case_small: Budgets are set by politics, and flagship commitments (HWO, the LISA contribution) lock in spending for a decade.
science-portfolio-shift.signpost: Terms of reference for the next astrophysics decadal survey addressing AI analysis capacity.
science-portfolio-shift.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: S2 Medium->Low; skeptic: S3 Medium->Low and S3 2029->2030 (decadal surveys and appropriations compress 1.0x; FY2027 cuts confound attribution). All three lenses: hard edge from science-hwo-design-closure made soft. Advocate: soft edges from physclock-dev-capital-cut, physclock-cheap-mass-customer and science-private-observatories accepted (bands unchanged by them).

struct-test-data-commons.title: AI-ready structural and thermal test data
struct-test-data-commons.description: Machine-readable databases of the physical evidence this domain runs on: shell-buckling tests with measured imperfections, fatigue and crack-growth spectra, thermal-vacuum correlation sets, microgravity two-phase flow data and deployment telemetry, opened to AI models inside agencies and large firms.
struct-test-data-commons.status_oct2026: Fragmented. NASA Shell Buckling Knockdown Factor (SBKF) test reports sit in NTRS as PDFs; Wagner released Monte Carlo knockdown databases and code on Zenodo (Jul 2026; doi 10.5281/zenodo.21630428); ISS flow boiling and condensation datasets were published 2024-2025; most company data are proprietary or export-controlled (general).
struct-test-data-commons.why: fc-position-2: this domain is limited by modeling fidelity, data and verification cost, not conjectures. Every physics node below (damage, two-phase flow, deployment, mid-frequency vibration) is data-gated: an AI that can build theory still needs validated tests with known uncertainties. Organizing existing evidence is cheap compared with new tests (a single 8-ft shell test or thermal-vacuum campaign takes months); under S2 the incentive to make data AI-readable is strong, so large organizations do it internally by 2028.
struct-test-data-commons.strongest_case_small: Export control, proprietary interest and poor metadata in legacy tests (unmeasured imperfections, uncertain boundary conditions) mean much historical data cannot validate anything; new tests are still needed.
struct-test-data-commons.signpost: NASA or ESA releases a structured, AI-queryable buckling, fatigue or thermal test database, or a major launch company says it validates models on its full flight-test archive, by 2028.
struct-test-data-commons.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor] Fact fix: the Zenodo knockdown record (Jul 27 2026) lists Wagner only, not 'Wagner and Huehne'. Now also a hard prerequisite of struct-cert-by-analysis [skeptic]. Years and bands unchanged. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'Analyst position (g):' replaced with the KB position id fc-position-2.

struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.title: Firmer math under elasticity, crack and inspection models
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.description: Independent confirmation of the release's elasticity and fracture results: smooth isotropic Lame moduli are uniquely determined by boundary measurements (372); metric and connection recovery from one boundary patch, plus a conductivity nonuniqueness theorem from full boundary data (365); regularity of planar Mumford-Shah crack sets (366); the 3D Ball-Evans approximation problem (368).
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.status_oct2026: 372, 366 and 368 are T1 (manuscript only). 365's Lean part (T3, unchecked by outsiders) is nonuniqueness for bounded measurable, uniformly positive scalar conductivities on a 3D ball: two conductivities differing on a set of positive volume have identical full Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps. The metric-and-connection recovery from one boundary patch is manuscript-only (T1). No outside Comparator report as of 2026-10-07. PDE formalization is weak in the release (3 of 16 PDE families).
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.premise_tier: T1 (372, 366, 368, and 365's recovery half); T3 (365 conductivity nonuniqueness)
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.why: These four families are the release's only direct contact with structural mechanics. 372 tells inspection engineers that full boundary data determine elastic stiffness in principle; it says nothing about how stably, and Calderon-type problems are typically only logarithmically stable (general), so it raises confidence without changing tools. 366 underpins the Griffith/Francfort-Marigo variational fracture energies behind phase-field fracture codes: minimizing crack sets are well-behaved in 2D. 368 is a technical tool for nonlinear-elasticity existence and approximation theory (invertible deformations), relevant to large-deformation finite elements. The conductivity half of 365 is a negative result: some bounded measurable conductivities cannot be recovered even from full boundary data (T3). This limits electrical-resistance damage sensing in carbon-fiber structures only if real laminate damage fields fall in such rough classes (judgment). Under S2, AI-assisted formalization of PDE catches up (2028), so confirmation by 2031 is likely. The 372, 366, 368 and 365-recovery parts are conditional (T1, no Lean main results), so bands are one step down.
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.strongest_case_small: Engineers already run elastography, guided-wave inversion and phase-field fracture codes without these theorems; uniqueness in principle is not stability; the counterexamples may live in coefficient classes (rough, anisotropic, non-generic) that real laminates never present.
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.signpost: An independent Comparator run on 365, or inverse-problems specialists endorsing 372 in a refereed venue, by end-2027; any SHM paper using 365's nonuniqueness construction to bound resistance-based damage sensing.
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.calibration_note: A3: T1 premise rule: three of the four families (372, 366, 368) are T1; only 365 is T3. One band down: Medium/High/High -> Low/Medium/Medium; why now marks the T1 parts conditional. This leaves its hard dependent struct-shm-inverse-limits (capability-driven, Medium/High/High) above it; that edge should become a soft edge (see notes).
struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [auditor] 365 statement gap (lean/docs/365.md, checked): the Lean part is scalar-conductivity nonuniqueness from the full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map (T3); metric-and-connection recovery from one patch is manuscript-only (T1). Description, status, why and premise_tier corrected; bands unchanged (already one step down).

struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.title: Hot spots conjecture (planar case) confirmed
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.description: Family 369 claims that on any simply connected planar domain, the slowest-decaying non-constant temperature mode of an insulated (Neumann) plate takes its maximum and minimum on the boundary, settling Rauch's 1974 conjecture for that class.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.status_oct2026: T1 (manuscript only). Human results cover special classes: all Euclidean triangles (Judge-Mondal, Annals 2020; erratum 2022), lip-type and symmetric domains in higher dimensions (TAMS-B Apr 2026), convex hyperbolic domains with small eigenvalues, trapezoids and kites. A certified-numerics project (cert-machine, Zenodo, Oct 5 2026, not refereed; machine-derived with Claude, not from family 369) certified a non-symmetric convex trapezoid case.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.why: A dead-end leaf for engineering, included to show the mapping honestly. Real radiators and panels are 3D, multi-material, with radiative (not insulated) boundaries, and thermal engineers compute their modes numerically for every geometry. The theorem confirms an intuition (slowest insulated thermal mode peaks at edges) and could inform sensor-placement heuristics for thin insulated plates; it changes no design. Effect on space thermal engineering: nil to negligible. Conditional: 369 is T1 (no Lean main result), so the band is one step below a checked result.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.strongest_case_small: This node is itself the strongest case: radiative boundary conditions, 3D geometry and numerical design make the planar Neumann theorem irrelevant to hardware.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.signpost: Expert acceptance (refereed version or endorsement by spectral-geometry specialists) by 2027. No engineering signpost is expected.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.calibration_note: A3: T1 premise rule: family 369 is T1 (no Lean). One band down: Medium/High/High -> Low/Medium/Medium; why now says conditional.
struct-hot-spots-thermal-modes.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [auditor] Status completed with the best-known human result (all Euclidean triangles, Judge-Mondal) and cert-machine provenance.

struct-worst-imperfection-theory.title: Worst-case imperfection theory for thin shells
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.description: Rigorous answers to the open question of which manufacturing imperfections (shape, amplitude, number, location) most reduce the buckling load of thin cylinders and cones, with provable lower bounds on the knockdown factor given a factory's measured imperfection statistics.
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.status_oct2026: Genuinely open. Ubamanyu, Blond, Hutchinson and Reis (arXiv, Jul 2026) show the localized dimple, nearly worst-case for spheres, is not worst-case for cylinders, and find a statistical size effect; Wagner et al. (Proc. R. Soc. A, 2025) propose a regime-aware mechanistic design curve; NASA SP-8007-2020/REV 2 added semi-empirical and analysis-based design approaches to the 1960s lower bounds, but no worst-case imperfection theory underlies them.
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.why: This is a nonconvex variational and stochastic problem in nonlinear shell theory (Koiter asymptotics, energy barriers, extreme-value statistics of defect populations): bespoke research-grade applied math of the kind S2 makes routine by 2028. A provable lower bound tied to measured imperfection spectra is what lets designers replace empirical lower-bound curves with tighter, defensible knockdowns (see struct-flown-lighter-structure, which it now gates, and struct-shell-knockdown-rules, which it accelerates).
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.strongest_case_small: Humans are converging anyway (mechanistic design curve, probabilistic knockdowns, SBKF); boundary conditions and load imperfections, not geometric theory, drive much of the test scatter; any bound is only as good as one factory's imperfection data.
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.signpost: A paper (AI-assisted or not) proving worst-case imperfection families, or computing certified lower bounds, for axially compressed cylinders by 2028.
struct-worst-imperfection-theory.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic, applied for consistency] status fact fix: SP-8007-2020/REV 2 is the current reference, not the 1960s bounds alone. Edges: now a hard prerequisite of struct-flown-lighter-structure [advocate+auditor] and a soft one of struct-shell-knockdown-rules [skeptic]. Years and bands unchanged.

struct-certified-uq-margins.title: Structural margins with certified uncertainty bounds
struct-certified-uq-margins.description: Reliability-based structural margins with rigorous rare-event probability estimates and quantified model-form error, as a defensible alternative to stacked deterministic factors (ultimate factors of ~1.25-1.4, model-uncertainty factors, test factors). Acceptance as a substitute for factors of safety is modeled in struct-cert-by-analysis.
struct-certified-uq-margins.status_oct2026: Practice is deterministic factors of safety (NASA-STD-5001 family, general) plus model-credibility assessment (NASA-STD-7009); probabilistic design used selectively. The release contains nothing on uncertainty quantification. 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, Lean, T3) is theory for the posterior sampling such methods use. NASA-STD-5001B FSR 17 already lets the delegated Technical Authority approve probabilistic criteria case by case, while noting that experience has shown deterministic criteria to be adequate; uptake has been limited (general).
struct-certified-uq-margins.pathway: P1 (method availability; acceptance as a substitute for factors is P6, modeled in struct-cert-by-analysis)
struct-certified-uq-margins.premise_tier: n/a (139 is T3 but peripheral; constants unknown, so P4 effect marginal)
struct-certified-uq-margins.why: Reliability methods, multifidelity Monte Carlo and Bayesian calibration are largely solved in principle but expensive and expert-scarce per program; model-form error and high-dimensional rare events remain open. On-demand AI applied math makes doing this properly on every program affordable. Replacing a stacked factor of ~1.4 with a reliability-equivalent margin is worth up to ~10% of mass on strength-critical members only; stiffness-, minimum-gauge- and buckling-critical parts gain less (general). The binding input is validation test data for model-form error, not method, hence the data gate.
struct-certified-uq-margins.strongest_case_small: Factors of safety cover unknown unknowns (workmanship, unmodeled load paths) that no UQ captures; crewed-system safety organizations will keep deterministic factors; the method is not the bottleneck, test data are.
struct-certified-uq-margins.signpost: A launch provider or NASA/ESA program publishes reliability-based margins with quantified model-form error, computed for a flight structure alongside its factors of safety, by 2029.
struct-certified-uq-margins.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor] Signpost re-scoped from a standards revision (regulator acceptance, capped Medium) to method use on a flight structure, so the High band grades capability; description and pathway say acceptance is modeled in struct-cert-by-analysis; FSR 17 added to status. [skeptic] binding_gate cognitive -> data (the node's own strongest case names test data as the bottleneck); mass claim limited to strength-critical members. Skeptic's S2 High -> Medium rejected once the signpost no longer needs acceptance (see debates).

struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.title: Closing the mid-frequency vibration gap
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.description: Error-controlled prediction of launch vibroacoustic response in the mid-frequency band (roughly a few hundred Hz to ~1-2 kHz), where finite-element models are too costly and statistical energy analysis is invalid, via hybrid FE-SEA and reduced-order models with a posteriori error bounds.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.status_oct2026: A long-standing open problem (general); practice envelopes predictions with margins and relies on acoustic and random-vibration tests. NASA NESC's Norton-Thevenin Receptance Coupling (2023-2024) cuts the cost of coupled loads analysis but does not address mid-frequency fidelity.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.why: Mid-frequency is hard because modal and statistical descriptions both break down. AI can design and prove error estimators for hybrid methods quickly under S2, but validation needs reverberant-chamber and flight data with quantified uncertainty. If solved, component random-vibration levels could be set from prediction with smaller margins, feeding struct-launch-env-margins.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.strongest_case_small: Qualification by test remains mandatory; uncertainty in the forcing (liftoff acoustics, transonic buffet) dominates structural model error, so even perfect structural models leave most of the margin in place.
struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics.signpost: A hybrid FE-SEA method with proven error bounds, validated against chamber data, ships in a commercial vibroacoustics code by 2029.

struct-shm-inverse-limits.title: Damage detection with proven detection limits
struct-shm-inverse-limits.description: Problem-specific stability estimates, optimal sensor placement and model-assisted probability of detection (MAPoD) for guided-wave, strain and electrical-resistance damage sensing, telling engineers what damage size a given sensor layout can and cannot see.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.status_oct2026: MAPoD for guided-wave SHM on composite cryogenic tanks for reusable launchers is active research (ONERA, Jul 2026); SHM is not yet qualified as an inspection replacement on launch vehicles (general). The release supplies a uniqueness claim (372, T1 per KB catalog, conditional) and a nonuniqueness result (365; only the 3D bounded-measurable scalar-conductivity part is formalized, T3), not stability constants.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 per KB catalog, conditional (repo lean/docs/372.md lists a Lean main result with a Comparator challenge, checked Oct 7 2026; T3 once the catalog is reconciled); 365 headline T1, formal scalar-conductivity part T3
struct-shm-inverse-limits.why: The question that earns inspection credit is not whether damage is identifiable in principle (372 claims yes, for smooth isotropic Lame moduli in 3D with full boundary data; conditional, and it does not cover anisotropic laminates or discontinuous damage) but how small a delamination N sensors detect at 90/95 confidence. That is quantitative stability plus statistics: solved in principle, expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. 365's formal part (T3) shows nonuniqueness only for rough (bounded measurable) scalar conductivities in 3D; thin sensing skins are effectively 2D, where uniqueness for bounded conductivities is classical (Astala-Paivarinta 2006, general), and CFRP is anisotropic, so 365 sets no practical ceiling. The practical limit is the classical logarithmic stability of the Calderon problem (general). The node's main pathway is capability; the catalog adds only conditional confidence.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.strongest_case_small: Real SHM is limited by sensor aging, bonding and temperature/cryogenic compensation, not inverse-problem theory; regulators and operators accept POD from physical specimen tests, not proofs.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.signpost: Published MAPoD/POD curves for a guided-wave SHM layout on a cryogenic composite tank, validated against seeded-defect specimens, by 2029; SHM papers citing 365 or 372.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.calibration_note: A3: Premise label only: the why says the main pathway is capability and the catalog adds confidence. A4: Hard edge from struct-elasticity-fracture-foundations made soft. That node is T1-premised (Low/Medium/Medium), and this one is capability-driven (Medium/High/High), as its own why says (the catalog adds confidence). A hard edge would have rated the dependent likelier than its prerequisite. B-certification: 'one ceiling' dropped; 365 sets no practical ceiling for 2D or anisotropic sensing.
struct-shm-inverse-limits.revision_note: B-certification: [auditor+skeptic] Grounding fixes: 372 worded as a conditional T1 claim limited to smooth isotropic moduli; 365's ceiling claim replaced (formal part is rough 3D scalar conductivity only, verified in lean/docs/365.md; sensing skins are 2D and anisotropic); 366 (Mumford-Shah regularity) dropped as irrelevant to detection limits; pathway P3+P5->P6 -> P1 (catalog P5, conditional). [skeptic] acceptance signpost moved to struct-shm-inspection-credit; signpost is now validated POD curves. Skeptic's S2 High -> Medium rejected once the signpost grades method output (see debates).

struct-verified-fe-solvers.title: Finite-element solvers with machine-checked error bounds
struct-verified-fe-solvers.description: Structural and thermal finite-element solvers (linear statics, modal, steady conduction-radiation) whose discretization and floating-point errors carry proved bounds (guaranteed a posteriori estimators plus verified arithmetic), so an analysis result ships with a certificate.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.status_oct2026: Guaranteed error estimators exist for model problems (general); verified floating-point toolchains are emerging at flight-software scale (verification domain); nothing at production FE scale; Mathlib coverage of PDE and numerics is thin.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.why: Certification by analysis rests today on solver verification by benchmark plus test correlation. Proof-carrying error bounds remove the code- and solution-verification layer of NASA-STD-7009-style credibility, freeing scarce reviewers for model-form questions. tl-position-6: formal verification is the bridge to safety-critical use, here applied to numerics rather than flight code.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.strongest_case_small: Discretization error is rarely the dominant uncertainty in structures (joints, boundary conditions, damping and loads are); a certificate on the wrong model is worthless (the specification problem).
struct-verified-fe-solvers.signpost: An open or commercial FE code ships certified error bounds for linear statics or modal analysis with a formal proof artifact by 2029.
struct-verified-fe-solvers.revision_note: B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'Analyst position (b):' replaced with the KB position id tl-position-6.

struct-damage-tolerance-physics.title: Predictive damage and fatigue models for reusable structures
struct-damage-tolerance-physics.description: Validated physics-based models of crack growth and composite damage progression under the low-cycle, high-amplitude, cryogenic and thermal-cycling spectra of reusable stages and tanks, replacing conservative empirical scatter factors and knockdowns.
struct-damage-tolerance-physics.status_oct2026: No consensus predictive theory for composite failure (general); NASA NESC documented limits of linear elastic fracture mechanics for small cracks in COPV liners (2020); reusable vehicles rely on inspection, fleet-leader experience and conservative life factors (general).
struct-damage-tolerance-physics.why: Damage physics is multiscale and data-hungry. AI theory-building (S2, 2029) can propose closures quickly, but each must survive coupon-to-subcomponent test campaigns (months per load spectrum; cryogenic fatigue rigs are scarce). Autonomous labs (S3) compress coupon testing by about a year, not subcomponent and full-scale tests.
struct-damage-tolerance-physics.strongest_case_small: Operators already reach reuse by test-fix-fly and inspection, so better theory changes margins not feasibility; composite damage modeling has absorbed decades of expert effort without converging because material variability, not cognition, is the limit. Overlaps the materials domain.
struct-damage-tolerance-physics.signpost: A damage model predicts a blind fatigue or residual-strength test series within stated bounds (a successor to the blind-prediction exercise format) by 2029.

struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.title: Predictive two-phase cooling physics in microgravity
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.description: Validated mechanistic models of flow boiling, condensation, critical heat flux and flow-regime transitions in microgravity pumped loops and heat pipes, at the heat fluxes 100-250 kW compute satellites need.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.status_oct2026: Correlation-based. ISS flow boiling and condensation results published 2024-2025 (Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer); microgravity onset-of-boiling studies 2026. Two-phase pumped loops and oscillating heat pipes have flown, but not at AI1's heat flux, quantity or cost (33FG, Jun 2026).
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.why: Two-phase transport cuts heat-transport mass (33FG model: ~2.0 kg/kW for Starlink-like transport to ~0.8 kg/kW loop-based) and lets radiators run nearer chip temperature, which matters through T^4; below ~5 kg/m2, radiators rest on two-phase pumped loops or oscillating heat pipes not yet flown at this flux or quantity (33FG). Designers carry margins for microgravity uncertainty. Flight data bind: an ISS campaign yields hundreds of test points, while compute-satellite fleets will stream telemetry from ~2028-29, which S2 AI can turn into models; whoever owns the fleet owns the model. AI1's published radiator is a deployable liquid radiator, possibly single-phase, so its telemetry may not be two-phase data.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.strongest_case_small: Engineers design around uncertainty with margin and favorable-orientation ground tests; the margin penalty may be only ~10-20% of heat-transport mass; SpaceX will iterate hardware faster than theory matures.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.signpost: Operator telemetry from AI1 or Starcloud-class two-phase loops published or used in an open model; a microgravity critical-heat-flux model validated within about 15% by 2029.
struct-two-phase-microgravity-models.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): All three lenses: node was a dead end; soft edges added to struct-radiator-optimization and struct-radiator-lightweight-production. Advocate: soft edges from struct-highflux-radiator-flight (fleet telemetry) and to struct-fsp-radiator-qual (heat-pipe radiators). Skeptic: telemetry date ~2027-28 -> ~2028-29 (first-flight slip) and single-phase caveat. Advocate's S2 2030 -> 2029 rejected (zero lag behind cap-physics-theory S2 2029; first fleet data 2028-29 and possibly single-phase). Years and bands unchanged.

struct-deployment-mechanics.title: Predictive simulation of large deployable structures
struct-deployment-mechanics.description: Validated models of deployment for 50 m to km structures: frictional contact and latching, stored-strain composite booms, tape-spring snap-through, membrane wrinkling and thermally induced vibration, where today's simulations lean on ground tests that gravity corrupts at scale.
struct-deployment-mechanics.status_oct2026: ACS3 (launched Apr 2024) deployed an ~80 m2 sail on 7 m composite booms; NASA says current booms support sails up to 500 m2 and follow-on booms up to 2,000 m2. Hinge misalignment in over-constrained deployable panels for space solar power is still being quantified (JSME, 2026). Rigid-body Coulomb friction has known existence and uniqueness pathologies (Painleve paradox, general).
struct-deployment-mechanics.why: At 100 m and beyond, gravity-offload rigs stop being representative, so qualification must be by analysis plus subscale and flight data, which requires models with understood error. AI supplies the math (nonsmooth dynamics, similitude scaling laws, tension-field wrinkling theory) quickly under S2, but validation needs flight deployments. Compute satellites will add many: each Starmind satellite deploys arrays on a ~75 m wingspan (up to 1,500 m2 of solar under the Sep 2026 filing), by the hundreds a year from ~2029, a far larger large-deployable dataset than today's few flights a year, though it covers the 50-100 m class rather than km scale and belongs to the operator.
struct-deployment-mechanics.strongest_case_small: Most deployment failures are workmanship and mechanism problems (snags, stiction, harness routing) that no model predicts; programs mitigate with simplicity and redundancy, not prediction.
struct-deployment-mechanics.signpost: A 500 m2-plus deployable flies with pre-flight predicted deployment shape and loads matched within stated bounds; NASA flies its follow-on boom technology.
struct-deployment-mechanics.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Advocate: soft edge from struct-highflux-radiator-flight (compute-satellite array deployments as flight data) and why updated. Advocate's S2 2030 -> 2029 rejected: zero lag behind cap-physics-theory (S2 2029), Starmind deployments at volume only from ~2029, and km-scale extrapolation remains. Years and bands unchanged.

struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.title: AI agents run and check structural and thermal analysis
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.description: AI agents set up, run, check and document finite-element stress, loads, buckling and thermal analyses end to end (meshing, boundary conditions, margins of safety, thermal-model correlation to thermal-vacuum data, coupled-loads cycles), with an engineer signing off.
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.status_oct2026: Research prototypes in 2026: LLM agents driving commercial FE codes through MCP (arXiv Sep 2026), multi-agent end-to-end FEA for solid mechanics (arXiv May 2026), PDE-Agents (arXiv Jun 2026). No public flight-program use (general).
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.why: tl-position-4: most engineering math is bespoke and easier than the catalog. The bulk of structures and thermal effort is setup, checking and correlation by scarce senior analysts: solved in principle, expert-scarce. Under S2 an analysis cycle costs several times less; a thermal-model correlation that takes weeks after a test could take days (assumption).
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.strongest_case_small: Analysis labor is a minority of program cost; export-control and data-access rules slow adoption at primes; accountability keeps human sign-off time roughly constant.
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.signpost: A NASA center, prime or new-space firm says AI agents produce flight-program stress or thermal analysis reports with human sign-off, by 2027-28.
struct-agentic-analysis-workflows.revision_note: B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): lettered citation 'Analyst position (a):' replaced with the KB position id tl-position-4.

struct-shell-knockdown-rules.title: Lighter buckling design rules for tanks and interstages
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.description: Probabilistic or mechanistic knockdown factors tied to measured imperfection statistics, beyond NASA SP-8007-2020's deterministic analysis-based approach, become routine agency and industry practice for cylinders and cones, including composite shells where a blanket 0.65 is still common.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.status_oct2026: NASA SP-8007-2020/REV 2 (Dec 2020, NESC) already updates the 1965/1968 monograph with semi-empirical and analysis-based design approaches (Secs. 4.2-4.3) and records analysis-based design buckling loads for the Shuttle SRB cases and External Tank and the SLS core stage; it is a design guideline, not a requirement. NASA SBKF developed and test-validated analysis-based knockdown approaches on 8-ft metallic and composite cylinders (2010s-2022); a NASA review warns the universal 0.65 composite factor can be unconservative; Wagner et al. (2025) report weight savings above 14% and up to 31% in optimized configurations with a mechanistic design curve. Probabilistic knockdowns tied to measured imperfection statistics are not yet standard practice.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.why: For unstiffened isotropic cylinders SP-8007 gives knockdowns of about 0.22-0.47 (R/t 1000-200), and buckling-critical wall thickness scales as KDF^-1/2, so raising a knockdown from 0.32 to 0.60 cuts that wall mass about 27%. 0.65 is SP-8007's recommended factor for moderately or heavily stiffened cylinders, whose load does not scale as t^2. Stiffened, sandwich and optimized shells see 14-31% with a mechanistic design curve (Wagner et al. 2025). Rules tied to measured imperfection statistics come from Monte Carlo on factory data plus certified margins; a worst-case imperfection theorem helps but is not required, since the analysis-based revision already happened without one. Standards and handbook revision (SP-8007, ECSS buckling handbook) and validation tests on representative shells bind, so the band is capped at Medium.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.strongest_case_small: Buckling-critical structures (interstages, intertanks, unpressurized barrels, adapters) are a minority of dry mass; new-space firms test to failure and do not follow SP-8007 strictly; a kilogram saved on a booster buys only ~0.1-0.2 kg of payload (general).
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.signpost: A NASA SP-8007 or ECSS buckling-handbook revision adopting regime-aware or probabilistic knockdowns, or a launch-vehicle program citing them, by 2029.
struct-shell-knockdown-rules.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Fact fix: SP-8007-2020/REV 2 already replaced the 1960s-only approach and analysis-based loads were used on SRB, ET and SLS core stage (text checked by resolver in the NTRS full text); description re-scoped to probabilistic knockdowns beyond it; scaling example corrected (0.65 is the stiffened-cylinder factor; unstiffened 0.22-0.47; 0.32 -> 0.60 cuts ~27%). [skeptic] struct-worst-imperfection-theory hard -> soft. Years and bands unchanged.

struct-launch-env-margins.title: Tighter launch vibration and acoustic environments
struct-launch-env-margins.description: Component and spacecraft random-vibration, acoustic and shock test levels set with a reduced qualification margin over a model-predicted maximum predicted environment (MPE), from error-bounded predictions calibrated on early flight data, for new vehicles where flight data are sparse; published by a launch provider or disclosed by a vertically integrated provider-customer for its own payloads.
struct-launch-env-margins.status_oct2026: Maximum predicted environments are already statistical (P95/50 normal tolerance limits per NASA-HDBK-7005, general), and qualification adds about +3 dB (GEVS) to +6 dB (launch-vehicle units) over the acceptance or MPE level (general). Environments are enveloped flight data plus fixed qualification margins (for example qualification at acceptance +3 dB, general); NESC's NTRC methods cut coupled-loads cost (2023-2024); each coupled-loads cycle with a launch provider takes weeks (general).
struct-launch-env-margins.why: Random vibration sizes brackets, secondary structure and electronics boxes; a 3 dB margin doubles the test PSD (about 1.4x g-rms). Stating environments as exceedance probabilities is already practice, and for high-cadence vehicles empirical P95/50 envelopes from abundant flight data do the job without predictive models, so the AI-attributable gain is on new vehicles with sparse data, where calibrated predictions could justify a smaller margin. Forcing uncertainty dominates structural model error, so mid-frequency structural fidelity accelerates rather than gates. Launch-provider user guides and agency test standards gate adoption, so Medium is the cap; S2 Low because providers have little incentive to tighten published environments and a vertically integrated provider (SpaceX launches about three quarters of its own mass to orbit) rarely discloses its own.
struct-launch-env-margins.strongest_case_small: Launch providers have little incentive to tighten published environments; forcing uncertainty dominates; savings fall on small parts and test-failure rates rather than vehicle mass.
struct-launch-env-margins.signpost: A launch provider publishes environments derived from flight-calibrated predictive models with stated exceedance probability and a reduced qualification margin, or a vertically integrated provider discloses such environments for its own payloads.
struct-launch-env-margins.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic] Fact: MPEs are already P95/50 statistical; description narrowed to reduced margins over model-predicted MPEs for new vehicles; struct-midfreq-vibroacoustics hard -> soft; S2 Medium -> Low (S3 Medium kept). [advocate] description and signpost add the vertically integrated provider-customer route; advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 rejected because abundant flight data make predictive models unnecessary for the high-cadence provider the argument relies on (see debates).

struct-radiator-optimization.title: AI-optimized radiators and heat transport
struct-radiator-optimization.description: Coupled conduction-radiation-two-phase design optimization (panel topology, heat-pipe and loop layout, cold plates and heat spreading, view factors to Earth and arrays, micrometeoroid segmentation, deployment structure) that cuts thermal-subsystem mass and the chip-to-radiator temperature drop at fixed hardware technology.
struct-radiator-optimization.status_oct2026: 33FG model: Starlink V3-like thermal ~19.4 kg/kW at 310 K; StarThink V2 ~3.0-3.4 kg/kW at 370 K with 2.5 kg/m2 two-sided panels; proven radiators run 2.5-5 kg/m2, and values below ~5 rest on two-phase hardware not yet flown at this scale. AI1 June 2026 spec: 110 m2 deployable liquid radiator (~3.7 kg/m2 implied by 33FG's ~410 kg radiator allocation); ~1,400 W/m2 (two-sided, per m2 of planform) is Musk's stated figure, not the spec sheet. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response caps the 250 kW-peak design below 200 m2 of radiator; 33FG's Oct 6 model needs ~134 C GPU logic and ~132 C HBM at 200 m2, or ~327 m2 to hold 105 / 95 C, unless heat spreading improves.
struct-radiator-optimization.why: The design space is large but well-posed (T^4 nonlinearity, view-factor coupling, MMOD puncture probability): expert-scarce, ideal for on-demand AI. At 765-1,400 W/m2 (from 33FG's Oct 2026 model holding HBM at 95 C up to Musk's June figure), a GW of waste heat needs ~0.7-1.3 km2 of panel, and each 1 kg/m2 of areal density is ~700-1,300 t per GW. If AI design cuts thermal mass 10-25% beyond SpaceX's own conventionally optimized second iteration (assumption; the AI-attributable increment may be nearer 5-15%), the saving is ~350-1,400 t per GW (~4-14 Starship flights at 100 t), ~2-9% of the ~16,000-18,000 t launched per GW. In cost terms, thermal is the largest single $/GW sensitivity in Mach33's orbital-data-center model (+/-30% thermal -> +/-8.9% $/GW), so a 10-25% cut is ~3-7% of $/GW, about 0.3-0.6 year on Mach33's base cost curve, which falls ~12% a year in 2028-31 (a single commercial forecaster's model). The biggest design lever is the chip-to-radiator temperature drop under the HBM limit: at the ~250 kW target, cold-plate and heat-spreading design set chip and HBM temperature and therefore chip life (33FG reference: 5.6 -> 3.4 years), so the gain shows up as service life and sustained draw as much as mass; how hot the chips may run is decided by qualification (struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification).
struct-radiator-optimization.strongest_case_small: Radiator physics is simple and SpaceX and Starcloud already optimize it with conventional tools; manufacturing cost per m2 at Starlink volume and chip-temperature limits matter more than design insight (33FG: thermal is not a physics blocker).
struct-radiator-optimization.signpost: A flown compute satellite discloses radiator areal density below 3 kg/m2; Starmind telemetry shows ~1,250-1,400 W/m2 sustained at stated chip and HBM temperatures.
struct-radiator-optimization.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic + auditor: prerequisites cap-applied-math and cap-research-math-public replaced by cap-design-optimization (same years; this is a multiphysics design tool); gate fabrication -> adoption; the 2.5 kg/m2 target moved out of the description (it belongs to struct-radiator-lightweight-production). Skeptic: radiator flux 1,400 -> 765-1,400 W/m2 per the Oct 2026 33FG model and counterfactual set to SpaceX's own second iteration. Auditor: arithmetic fixed (2.5-6% was 2.5-9%; now ~2-9% on the revised mass per GW); 1,400 W/m2 attributed to Musk; chip-life channel added. Advocate: $/GW framing (Mach33 thermal sensitivity, verified) added; soft edges from struct-agentic-analysis-workflows, struct-two-phase-microgravity-models (all three lenses) and the new hot-chip node. Years and bands unchanged.

struct-cert-by-analysis.title: Qualification by analysis replaces some structural tests
struct-cert-by-analysis.description: Agencies (NASA, ESA, Space Force) accept AI-produced, uncertainty-quantified analysis in place of a strength qualification test beyond what NASA-STD-5001B already allows: for composite or bonded primary structure, or for metallic structure at tested-hardware factors of safety instead of the larger no-test factors. Derivative structure with correlated heritage test data comes first.
struct-cert-by-analysis.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009 provides a credibility framework. NASA-STD-5001B (Change 3, Oct 2022) already allows prototype or protoflight strength testing and, for metallic structures only, an analysis-alone (no-test) option with an engineering rationale and Technical Authority approval, generally at larger factors of safety; its example criteria include similarity to a test-verified predecessor with good test-analysis correlation (FSR 15-16, Sec. 4.1.2.3). It allows probabilistic criteria case by case (FSR 17). Composite, bonded and most new primary structure are still strength-tested (general).
struct-cert-by-analysis.why: A dedicated qualification article for launch-vehicle primary structure costs tens of millions of dollars and up to a year (general); a spacecraft unit's qualification model costs far less. The institutional route already exists for metals at a mass penalty, so what is new is credit at standard factors and for composites. It rests on certified UQ, AI-run test correlation and correlated heritage test data (5001B's no-test criteria lean on similarity and test-analysis correlation, hence the hard edge from struct-test-data-commons). Proof-carrying solver bounds help but do not gate, because discretization error is rarely the dominant uncertainty (struct-verified-fe-solvers). Chain (S2): credibility directive 2029 -> first use at a program's test-plan milestone 2030. Needs agency acceptance, so capped at Medium; S2 Low because the re-scoped step is harder than today's allowances and has one or two years of window after the rulebook (judgment, not a computed probability).
struct-cert-by-analysis.strongest_case_small: Test failures routinely expose what analysis missed (joints, workmanship); no agency will drop tests on first-of-kind primary structure; savings concentrate on derivatives.
struct-cert-by-analysis.signpost: A NASA, ESA or Space Force program grants model-based qualification credit, citing AI-produced analysis, in place of a planned strength test for composite or bonded primary structure, or for metallic structure at tested-hardware factors, by 2030-31.
struct-cert-by-analysis.revision_note: B-certification: [skeptic+auditor] Fact fix: the status said tests are mandatory for primary-structure qualification; NASA-STD-5001B Change 3 Sec. 4.1.2.3 (FSR 15-16) already allows metallic no-test verification and FSR 17 allows probabilistic criteria (text checked by resolver). Description and signpost re-scoped to credit beyond those allowances (otherwise the node is met today with no AI attribution). [skeptic+advocate] struct-verified-fe-solvers hard -> soft. [skeptic] struct-test-data-commons added as hard prerequisite (5001B no-test criteria require similarity and correlation evidence). [skeptic] S2 band Medium -> Low because the re-scoped event is strictly harder; skeptic's year slip (S2 2031, S3 2030) not taken because the credibility standard stays at S2 2029; advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 rejected (depended on a 2028 rulebook).

struct-fsp-next-gen-design.title: Second-generation fission power designs
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.description: AI multiphysics optimization of reactor, shield, Brayton converter, radiator and lander integration for follow-on fission systems (lower kg/kWe at 100 kWe-plus, Mars or nuclear-electric variants) after the first unit's design is frozen.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.status_oct2026: NASA directive (Jul 31 2025): at least 100 kWe, closed Brayton cycle, heavy lander with up to 15 t available, launch-ready by Q1 FY2030, awards to two providers within six months of the RFP; reactor under ~6 t (New Space Economy, Apr 2026). The final RFP was never issued: NASA made the draft Space Act Agreement path inactive on Mar 26 2026 and tied Lunar Reactor-1 to SR-1 experience. NASA spent over $200M since 2000 on 1-200 kWe concepts without flight readiness (directive).
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.why: A timing trap: first-of-a-kind systems freeze their designs (PDR not before ~2028, no provider yet) before AI multiphysics design capability matures (S2 ~2029), so AI-math gains land in second units, and a second-generation study presupposes a first unit under contract and frozen. Shield design rests on radiation transport, which the release does not touch; AI applied math helps there only under S2.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.strongest_case_small: Space nuclear power is bounded by fuel supply, launch approval, nuclear ground testing and budgets, not design insight; a second-generation program may not be funded before the first unit operates.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.signpost: NASA restarts the LR-1 procurement, awards providers and announces a follow-on (Mars-class or 200 kWe-plus) design study, ideally naming AI-assisted multidisciplinary optimization.
struct-fsp-next-gen-design.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor: status corrected (final RFP never issued; Mar 26 2026 reset); PDR ~2027 -> not before ~2028; bands S1 Low -> Speculative, S2/S3 Medium -> Low. Years unchanged.

struct-flown-lighter-structure.title: First flight structure sized with AI-certified margins
struct-flown-lighter-structure.description: A launch-vehicle barrel, interstage or large spacecraft primary structure flies after being sized with AI-derived knockdowns tied to measured imperfection statistics and certified uncertainty margins, beyond SP-8007-2020's analysis-based approach, at 10-30% lower mass for its buckling-critical parts. Commercial builders need no standards revision to do this.
struct-flown-lighter-structure.status_oct2026: No such flight attributed to AI-derived design rules. Human analysis-based design buckling loads were already used for the Shuttle SRB cases and External Tank and for the SLS core stage (first flown Nov 2022), per SP-8007-2020; new-space firms rely on test-to-failure (general).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.why: Chain (S2): worst-case imperfection theory and certified margins (2028) -> in-house design rule 2029 -> build and validation test of a primary-structure flight article (2-3 years for a new launch-vehicle subsystem, lag ladder) -> flight 2031. A standards revision (struct-shell-knockdown-rules) accelerates but does not gate, because commercial builders are not bound by SP-8007 or ECSS handbooks and the FAA does not certify structure. S3 gains little because the build-and-test cycle binds; its 1.3-1.5x physical speed keeps 2031 but raises the odds to Medium. Since human analysis-based knockdowns have already flown, the AI-attributable step is a further margin cut on a minority of dry mass. Vehicle-level payoff is modest: ~1-3% payload on an upper-stage-limited vehicle (analyst estimate).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.strongest_case_small: Attribution is nearly impossible because companies already push margins via test; vehicle-level mass savings of 1-3% are within normal design-iteration noise.
struct-flown-lighter-structure.signpost: A launch or spacecraft program publicly states that a flown structure was sized with AI-derived probabilistic or mechanistic knockdowns (by 2031).
struct-flown-lighter-structure.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder: primary structure. A launch-vehicle barrel, interstage or primary structure designed on 2028-29 AI capability flies 2031+ in S2 (new LV subsystem 2-3 years). Chain (S2): imperfection theory 2028 -> knockdown rules 2029 -> flight-article build and validation test 2-3 years -> flight 2031. S2 2030 -> 2031 (Medium -> Low); S3 2030 -> 2031 (1.3-1.5x physical speed still lands 2030-31; Medium kept); S1 unchanged. A4: Why text updated to match the A3 years and bands; it had still described the v0 values. A3's conditional sentence is kept.
struct-flown-lighter-structure.revision_note: B-certification: [advocate+auditor] struct-shell-knockdown-rules hard -> soft; struct-worst-imperfection-theory and struct-certified-uq-margins added as hard prerequisites (a flown commercial structure needs no standards revision). [skeptic] description re-scoped beyond SP-8007-2020; status records the human analysis-based SRB/ET/SLS precedent. [auditor] signpost date 2030 -> 2031 to match the S2 year. Advocate's S2 2030/Medium and skeptic's S3 Medium -> Low both rejected; years and bands unchanged (see debates).

struct-shm-inspection-credit.title: Sensor-based inspection credit for reusable stages
struct-shm-inspection-credit.description: Built-in structural health monitoring with quantified probability of detection replaces scheduled teardown or scanning inspection for defined zones of reusable stages or tanks between flights.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.status_oct2026: Demonstrated on specimens and subscale composite cryotanks (ONERA, 2026); an SHM payload for in-flight re-certification was prepared for ISS exposure (SPIE, Apr 2026); no launch vehicle uses SHM as formal inspection credit (general).
struct-shm-inspection-credit.why: Inspection is a large part of reuse cost: non-destructive testing of large structures is slow and access-limited (ONERA, 2026). Proven detection limits plus certified margins let operators set inspection intervals from data. Sensor qualification under thermal-cryogenic aging binds, which no amount of cognition compresses. Chain (S2): applied math public 2027 -> proven damage-detection limits and certified structural margins (2028) -> sensor systems qualified under thermal-cryogenic aging 2029 -> an operator sets inspection intervals from sensor data on a reusable stage 2030 (Medium; no regulator needed for an operator carrying its own risk).
struct-shm-inspection-credit.strongest_case_small: Commercial operators set their own regimes and may find visual and borescope inspection plus fleet leaders cheap enough; sensor reliability, not math, limits SHM.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.signpost: An operator or NASA program announces SHM-based inspection credit for a reusable stage or tank (POD curves accepted in place of a scheduled NDE inspection) by 2030.
struct-shm-inspection-credit.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder. Built-in SHM on a reusable stage is a new launch-vehicle subsystem (2-3 years from design-complete to flight, 1.5-2 years at S3 speed) and its own why says sensor qualification under thermal-cryogenic aging binds. Chain (S2): detection limits and certified margins 2028 -> sensor network design and qualification -> inspection credit on flying stages 2030. S1 2031 -> >2031, S2 2029 -> 2030, S3 2029 -> 2030; bands unchanged.

Advocate's S2/S3 2030 -> 2029 rejected: the A3 lag ladder (new launch-vehicle subsystem 2-3 years; sensor aging qualification binds) still holds for commercial operators (see debates).

struct-highflux-radiator-flight.title: 100-kW-class deployable radiators fly on compute satellites
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.description: First flights of deployable liquid or two-phase radiators rejecting 100-250 kW per spacecraft (SpaceX Starmind: the June 2026 AI1 spec had 110 m2 at Musk's ~1,400 W/m2 for 150 kW; the Aug-Sep 2026 revision runs 175 kW average / 250 kW peak inside a filed radiator envelope under 200 m2, i.e. at least ~1,250 W/m2 at 250 kW unless the envelope grows; Starcloud-3, ~200 kW), on the physical clock and largely independent of AI mathematics.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.status_oct2026: June 2026 AI1 spec (150 kW peak, 120 kW average, 110 m2 radiator, 70 kW/t target, 70 m wingspan) superseded. SpaceX product page (Aug 2026): 175 kW average / 250 kW peak on a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72, 75 m wingspan. SpaceX FCC response (Sep 16 2026): under 4,000 kg, under 200 m2 radiator, under 1,500 m2 solar. Musk (Oct 1 2026): cautiously optimistic of ~250 kW average via Nvidia co-design. 33FG Oct 6 model: 250 kW in 200 m2 implies ~134 C logic / ~132 C HBM (with a higher-rated GPU package); holding 105 / 95 C needs ~327 m2. SpaceX targets first Starmind launches in Q4 2027 (Musk, Aug 25 2026); the design is not frozen. Starcloud-1 ran an H100 in orbit from Nov 2025; Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship; Starship reached orbit Sep 28 2026 deploying 26 Starlink V3.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.why: Anchor node for the orbital-compute chain: the hardware arrives regardless, sized with conventional tools. 33FG's June reconstruction puts AI1's thermal system (June spec) at ~532 kg of 2.1 t (25%) and notes that below ~5 kg/m2 it relies on two-phase hardware SpaceX does not yet build in-house; the October reference satellite is ~4.0-4.5 t. Between June and October 2026 the power point moved twice and the radiator envelope grew from 110 to up to 200 m2, with thermal closure (HBM temperature) still open. With design-complete at best ~Q1 2027, a 12-18 month lag from design-complete to flight for a derivative payload (physclock lag ladder) and announced SpaceX schedules running 1.5-3x long, first flight lands in 2028 in every scenario. AI-math effects enter on the second iteration.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.strongest_case_small: This node is the counterfactual baseline: everything here happens without any AI mathematics.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.signpost: First Starmind launch (Q4 2027 target) with published thermal telemetry: sustained ~1,250-1,400 W/m2 of planform, GPU and HBM temperatures.
struct-highflux-radiator-flight.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Auditor + advocate + skeptic: status and description updated from the superseded June AI1 spec to the Aug 2026 product page, Sep 16 2026 FCC envelope and Oct 2026 statements; 'launch date not published' corrected (SpaceX targets Q4 2027). Skeptic: years 2027 -> 2028 in all scenarios (design not frozen, 12-18 month lag ladder, 1.5-3x slip calibration; same practice the trunk resolver applied to launch-clock nodes). Advocate's reliance on a Q4 2027 first flight rejected on that calibration. Bands High unchanged. New soft edges out to two-phase, deployment and sail nodes (fleet data and deployable supply base).

struct-radiator-lightweight-production.title: Ultralight radiators in serial production
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.description: Two-phase or oscillating-heat-pipe deployable radiators at or below 2.5 kg/m2 planform, running at ~370 K chip temperature, built at Starlink-like volume (thousands of m2 per month).
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.status_oct2026: Lab and prototype panels reach ~1.9-3.9 kg/m2 (33FG survey of NASA and industry prototypes); commercial deployables ~3.5-4.9 kg/m2 (Redwire Q-Rad per 33FG); none in mass production at this areal density (general).
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.pathway: P7 (manufacturing; AI design and two-phase models accelerate via P1)
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.why: Going from ~3.7 kg/m2 (AI1 implied) to 2.5 kg/m2 saves ~850 t of radiator per GW at 1,400 W/m2 (~1,550 t at ~765 W/m2), ~9-16 Starship flights at 100 t. Prototypes already reach ~1.9-3.9 kg/m2 without AI design, so serial production is a manufacturing and insourcing problem; AI design (2028 in S2) and validated two-phase models shorten iteration but are not prerequisites. The manufacturing ramp and qualification bind, so S2 and S3 tie at 2030 (first flight of the new panel in 2029, then the production ramp). Economic pull is modest: 33FG finds the radiator is the subsystem with room to spare (each kg/m2 off the ~600 m2 solar array buys ~6x what the same cut buys on the radiator), and the October design is short of radiator area, not areal density. S3's AI-run factories speed a ramp but do not create demand for it.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.strongest_case_small: The gain rides on manufacturing learning curves and supplier insourcing, where AI mathematics plays a small role; 70 kW/t may already be economic without it.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.signpost: SpaceX insources two-phase radiator production (33FG expects within a few years of first purchase) and discloses areal density for a Starmind version.
struct-radiator-lightweight-production.calibration_note: A3: Lag ladder. Serial production at thousands of m2 per month comes after first flight of the new panel, which itself takes 12-18 months from the 2028 design (production ramp compresses only 0.9x in S2, 0.7-0.8x in S3). Chain (S2): AI-optimized radiator design 2028 -> first flight mid-2029 to 2030 -> serial production 2030. S1 2031 -> >2031 (Medium -> Low; S1 design lands 2030), S2 2029 -> 2030, S3 2029 -> 2030; S2/S3 bands unchanged. A4: Why text updated to match the A3 years and bands; it had still described the v0 values. A3's conditional sentence is kept.
