Skeptic: RCC-319 revision dropped as a pre-2031 signpost. Advocate (mechanism checked against 14 CFR 450.35, which lists 450.145(b) but not 450.141): hard edge from infra-tool-qualification made soft and hard edge from verif-code-proof-agents added; advocate's S2 2030 -> 2029 and S3 2029 -> 2028 rejected because the flight safety system still needs an FAA-accepted means of compliance and no lens other than the advocate saw a 2029 incentive. Years unchanged.

verif-assurance-cost-collapse.title: Verified flight code 15-120x cheaper per line
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.description: The cost per functionally verified line (seL4-class full functional proof) falls from about $300-600 to roughly $5-20 under S2, a 15-120x fall (central about 35-40x), because spec review dominates what remains and compute costs cents per line. Turnaround to re-verify a small change drops from weeks to days. Program-level savings, which physical integration testing caps at about 2x, are tracked in astro-gnc-assurance-cost.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.status_oct2026: Baseline: DO-178 certification runs about $25-100 per line (Level A at the top of the range); verification can reach 80% of a DO-178B Level A project, and effective productivity is under 10 lines per person-day (Coverity/Black Duck whitepaper). seL4-class full functional proof costs roughly $300-600 per line (general, derived from about 25 person-years, including design and implementation, for 8.7 KLOC). Early evidence on unit cost: AI agents wrote an Ada/SPARK security stack whose 49,280 proof obligations GNATprove discharged at a claimed 20-40x lower supervision cost than hand verification (arXiv 2607.14340, Jul 2026 preprint; security software, not a flight program).
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.why: Per-line cost model (general, our assumptions; verification-domain cost table, values 'by 2029'): proof labor, the dominant cost of seL4-class verification, becomes agent compute, and the residual is human spec review and accountability. Under S1 the per-line cost falls to about $50-150 (2-12x); under S3 to about $1-5. Chain (S2): proof agents, spec drafting and FDIR model checking 2027 -> adoption on uncrewed programs that need no certification credit 2028 -> vendor or program case studies showing more than 50% fewer verification hours 2028-29. The per-line effect is measured on code, not on certified programs, so it needs no regulator; S2 returns to High now that the program-level claim, which waited on certification credit (A3), has moved to astro-gnc-assurance-cost. S3 equals S2 through 2028, so S3 is 2028, not 2027. The larger effect is assurance level per dollar and change turnaround.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.strongest_case_small: Software is a modest share of mission cost and schedule. HIL rigs, environmental testing and integration remain physical and set program pace.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.signpost: Program cost reports or vendor case studies showing more than 50% reduction in verification hours on a safety-critical flight program.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.calibration_note: A3: Tier-7 rule: the 30-100x cost of a verified line follows directly from S2, but the programme-level "about 2.4x cheaper" claim needs programmes to adopt and finish, and any certified programme waits for first certification credit (S2 2030). S2 High -> Medium; S3 High kept.
verif-assurance-cost-collapse.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: All three lenses: program-level '2.4x certified program' claim and its cost model moved to astro-gnc-assurance-cost; node rescoped to per-line cost. Skeptic: arithmetic corrected ($300-600 -> $5-20 is 15-120x, not 30-100x). Skeptic + auditor: S3 2027 -> 2028 (S3 equals S2 until 2028). Auditor + advocate: S2 band Medium -> High, since A3's downgrade applied only to the certified-program claim that moved out. Skeptic's S2 2028 -> 2029 rejected: the domain table's '2029' is a 'by' date, two lenses keep 2028, and 2026 SPARK evidence already shows 20-40x supervision savings. Auditor: status cost figures scoped to their source.

verif-new-entrant-advantage.title: Assurance stops being a moat for primes
verif-new-entrant-advantage.description: Small teams (lander and constellation startups) reach assurance levels that once required large verification departments, on uncrewed commercial and government work that needs no certification credit. Primes' advantage shifts from process capacity to certification relationships, which still matter for crewed and certified work, while qualified-checker vendors and AI-model providers capture new value.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.status_oct2026: Primes hold certification know-how and large V&V departments. New entrants run small teams and account for most recent software-caused lander losses and near-losses (Beresheet and Hakuto-R M1 lost; IM-1 landed but tipped over after a configuration and patch error).
verif-new-entrant-advantage.why: Uncrewed commercial missions have no certifying regulator for mission software, so new entrants can adopt as soon as the tools work, while primes on cost-plus contracts have weaker incentives to cut verification hours. Value concentrates where trust is scarce: in the small set of qualified checkers (AdaCore, AbsInt, TrustInSoft and similar) and in access to frontier models. Chain (S2): per-line cost collapse 2028 -> new entrants bid formal assurance as a discriminator 2028-29 -> a NASA, ESA or defense award citing it 2030; procurement runs 1-2 years from RFP to award, and politics and appropriations do not compress. Certification credit accelerates the effect on certified work but does not gate it.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.strongest_case_small: Primes adopt the same tools quickly (Airbus led formal methods in avionics) and keep the regulator relationships. Value may accrue to AI labs and checker vendors rather than to either group of space companies.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.signpost: A new entrant winning a NASA, ESA or defense contract with formal assurance as a cited discriminator; a prime reorganizing its V&V department around spec engineering.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.calibration_note: A1: its hard prerequisite verif-checker-not-generator was merged into infra-tool-qualification (>2031/2030/2029, the scenario premise for regulator credit), so the moat cannot fall before certification credit for AI proofs exists. Superseded by B-verified-autonomy: the hard edge from infra-tool-qualification is now soft, because the node is rescoped to work that needs no certification credit; years kept on a procurement-lag chain.
verif-new-entrant-advantage.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic (alternative) + advocate: hard edge from infra-tool-qualification made soft and scope limited to work that needs no certification credit, since the node's own why says uncrewed work has no certifying regulator. Years and bands kept: skeptic's S2 2031/S3 2030/S2 Low depended on the zero lag after credit, which no longer applies, and advocate's S2 2029/S3 2028 ignores the 1-2-year procurement lag (politics 1.0x). Auditor: IM-1 is a near-loss, not a loss.

verif-mission-loss-rate.title: Fewer missions lost to software logic (hard to see by 2031)
verif-mission-loss-rate.description: The share of mission losses caused by software logic, configuration and fault-management errors falls measurably.
verif-mission-loss-rate.status_oct2026: Of the 12 notable losses and near-losses in our failure table (1996-2025), 9 were primarily or partly software, logic or configuration errors. Of the six commercial lunar missions in the table since 2019, three losses (Peregrine, Resilience, Athena) were primarily hardware or sensor physics. The table lists failures only. Successes in the same period include Chandrayaan-3 (2023), SLIM (2024, landed on its nose) and Blue Ghost M1 (Mar 2025), and agency losses with logic or GNC causes include Chandrayaan-2's Vikram (2019) and Luna-25 (2023) (general).
verif-mission-loss-rate.why: Even if verified software works as intended, only a few dozen lander and RPO flights will occur by 2031, too few to separate a lower software-caused loss rate from noise. Three of the six commercial lunar missions in the failure table (2019-25) had software- or logic-related causes (with Blue Ghost M1 added, p0 is about 0.4-0.5). With zero software failures in n verified landings the one-sided p is about 0.6^n, so at least 6 verified landings are needed for p < 0.05. S2 gives a first verified lander in 2029 and perhaps 2-5 by 2031, confounded by non-AI learning (Blue Ghost M1 succeeded without proofs), so S2 is Speculative, the P7 default; S3 stays Low. All 9 software-related cases in the table were assumption, spec or process misses, so the outcome also hinges on validated environment assumptions (verif-environment-assumption-models, now a hard prerequisite), not only on proof flights. Hardware and sensor failures keep the total loss rate high.
verif-mission-loss-rate.strongest_case_small: With cheap proofs, teams may ship more ambitious autonomy faster, keeping the loss rate flat while capability rises (risk homeostasis, general).
verif-mission-loss-rate.signpost: Root-cause reports of 2027-2030 lander or RPO failures: a shift from logic and configuration causes toward hardware and sensor causes would support the chain.
verif-mission-loss-rate.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: Skeptic + auditor: S2 band Low -> Speculative (P7 default; at least 6 verified landings needed to see the effect). Auditor's S3 Low -> Speculative and S3 2031 -> >2031 rejected to keep a scenario spread: S3 adds lander flights and near-free cognition from 2029, which makes Low (10-30%) defensible. Skeptic: hard edge from verif-environment-assumption-models added (the direct edge from verif-assumption-falsification is omitted because it already sits upstream through the lander node). Auditor: success denominator added.

capability-random-sample-audit.title: Published error rate for openai/math results
capability-random-sample-audit.description: An independent expert team audits a random sample of 30 or more openai/math families (formalized and unformalized), checking statements against manuscripts and proofs or Comparator runs, and publishes an error and scope-gap rate. This turns the catalog-wide trust level from an assumption into a measured number.
capability-random-sample-audit.status_oct2026: Not yet. The only audit of an earlier OpenAI release covered ten results (arXiv 2608.14673); the first outside Comparator run (Kingy AI, Oct 6, 2026) covered three targets with no statement audit and found the Pi Exponent formal statement omits a manuscript consequence. Hexagon (beta, launched Oct 6, 2026; Buzzard on its advisory board) and AGMAI (guidelines Sep 29, 2026) supply venues and norms but hold no OpenAI deposits.
capability-random-sample-audit.pathway: P2/P3 (verification of the premise base, not certified use)
capability-random-sample-audit.premise_tier: n/a (measures the trust tier of the T1 and T3 catalog families)
capability-random-sample-audit.why: A measured error and scope-gap rate decides whether the 245 unformalized families (T1) stay 'conditional' in every downstream node and calibrates capability-cheap-trust; statement gaps are already visible in the first outside run. It is a human-bandwidth task (a few expert-days per family, general), so its year does not depend on the scenario; AI-assisted checking in S2 and S3 makes it cheaper, not earlier. Band above the P2 default because this is a research audit, not certified use.
capability-random-sample-audit.strongest_case_small: Experts may prefer headline families or their own research; a sample of 30 across many fields needs dozens of specialists; a low error rate on lab-chosen, mostly discrete problems says little about engineering statements.
capability-random-sample-audit.signpost: A published random-sample audit of 30 or more openai/math families (Hexagon, AGMAI, Epoch or an academic group) reporting proof-error and statement-gap rates.
capability-random-sample-audit.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the auditor (proposed as verif-random-sample-audit; renamed to the trunk's domain prefix). Mechanism sound and not a duplicate: verif-independent-check covers headline families only; the random-sample signpost existed only as text in cap-research-math-internal.

capability-compute-launch-demand.title: AI compute becomes Starship's second anchor customer
capability-compute-launch-demand.description: Orbital-compute satellites (SpaceX Starmind AI1 and peers) fill at least 10 Starship flights in one calendar year, so Starship cadence and production learning depend on AI compute demand as well as Starlink. This couples the launch clock to the AI capability curve through demand, not through mathematics.
capability-compute-launch-demand.status_oct2026: Not yet. SpaceX disclosed AI1's first specification in Jun 2026 (150 kW peak; about 2.1 t per Mach33's reconstruction; modular, interchangeable chip inserts), then raised it on its Aug 2026 product page to 175 kW average / 250 kW peak; its Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds each satellite under 4,000 kg, and 33FG's Oct 2026 reference satellite is about 4.0-4.5 t and partnered with Nvidia on its compute payload (Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs; SpaceX, Aug 4 2026, via 33FG). Mach33 reports the power target rising to about 250 kW by Oct 2026 and calls space datacenters the largest uncertainty in its Starship launch-revenue model (Sep 2026). 100-kW-class radiators first fly in 2028 in every scenario (struct-highflux-radiator-flight; SpaceX targets Q4 2027).
capability-compute-launch-demand.pathway: P7 (demand coupling from AI capability, not an AI-math effect)
capability-compute-launch-demand.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous demand: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
capability-compute-launch-demand.why: Full chain (S2): both Starship stages reflown 2027 -> first 100-kW-class compute satellites flown 2028 (struct-highflux-radiator-flight) -> paying 100-kW-class operations in orbit 2029 (materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops) -> internal launch cost under ~$300/kg, Mach33's orbital-compute base-case input, 2029 -> 10 or more compute flights in one year, 2030, with little slack. At about 4.0-4.5 t per AI1-class satellite (Oct 2026 reference), 10 flights of 100 t carry roughly 220-250 satellites, about 40-60 MW at 175-250 kW each. This is where the AI curve meets the launch clock: frontier training compute grows ~5x a year and a GW-scale ground site takes ~2.1 years (Epoch), so S2 and S3 raise demand for compute that needs no grid interconnection. S3 is a year earlier because demand and the physical multiplier both rise from 2028; S1 is later because a capability plateau slows the build-out. More flights also speed Starship production learning. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
capability-compute-launch-demand.strongest_case_small: The economics are unproven and Mach33 itself treats space datacenters as the largest uncertainty in launch revenue; running chips hot shortens their life (33FG's Oct 2026 model puts logic near 134 C at 250 kW in a 200 m2 radiator; struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification); Starlink V3 competes for the same flights through 2028; and ten compute flights in a year is a SpaceX demand decision it can defer.
capability-compute-launch-demand.signpost: First AI1 launch and on-orbit operation; SpaceX disclosure of a compute-satellite production rate; Starship flights carrying compute satellites in 2029 (5 or more keeps S2 on track).
capability-compute-launch-demand.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (proposed as physclock-compute-manifest-anchor; renamed to the trunk's domain prefix). Years moved one year later than proposed (S1 2031 / S2 2030 / S3 2029) to follow physclock-cheap-mass-internal (now 2029) and the launch-slip calibration; S3 High -> Medium (economics unproven). Labelled as an AI-capability demand effect, not AI math. Not a duplicate: struct-gw-orbital-compute is the 1 GW cumulative outcome downstream. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): status, chain and strongest case re-based on the orbital-compute branch: radiator first flight 2028 and paying ops 2029 (was 2027/2028), AI1 ~4.0-4.5 t (was 2.1 t), 10 flights ~220-250 satellites / ~40-60 MW (was ~450 / 70-110 MW); soft edge to struct-gw-orbital-compute added. Years and bands unchanged (S2 2030 Medium matches the GW node chain).

frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.title: Clay rules on the forced Navier-Stokes breakdown claim
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.description: The Clay Mathematics Institute states whether OpenAI's Sep 8, 2026 forced blowup result satisfies its official breakdown statements (C)/(D), which permit a smooth, decaying force. Clay rules need publication in a qualifying outlet, two years, and general acceptance. OpenAI says it will not claim the prize, so the ruling may come only as a change to Clay's 'unsolved' listing. This is the event readers will hear as 'AI solved Navier-Stokes'. Its engineering effect is nil.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.status_oct2026: Clay still lists Navier-Stokes as unsolved; its president Martin Bridson called the evaluation 'deliberately unhurried' and 'absolutely rigorous'. OpenAI says the result establishes statement (C), and also (D), and will not pursue the prize. The underlying Lean claim is T3 with no independent Comparator run or statement audit; the manuscript is not yet published in a refereed outlet.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.premise_tier: T3 (forced NS Lean claim, pending independent check)
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.why: Chain: a Comparator run and statement audit (prop-ns-forced-verified, T4), then refereed publication (earliest 2027), then the two-year rule and general acceptance, then a Clay statement. The institutional clock runs at 1.0x in every scenario, so the earliest year is 2029 in all three. Band Low (judgment, not a computed probability): the check is likely, but publication of a 166-page manuscript, Clay's unhurried review, open questions about whether the force meets (C)'s decay conditions on [0, infinity), and the lack of a claimant make a Clay statement by 2031 less likely than not. Separates the reader-facing 'Millennium problem' headline from frontier-ns-unforced, the force-free question most analysts mean. Engineering effect nil (tl-position-2).
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.strongest_case_small: Clay may never rule if nobody claims the prize, and most mathematicians already treat the unforced question as the real problem, so the ruling changes nothing for mathematics or engineering beyond headlines.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.signpost: A Clay Institute statement, or a change to its Millennium Problems listing, on whether the forced result satisfies (C)/(D); a refereed publication of the OpenAI manuscript starts the two-year clock.
frontier-ns-clay-cd-ruling.revision_note: B-math-frontier: [auditor] New node: separates the Clay (C)/(D) ruling on the forced claim from the unforced question. Band lowered from the auditor's Medium to Low (publication plus two-year rule plus unhurried review plus no claimant; 1.0x institutional clock). Clay facts checked (implicator.ai).

verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.title: Reusable launchers re-prove flight software every flight
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.description: A reusable launch operator flies engine-control, redline, abort, fault-management and termination-interface logic whose key invariants are machine-checked, and re-proves them automatically on every software change between flights, and says so publicly. No certification is required: Part 450 reaches only public-safety computing items. This is the uncertified, flown counterpart of prop-verified-engine-software.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.status_oct2026: None known publicly. Falcon 9 flew 165 times in 2025 with no failures, and Starship flew at 48-91-day intervals in 2025 and 63-66 days in 2026 with software changes between flights (physical-clock domain). Under 14 CFR 450.35(a) the FAA requires an accepted means of compliance for the flight safety system (450.145(b)) but not for computing-system safety items (450.141). Newsletter commentary named a sensor trip as one hypothesis for the 2026 Raptor 3 boostback shutdowns (unverified). The largest launch operator owns a frontier AI lab (SpaceX acquired xAI, Feb 2026).
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.why: Two curves combine. The launch exponential means reusable vehicles fly often and change software between flights, so a regression in redline or abort logic is a recurring risk and re-verification sits on the turnaround path. The cognitive exponential cuts re-verification of a change from 2-6 weeks to 1-3 days, with proof repair in hours (verification-domain cost table), and software-only changes avoid the hardware lag ladder. Launch mission software has no certifying regulator beyond 450.141, and the leading operator owns a frontier lab. Chain (S2): proof agents, spec drafting and FDIR model checking 2027 -> integration into a vehicle software pipeline with reviewed invariant specs 2028 -> first publicly stated flight with re-proved engine and abort logic 2029. S3 equals S2 through 2028, and the binding gates (adoption and disclosure) do not move with cognition, so S3 is also 2029 and Medium. Most launch failures are hardware, so this changes software risk per flight, not cadence.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.strongest_case_small: Most launch failures are hardware; simulation plus HIL regression is already fast at leading operators; and adoption may never be disclosed, which is why S2 is Medium, not High.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.signpost: A launch operator stating, in a mishap report, conference paper or hiring material, that engine-control or abort logic is machine-checked on every release; an FAA license modification citing formal verification of computing-system safety items.
verif-launch-fsw-per-flight.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: New node from the advocate (the uncertified counterpart of prop-verified-engine-software, joining the launch-cadence and cognitive curves). Advocate's 2030/2028/2028 Low/Medium/High tempered to 2031/2029/2029 Low/Medium/Medium: the A3 lag ladder puts proof-carrying flight software in flight at S2 2029, S3 equals S2 through 2028, and disclosure, not cognition, binds the public signpost. physclock-flight-test-cadence made soft, because Falcon 9 already gives a reusable vehicle with frequent software changes. Not a duplicate: prop-verified-engine-software is the certified crewed-program version and astro-proof-backed-flight-software-ops covers spacecraft, not launch vehicles. Soft unlocks are limited to this branch's nodes; edges into external nodes (physclock-test-loop-monthly) are left to that branch. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): Starship interval aligned with physclock-flight-test-cadence (48-91 days in 2025; 63-66 in 2026).

verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.title: Onboard AI agents fly under proof-checked command guards
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.description: An operational spacecraft (not a shadow-mode experiment) lets an unverified learned or language-model agent issue commands directly (tasking, health management, pointing, conjunction response, surface operations), with every command passing through a small guard whose invariants are machine-checked: a recoverable-set or barrier check, resource and keep-out invariants, and command authentication. The agent is never verified; the guard and its isolation are. This applies Simplex runtime assurance to generalist agents.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.status_oct2026: Unverified guards already fly. Shield AI's Hivemind managed imaging tasking, health diagnostics, battery state of charge and pointing onboard a NOVI Space satellite, with 189 autonomous commands validated by Sedaro's SAFE edge framework, which is simulation-based rather than formal (Satnews, Aug 24 2026). An LLM agent supervised a reinforcement-learning thermal controller on flight-heritage hardware aboard the ISS (ASTREA, arXiv 2509.13380). AFRL flew neural-network attitude control with watchdog and guardrail runtime assurance in shadow mode (Jul 28, 2026). NASA's core Flight System has been ported to seL4, an isolation base.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.why: Three curves meet. Cheap proofs make a small guard verifiable at compute cost; onboard compute and cheap launch put capable models in orbit; and fleet scale (more than 355,000 avoidance maneuvers a year at Starlink) and cislunar latency create demand for autonomy. Chain (S2): runtime-assurance proofs 2028 -> guard with machine-checked invariants uploaded to an existing smallsat bus (or flown on a new one, with a verified separation kernel if agent and guard share a processor) -> first operational mission with an agent commanding through the guard 2029. No certifying regulator is involved for uncrewed missions. S3 equals S2 through 2028, so S3 is 2029, but near-free cognition from 2029 and fast-moving defense and commercial demand make it High.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.strongest_case_small: Conservative guards veto most useful agent actions, and a guard over a wrong recoverable-set model is still unsafe; if agent and guard share a multicore processor, timing isolation is measured, not proven; verification of neural perception stays open (verif-nn-verification-scale).
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.signpost: A satellite operator or defense program stating that an onboard AI agent commands the spacecraft in operations through a formally verified guard (machine-checked invariants), rather than in shadow mode or behind a simulation-only check.
verif-onboard-ai-guardrails.revision_note: B-verified-autonomy: New node from the advocate (onboard AI agents under proof-checked guards; the operational instance of verif-runtime-assurance for generalist agents). Kept the advocate's bands Low/Medium/High; S3 2028 -> 2029 because S3 equals S2 through 2028 and its prerequisite runtime assurance is 2028 in both. verif-verified-onboard-stack made soft rather than hard, because the guard can run on the existing flight computer while the agent runs on a payload computer, as current demonstrations do. Evidence checked: Satnews Aug 24 2026 (SAFE is simulation-based, not formal), ASTREA arXiv 2509.13380. Not a duplicate: verif-runtime-assurance is the tier-4 tool, and the auton nodes cover surface robots. Soft unlocks into external nodes (astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale, auton-*) are left to those branches.

comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.title: AI shrinks the quantum computer needed to break today's crypto
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.description: AI-designed quantum error-correcting codes (qLDPC and bivariate-bicycle families), logical instruction sets and arithmetic circuits lower the published spacetime cost (physical qubits x runtime) of Shor's algorithm for RSA-2048 or P-256 by at least 2x below the Oct-2026 best estimates for the same hardware assumptions: under 100,000 superconducting qubits (Pinnacle) or 10,000-26,000 neutral atoms (Cain et al.). Achieved means a published resource estimate that credits an AI-found code or circuit. This lowers the bar hardware must clear; it does not build the hardware.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.status_oct2026: Human work cut RSA-2048 estimates from about 20 million noisy qubits (2019) to under one million (Gidney, arXiv 2505.15917, May 2025), to under 100,000 physical qubits with qLDPC codes at 1e-3 error and 1 us cycles (Pinnacle, arXiv 2602.11457, Feb 2026), and to as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atoms (Cain et al., arXiv 2603.28627, Mar 2026). LLM-guided search found new bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes for about $400 of inference (arXiv 2606.02418). We know of no published Shor estimate that credits an AI-found code or circuit (not searched exhaustively).
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.premise_tier: n/a (capability; no catalog family is load-bearing)
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.why: The 2019-2026 gains came from code choice, arithmetic tricks, magic-state factories and layout: expert-scarce search of exactly the kind AI already does (the $400 qLDPC search). This is the main route by which AI mathematics moves the code-breaking threat to satellite links, and it runs against defenders: it raises the urgency of crypto-agility without changing the fabrication gate on comms-crqc-before-2031. In S2, research-grade applied math is public in 2027 and a resource-estimate paper takes about a research cycle, so 2028; S3 follows S2 through 2027. Bands are judgments on the P1->P4 convention for a negative (for defenders) result.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.strongest_case_small: Estimates were already falling fast through human work, so AI credit may be marginal. The dominant costs (physical error rates, cycle times, connectivity, decoding latency) are hardware, a lower estimate does not change when a machine exists, and the 2026 estimates already assume hardware no one has at scale.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.signpost: A resource-estimate paper for RSA-2048 or P-256 crediting an AI-found code, magic-state factory or arithmetic circuit; a quantum-hardware vendor roadmap citing AI-designed codes.
comms-ai-crqc-resource-cuts.revision_note: B-networks resolver: New node (auditor proposal; advocate's crqc finding names the same error-correction channel). No duplicate in node-index-v1. Resolver changed years from 2029/2027/2027 to 2029/2028/2028 (a published estimate trails public applied math by a research cycle). Soft edges into comms-crqc-before-2031 and comms-crypto-agile-architecture.

revisions.from: AI-found codes and circuits cut code-breaking quantum resource estimates

comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.title: Real-time spectrum sharing among rival constellations
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.description: Three or more NGSO operators in a shared band exchange ephemerides and beam plans and coordinate beams and power dynamically, under a protocol that carries machine-checked bounds on each party's throughput degradation (the FCC's 3% / 0.4% criteria) and proven convergence and fairness, replacing static band-splitting and exclusion angles. Achieved means such an arrangement operates in at least one band in at least one jurisdiction.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.status_oct2026: NGSO-NGSO sharing under FCC 24-117 uses 3% time-weighted throughput degradation and 0.4% added unavailability judged by orbital simulation (Roberts, arXiv 2609.36122); FCC 26-26 (Apr 2026) extended performance-based criteria to NGSO-GSO sharing. Game-theoretic power control for equal-priority NGSO coexistence has convergence and Nash-uniqueness conditions (arXiv 2609.38935); tight guarantees for three or more equal-priority operators remain open (comms research). Amazon filed for a 5,105-satellite direct-to-cell constellation in Jul 2026 (Roberts). No dynamic multi-operator arrangement is known.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.why: Multi-operator coexistence guarantees are genuinely open math, a cognitive bottleneck that S2 attacks (P1), and certified bounds that every party can re-check remove the trust barrier to sharing proprietary beam plans (P2). As filings multiply (Starlink, Amazon Leo, AST, Chinese filings), pairwise static coordination wastes spectrum. But the arrangement needs rival operators and a regulator to accept it, which caps the band at Medium, and commercial and political acceptance runs at 1.0x in every scenario: math solved around 2028 (S2), protocols and trials 2029-30, operation 2031 at the earliest. Low in S2 and S3.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.strongest_case_small: Operators prefer bilateral agreements and band segmentation that protect proprietary beam plans; the largest incumbent gains little from sharing; real-time exchange raises antitrust and security concerns; and static rules may be good enough at 2031 densities.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.signpost: Three or more NGSO operators announcing a dynamic coordination or data-exchange protocol; an FCC or ITU-R WP4A contribution proposing dynamic multi-operator sharing with verifiable bounds.
comms-multi-operator-dynamic-sharing.revision_note: B-networks resolver: New node (advocate proposal, resolver-modified). Mechanism grounded in research/comms.json ('genuinely open: tight guarantees for coexistence among three or more equal-priority operators'); distinct from comms-d2d-coexistence-scheduling (one operator scheduling against budgets) and the ITU regime node. comms-certified-network-optimization moved from hard to soft (sharing does not need mesh routing). Years and bands lowered from >2031/2030/2029 and Low/Medium/Medium to >2031/2031/2030 and Speculative/Low/Low: rival and regulator acceptance does not compress.

physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.title: Operators fly new hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.description: A commercial operator or bus vendor that carries its own risk (no regulator, insurer or government customer accepts the evidence) flies a new-design, not heritage-derived, spacecraft subsystem or structure whose qualification rests mainly on AI-produced analysis with stated uncertainty plus development tests and acceptance-level workmanship screening, skipping protoflight- or qualification-level environmental tests that its own practice would otherwise run. Today's common practice of protoflight testing instead of a dedicated qualification unit does not count.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.status_oct2026: Not yet attributed to AI. Commercial operators already set their own test programs: FAA Part 450 licenses public safety, not vehicle or payload qualification (CRS R48582), and FCC licensing does not review structural qualification (general). Protoflight testing of new designs is common commercial practice, and some risk-tolerant smallsats skip thermal-vacuum testing (general). Most mass to orbit belongs to an operator that answers to no qualification authority: Starlink carried 1,975 t in 2025 against a contested external market of 347 t, about 5.7:1 (research/physclock.json, Mach33).
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.pathway: P1 (process outcome; flight step written out as a chain)
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.why: Chain (S2): AI agents run and check structural and thermal analysis (2027) -> information-optimal development tests (2028) -> a new subsystem designed and qualified mainly on that evidence in 2028 -> 12-18 month smallsat or derivative build (lag ladder) -> flies 2029-30. No Medium cap applies because the operator, not a regulator or customer, accepts the evidence. The AI-attributable step is extending test skipping from heritage derivatives to new designs on the strength of checked analysis. For constellation operators the fleet itself can serve as the test stand (in-orbit statistics from hundreds of units), which counts here when it replaces ground tests on a new design. S2 Medium, not High (judgment, not a computed probability): tests catch workmanship and unmodeled behavior that analysis cannot, a fleet-wide defect costs far more than a protoflight campaign, and the step must be stated publicly to count. S3 High: near-free cognition from 2029 makes analysis-led qualification the default for AI-native builders. Workmanship screening and thermal-vacuum time constants remain.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.strongest_case_small: Risk-owning operators already skip tests they judge not worth it (protoflight, minimal smallsat testing) without AI, so attribution will be murky; an operator that loses hardware to an analysis miss will revert; insurers of commercial GEO satellites require qualification evidence (general).
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.signpost: An operator or bus vendor states that a new-design subsystem flew without protoflight- or qualification-level environmental testing on the strength of AI-produced analysis, by 2030.
physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.revision_note: B-certification: New node from the advocate (commercial self-risk track). Resolver re-scoped it beyond today's protoflight practice (otherwise met today), set S2 High -> Medium, and S3 2028 -> 2029 (S3 equals S2 through 2028; a 2028 flight needs 2027 design). Soft edges into external nodes (capability-program-cycle-compression, physclock-satellite-gen-cadence, physclock-dev-capital-cut) left as cross-branch requests.

physclock-reliability-priors-credit.title: Models count toward reliability, cutting certification flights
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.description: Launch and spacecraft certifiers (Space Force NSSL new-entrant certification, NASA Launch Services Program risk categories, human-rating boards, or component reliability demonstrations) accept AI-produced, credibility-graded physics and flight-data models as Bayesian priors in reliability demonstration, cutting the certification flights or zero-failure trials needed for a stated reliability and confidence.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.status_oct2026: Reliability demonstration by test needs about 230 zero-failure trials for 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence (n = ln(1-C)/ln R); the physical-gate table marks this unchanged unless model-based priors are accepted (then 0.3-0.6x), and no node used that row. Certifiers already trade flights for insight: Space Force certified Vulcan for NSSL in Mar 2025 after two certification flights, and the New Entrant Certification Guide pairs flight-count options with design review (general). NASA-STD-5001B FSR 17 allows probabilistic structural criteria case by case.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.why: Chain (S2): certified rare-event methods 2027-28 -> credibility directive 2029 -> a certifier accepts model priors in a reliability case at its next review cycle 2030. Statistics, not physics, bind: with accepted priors the zero-failure trials needed fall 0.3-0.6x (physical-gate table). Capped at Medium because it is certifier acceptance; S2 Low because it chains on a Medium rulebook with one or two years left, and certifiers already accept two-flight certification with heavy insight, so the next step is small and slow (judgment, not a computed probability).
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.strongest_case_small: Certifiers count flights because priors can be tuned to any answer, and rare-event model-form error is what NASA's 2024 UQ position paper calls unsolved (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20230016541).
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.signpost: A Space Force, NASA LSP or human-rating certification plan, or a component reliability demonstration, that cites model-based priors from AI-produced analysis to reduce required flights or trials, by 2030.
physclock-reliability-priors-credit.revision_note: B-certification: New node from the auditor (uses the physical-gate table's reliability-demonstration row). Resolver set S2 Medium -> Low (chains on a Medium rulebook with little window). Soft edge into external physclock-critical-payload-reuse-acceptance left as a cross-branch request.

revisions.from: Fewer certification flights via accepted model-based reliability priors

prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.title: Public flight data on storing cryogenic propellant in orbit
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.description: NASA and Eta Space's LOXSAT (Electron launch, nine months in LEO) completes its liquid-oxygen demonstration of zero-loss storage, high-accuracy gauging, automated pressure control and transfer, and NASA publishes comparisons of its predictive models against the flight data.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.status_oct2026: Integration was finalized in May 2026 for a launch no earlier than Jul 17, 2026 on Electron; the mission is to validate 11 cryogenic fluid management technologies over nine months and inform Eta Space's Cryo-Dock depot (target 2030) (satnews, May 17, 2026). Whether it has launched could not be confirmed (unverified). NASA's CFM portfolio lists maturing predictive models through flight comparisons as an objective.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.why: A physical-clock anchor with nil AI-math effect on its date. It supplies public microgravity validation data that does not depend on SpaceX releasing its Starship transfer data, which prop-cfm-models' strongest case says SpaceX will keep. Chain: Electron launch (NET Jul 2026, unverified) -> nine months of LOX storage, gauging and transfer tests (to about mid-2027) -> NASA model-versus-flight comparisons published (2028 at the earliest). The data are small-tank and LOX-only, so they calibrate models (soft links to prop-cfm-models and prop-mass-gauging) rather than validate Starship-scale methane behaviour. Medium, not High, in every scenario: launch, spacecraft performance over nine months and publication must all go right (the 2019 Robotic Refueling Mission 3 lost its methane early when its cryocooler failed, general).
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.strongest_case_small: Small tanks and LOX only: scale-up to depot-class tanks and methane still needs Starship data, so the public dataset may not move operational margins.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.signpost: Confirmed LOXSAT launch and nine-month operations, then NASA or Eta Space papers comparing model predictions with flight pressure, boil-off and gauging data.
prop-loxsat-cfm-flight-data.revision_note: B-engines-materials resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the auditor, accepted: not a duplicate (no LOXSAT or public-CFM-data node in node-index-v1), mechanism sound, all fields filled; bands set to Medium rather than the auditor's High because launch is unverified and nine-month operations and publication must all succeed. Links are soft, as the auditor specified.

hyper-model-form-error-bounds.title: Error bounds for carrying ground-test heating data to flight
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.description: Rigorous or coverage-calibrated bounds on the error of aerothermal and material-response models when extrapolated from arc-jet and shock-tube conditions to flight, so that a probabilistic TPS margin can carry model-form error with stated coverage instead of a judgment factor. Achieved when a published TPS sizing carries a ground-to-flight model-form term calibrated against instrumented flight bondline or heating data.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.status_oct2026: Open. The SRL alternative-margining Monte Carlo sampled aerothermal error only between 1 and the existing factors (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20260005218/downloads/SRL_TPS_IPPW.pdf, slide 13), while at the same 8 km/s entry baseline simulations under-predicted VUV by up to 2x against EAST and three UQ methods disagreed between 30% and 100% (Hansson, ESA, 24 Sep 2026). BOLT-1B showed flight transition differs from tunnel transition (Jan 2026). Paired ground-flight datasets are starting to exist: W-6 (May 2026) flew two NASA Ames instrumented eChar tiles.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.why: AI doing research-grade applied math can derive model-discrepancy frameworks with coverage guarantees cheaply (P1), but demonstrating coverage needs paired ground and flight datasets (Varda/Ames instrumented tiles, BOLT-class flights, Orion), which accrue at flight cadence. This is what decides whether the ~25% SRL-style thinning survives once aerothermal error is not assumed to sit inside the existing factors. It matters most where radiation is significant (Mars, Venus, 12+ km/s return) and least for convectively dominated LEO capsules. S2 lands the method by ~2029 and the first flight-calibrated application by ~2030; S1 lacks both the capability and the data in time.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.strongest_case_small: Model-form error under extrapolation may be irreducible without flight data at the exact condition; a few paired datasets a year may not support stated coverage, and engineers may keep judgment factors regardless.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.signpost: A published TPS sizing whose ground-to-flight model-form error term is calibrated against instrumented flight bondline data (e.g. Varda W-6 Ames tiles, Orion) and carried through to a reliability statement.
hyper-model-form-error-bounds.revision_note: B-entry: New node. [auditor] Split from hyper-certified-margin-uq, whose own why called model-form error 'genuinely open'. [skeptic] Signpost and data gate taken from the skeptic's certified-margin finding. Links to hyper-probabilistic-tps-sizing and hyper-12kms-entry-design-basis are soft, as the auditor proposed: LEO capsules can size probabilistically without it.

revisions.from: Model-form error bounds for ground-to-flight aerothermal extrapolation

hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.title: Fleet-trained reentry heating model for one reusable vehicle
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.description: A physics-constrained model of reentry heating and TPS thermal response specific to one reusable vehicle family (Starship first), assimilated from 50 or more instrumented orbital reentries of that family (thermocouple and load-sensing tiles, imagery, trajectory reconstruction). It predicts per-zone heating for the next flight within ~+/-15-20% and is used to shape entry trajectories and plan tile work. For the owner it turns the open transition and SBLI problems into a fitting problem inside the flown envelope; it does not transfer to other vehicles or to CO2 (Mars) entry. Achieved when the operator states that entries are shaped or tile work is planned from such a model.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.status_oct2026: Starship ships have re-entered on most integrated flights since 2024; Flight 10 (Aug 2025) deliberately removed tiles and flew metallic and actively cooled tiles, and Flight 13 (Jul 2026) flew load-sensing and reflown tiles in a heat-shield stress test. Starship flew 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7; physclock-flight-test-cadence expects 12+ a year from 2028 (2027 about a coin flip), and Mach33's reference case has ~90 flights in 2028. SpaceX does not publish its heating models; no ship has been caught.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.why: Two curves combine. Launch cadence supplies the owner with the flight data that the general tier-3 closure nodes lack: roughly 8-10 ship reentries with data through Oct 2026 (general count), about a dozen flights a year from 2028 (physclock-flight-test-cadence; 2027 is about a coin flip) and more once physclock-heavy-cadence-100 is reached (S2 2030, S3 2029), so ~50 instrumented reentries of one family accumulate around 2029. On-demand applied math (S2 2027) makes data assimilation, inverse heat conduction and Bayesian updating cheap to build and maintain. The general transition and SBLI nodes exclude per-vehicle tuning by definition, yet per-vehicle tuning is what an operator needs, so for the owner the open physics leaves the critical path while it stays open for everyone else. The data clock is the launch curve, which is largely independent of AI (S3 runs 0.5-1 year ahead), so S1 and S2 share a year. P6 defaults to Low; Medium because the owner needs no outside acceptance, held below High because the operator may never say it uses such a model.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.strongest_case_small: SpaceX builds this with or without frontier AI mathematics, so AI pulls it forward by months, not years. A per-vehicle fit can fail outside the flown envelope (new trajectories, Mars entry), and the operator may never disclose it.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.signpost: SpaceX or another reusable-vehicle operator states that entry trajectories or tile replacement are set from a model trained on its own fleet's reentry data, or publishes per-zone predicted-versus-measured heating.
hyper-fleet-aerothermal-twin.revision_note: B-entry: New node from the advocate, narrowed. Carries the owner-data curve that the skeptic and auditor removed from hyper-flight-data-pipeline. Scoped to heating so it does not duplicate hyper-tile-damage-accumulation (tile fatigue) or physclock-twin-reflight-clearance (reflight clearance); hard prerequisite is the flight-cadence node rather than ship reuse because reentries accrue on expended ships too. Advocate's bands Medium/High/High and years 2029/2028/2028 lowered to Medium x3 and 2029/2029/2028: disclosure risk does not vary by scenario, and the launch curve moves S2 by at most 0-0.5 year. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): S3 2028 -> 2029 and why/status re-based on B-trunk's launch clock (12+ flights a year from 2028, not 2027; heavy cadence S3 2029): ~50 instrumented reentries accrue around 2029 at the earliest in every scenario. Soft edge from physclock-heavy-cadence-100 removed: it lands after this node in every scenario and closed the only soft loop in the graph (heatshield -> heavy cadence -> this node -> heatshield); the later data growth stays in the why.

struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.title: AI chips and memory qualified to run hot in orbit
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.description: Accelerator logic and HBM stacks are shown, by accelerated life tests, physics-of-failure models (electromigration, gate-oxide breakdown, bias-temperature instability, HBM retention and refresh, solder and through-silicon-via fatigue, combined with dose) and on-orbit telemetry, to survive a 3-5 year orbital mission at elevated temperature (roughly 110-135 C logic and 110-130 C HBM, against the ~105 C / 95 C comparison limits in 33FG's model), so compute-satellite radiators can run hotter and smaller.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.status_oct2026: 33FG's Oct 6 2026 StarMind model fits 250 kW in the filed radiator envelope under 200 m2 only at ~134 C logic / ~132 C HBM (with a higher-rated GPU package); holding 105 / 95 C needs ~327 m2. 33FG found no publicly disclosed flight-qualified part with the required characteristics and estimates chip wear-out life falls from 5.6 to 3.4 years when the stock chip is pushed harder. Musk (Oct 1 2026): the SpaceX version of the VR72 is co-designed with Nvidia for ~250 kW average. Commercial HBM is specified for operation near 85-105 C (general).
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.pathway: P7 (vendor qualification; AI applied math accelerates via P1/P5 accelerated-life models)
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.why: Radiator area scales as 1/T^4 of the radiating temperature, so allowable chip and HBM temperature is the largest thermal lever. Raising the radiating temperature from ~368 K (95 C) to ~407 K (134 C) cuts panel area ~33% at fixed heat (calculation); 33FG's model puts the gap at ~200 versus ~327 m2 for a 250 kW satellite. At ~3.7 kg/m2 that is ~470 kg per satellite (~10% of a ~4.5 t satellite), or ~1,900 t (~19 Starship flights at 100 t) per GW of 4,000 satellites, more than the whole AI radiator-design lever (~350-1,400 t per GW). Physics stays fixed: DRAM retention roughly halves per ~10 C, so hotter HBM needs faster refresh at a bandwidth cost, and Arrhenius wear-out shortens life (general), so the trade is service life (3-5 years, matching chip obsolescence) against radiator mass. The AI-math role is P1/P5: hierarchical Bayesian accelerated-life models, competing-risk wear-out and optimal accelerated-test design let qualification rest on weeks of high-temperature operating life tests (~1,000 h, general) plus first-flight telemetry rather than years of exposure. Chain (S2): first 100-kW-class flights 2028 -> life tests and telemetry 2028-29 -> vendor re-specification of HBM and a published orbital operating envelope 2029. The gate is qualification by the operator and chip vendors, with no regulator, so S2 and S3 tie.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may simply accept a shorter first-generation chip life (33FG notes a first generation could trade life for earlier deployment and data), enlarge the radiator or its filing envelope, or use a cooler-running package; vendors, not AI mathematicians, own HBM reliability data, and the qualifying evidence is life tests and telemetry, not proofs.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.signpost: A published orbital operating envelope above standard junction limits (HBM at 110 C or more) backed by accelerated-life data, or Starmind telemetry showing sustained chip or HBM temperatures of 110 C or more, by 2029-30.
struct-hot-chip-hbm-qualification.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): New node merging the skeptic's materials-hot-hbm-qualification (T5, qualification) and the advocate's materials-hot-chip-wearout-models (T3, P1->P5); renamed to the branch's main domain prefix. Both lenses identify allowable chip/HBM temperature as a bigger thermal lever than radiator design (verified in 33FG's Oct 6 2026 model). One node, not two: physics-of-failure models already exist at vendors, and validation needs life tests and flight telemetry, so the advocate's High-by-2028 model node overstated the AI-math share; the AI role is kept as soft accelerators. Not a duplicate (no chip-temperature node in the graph).

struct-light-solar-array-production.title: Lightweight solar arrays at compute-constellation volume
struct-light-solar-array-production.description: Flexible or roll-out arrays at array-level specific power of roughly 125-140 W/kg or better (for example silicon at ~250 W/m2 on ~1.8-2 kg/m2 blankets) built at compute-constellation volume, hundreds of thousands of m2 a year. This is the mass lever 33FG identifies as the primary constraint on compute satellites, and the non-AI baseline against which the perovskite and specific-power chain is measured.
struct-light-solar-array-production.status_oct2026: 33FG's June 2026 AI1 reconstruction: array ~1,178 kg, 56% of the implied 2.1 t, ~127 W/kg over ~600 m2; the 2.1 t budget closes only if the array reaches ROSA-class ~1.8-2 kg/m2. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response allows up to 1,500 m2 of solar under 4,000 kg per satellite. Roll-out arrays fly today at kilowatt to tens-of-kilowatt scale per wing (general); none is produced at hundreds of thousands of m2 a year.
struct-light-solar-array-production.pathway: P7 (not AI-math-driven; AI touches array structural and deployment design only, marginal P1)
struct-light-solar-array-production.why: Solar is the largest mass block on a compute satellite; every kg/m2 off a ~600 m2 array buys ~6x what the same cut buys on a ~110 m2 radiator (33FG). At ~1,000-1,500 m2 per 250 kW satellite, 1 GW needs ~4-6 km2 of array, many times Starlink's yearly array output (assumption), so array production rather than radiator design is the fabrication gate at GW scale. Reaching 100 kW/t needs this and more: the June AI1 design already assumed ROSA-class arrays to reach ~70 kW/t, so 100 kW/t also needs thinner or higher-efficiency cells (materials-perovskite-primary-power) and hotter chips. Chain (all scenarios): first Starmind flights 2028 -> serial satellite production with arrays at constellation volume 2029. Medium rather than High because the filing allows a heavier 1,500 m2 array within 4,000 kg, so SpaceX may not need the light blanket at volume.
struct-light-solar-array-production.strongest_case_small: SpaceX already builds Starlink arrays in-house at scale and the filing allows a heavier array within the mass envelope, so volume may come with modest areal density; this node is the counterfactual baseline that happens without AI mathematics.
struct-light-solar-array-production.signpost: SpaceX discloses array areal density or W/kg for a Starmind version, or a Starmind production rate implying hundreds of thousands of m2 of array a year.
struct-light-solar-array-production.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the auditor (verified against 33FG's AI1 reconstruction: solar 56% of mass, 'primary constraint is solar areal density'); defined by array specific power so the hard edge to struct-100kw-per-tonne-fleet is a necessary condition. Years moved from the proposed 2028 to 2029 to follow the first-flight slip to 2028. Not a duplicate: the perovskite chain is the materials route; this is the architecture and production route.

struct-formation-compute-clusters.title: Tight-formation compute clusters operate in orbit
struct-formation-compute-clusters.description: Operational clusters of about 10 or more compute satellites holding station within a few hundred metres (inside ~750 m), linked by terabit-class optical crosslinks (~10 Tbps per cluster per SpaceX), running models too large for one satellite. Formation flying is the route to large coherent compute in place of km-scale monolithic structures.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.status_oct2026: SpaceX VP Michael Nicolls (Oct 6 2026): Starmind needs clusters of ~10 satellites in tight formation with ~10 Tbps between them (via 33FG). Google Suncatcher's design places 81 satellites within a 1 km radius at ~100-200 m spacing; its first prototype launched on Transporter-18 on Oct 1 2026 and a two-satellite laser-link test is planned for 2027. Close formation at hundreds of metres has flown since TanDEM-X (2010, general).
struct-formation-compute-clusters.pathway: P7 (not AI-math-driven; AI math second-order via P2 collision-safety proofs and certified link scheduling)
struct-formation-compute-clusters.why: Forcing a frontier model into one satellite forgoes up to 44% of achievable serving output (33FG, Jul 2026); tight clusters recover much of it, and microsecond-scale synchronization bounds a coherent domain to under ~750 m (Mach33). Chain (S2): first 100-kW-class Starmind flights 2028 -> a batch of ten or more satellites launched and phased into formation, with Google's two-satellite link test (2027) as a precursor -> operational cluster 2029-30. AI math lowers risk and operations cost (machine-checked collision safety for dense multi-year formations under thruster faults and communication loss; certified gaps for link scheduling) but does not set the date. Physical gates do not move: optical-terminal throughput, differential-drag and J2 station-keeping propellant, and the debris consequence of a dense cluster. S3 equals S2 in band because the gates are physical and no cluster has flown.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.strongest_case_small: Software (smaller or satellite-sized models, better parallelism) may shrink the single-satellite penalty toward parity (33FG), removing the need for tight formations; dense clusters raise collision and debris risk that licensing may restrict.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.signpost: Ten or more compute satellites holding sub-km formation with terabit-class crosslinks in operation; Google's 2027 two-satellite link test meeting its bandwidth target.
struct-formation-compute-clusters.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (verified: SpaceX 10-satellite cluster statement and Suncatcher Transporter-18 plan via 33FG news). Not a duplicate: struct-km-monolith covers the structure route and only mentions formation flying as its competitor. Advocate's S3 High lowered to Medium (first formation statement Oct 6 2026, no cluster flown, physical gates); S1 2031 -> 2030 since the node is not AI-math-driven.

auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.title: Heavy cargo landed on the Moon
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.description: A refueled Starship or Blue Moon Mk2 cargo lander delivers at least 15 t of useful payload to the lunar south-pole region in one landing. This is where the launch-cost exponential enters the lunar chain: reactors, LTVs, ISRU pilot units, habitats and spares. Smaller Mk1-class deliveries (about 3 t; VIPER, LTVs) are covered in the ground-truth and base chains.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.status_oct2026: No heavy lunar cargo landing yet. Starship reached orbit on Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026), and ship-to-ship propellant transfer is expected in early 2027. In Feb 2026 SpaceX made a lunar 'self-growing city' its priority and told investors it targets an uncrewed lunar landing in Mar 2027 (WSJ via NBC News). NASA's Moon Base plan says heavier infrastructure arrives as cargo-capable HLS come online, and bulk launch buys pairing 4-5 rockets with commercial landers were reported near (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6, 2026). Blue Origin's lunar schedule is exposed to the May 28, 2026 LC-36 loss. struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe names a ~15 t lander as its binding gate.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.pathway: P7 (physical exponential, largely independent of AI math)
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.why: Launch cadence and refueling, not cognition, set this date. AI contributes at the margin through boil-off and transfer models (prop-cfm-models), faster anomaly closure and PSI-informed site selection: 0-0.5 year in S2 and 0.5-1 year in S3 (physclock launch row). Chain (S2): ship-to-ship transfer 2027 -> full refuel campaign 2029 -> uncrewed or cargo-configured landing carrying 15 t or more 2029, under the Moon Base bulk-buy model. Chain (S1): the same curve without AI-assisted anomaly closure -> 2030. Chain (S3): refuel 2028 -> cargo landing 2028. The band is Medium in every scenario: it cannot exceed the refuel campaign's Medium in S1 and S2, announced schedules slip 1.5-3x, and a first landing of a new vehicle class on south-polar terrain carries real tip-over risk even in S3. Second-order unlock where the two curves combine: once landed mass is cheap and design iterations cost almost nothing, lunar hardware can be built mass-tolerant and rich in spares. That shifts reliability gates (ECLSS MTBF, MRE anode life) from 'demonstrate MTBF' toward 'carry spares and let robots swap them'.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.strongest_case_small: This node is almost entirely SpaceX's and Blue Origin's physical program; AI math moves it by months at most, and a single landing failure or refuel-campaign slip costs a year regardless of analysis speed.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.signpost: A Starship or Blue Moon Mk2 landing on the Moon with a declared payload of 15 t or more; NASA bulk lunar-delivery contracts naming heavy cargo flights.
auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing.revision_note: B-moon-mars: New node. It merges the advocate's auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing with the auditor's physclock-lunar-heavy-cargo; the advocate's 15 t threshold is kept because that is the gate struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe names and the one base infrastructure needs. The advocate's 2030/2029/2028 years are kept. Its S3 High is tempered to Medium (auditor's Medium; announced schedules slip 1.5-3x; landing risk), and the 'second landing within 12 months' clause is dropped so the year marks a single event. Not a duplicate: prop-hls-refuel-campaign is the propellant campaign, and no node covered landed heavy cargo. Edges into external nodes (a hard edge into struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe) are left for the struct branch.

auton-moon-base-infrastructure.title: Moon Base Phase 2 infrastructure on the surface
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.description: At one south-polar site, the following are landed and operating: night-surviving surface power of tens of kW (ridge-site solar with storage, or fission), surface communications, LTVs and a logistics cache, plus at least one semi-habitable element. This is the physical base that 'runs itself between crew visits' would maintain. It has no AI-math pathway and exists to show the gate.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.status_oct2026: NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 24, 2026) has three phases: Build, Test, Learn (CLPS and LTVs, up to 30 robotic landings from 2027); Establish Early Infrastructure (semi-habitable infrastructure and regular logistics); and long-duration presence once cargo-capable HLS come online. Reporting dates Phase 2 to 2029-2032 and Phase 3 to 2032 onward (NBC; NASA's release gives no years). Budget reported at ~$30B (Bloomberg via 33FG). LTV awards in May 2026 (Astrolab $219M, Lunar Outpost $220M). Lunar Reactor-1 is to land in 2030. Astrobotic's LunaGrid-Lite (1 kW over 1 km of cable) is a power-distribution precursor.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.why: This is the gate auton-crew-optional-lunar-ops names for itself: there must be enough base to operate. Phase 2 runs 2029-2032. Politics and appropriations compress 1.0x, government flagships slip 2-7 years (physclock), and the first crewed landing has already slipped about four years. Chain (S2): refuel campaign and first heavy cargo landing 2029 -> Phase 2 power, LTVs, logistics cache and a semi-habitable element delivered over several heavy and CLPS landings 2030-31 -> all operating at one site by late 2031 (Low). Chain (S3): heavy cargo 2028 -> launch cadence 0.5-1 year earlier plus near-free design -> operating 2030 (Medium). Chain (S1): the same as S2, with the 2030 heavy-cargo date making 2031 the edge of the horizon (Low). SpaceX's Moon-first priority is an upside a NASA-only schedule would not show.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.strongest_case_small: Nothing here depends on AI mathematics; the base is built when appropriations, landers and landing success allow, and AI only trims engineering labor.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.signpost: NASA Moon Base Phase 2 contracts for a semi-habitable element and surface power with named delivery dates; a surface power system of 10 kW or more operating through more than one lunar day at the south pole.
auton-moon-base-infrastructure.revision_note: B-moon-mars: New node from the skeptic: the binding gate auton-crew-optional-lunar-ops names for itself was missing from the graph. The skeptic's years and bands (2031/2031/2030, Low/Low/Medium) are kept. The hard prerequisite is auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing instead of prop-hls-refuel-campaign directly (the refuel gate is reached through it). The advocate's separate auton-lunar-solar-grid node was folded in as the 'night-surviving surface power' component and not added: a 1 t/yr oxygen pilot can carry its own ~3-6 kW array, so a stand-alone grid node is not a gate for anything in this branch. Not a duplicate of struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe (one power source, here a soft input).

auton-robotic-landing-pad.title: First robot-built landing pad or blast berm on the Moon
auton-robotic-landing-pad.description: Autonomous machines build a landing pad or blast berm of tens of square meters or more from local regolith on the Moon (sintered, melted or 3D-printed), using process windows from auton-sinter-process-control. The structure then survives the plume of a lander or a dedicated plume-test thruster.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.status_oct2026: NASA's MMPACT work with ICON (Project Olympus, $57.2M) aimed at a south-pole pad and blast-shield demonstration, originally targeted for about 2026, and no flight is manifested as of Oct 2026 (general). Lunar construction startups: Lunar Forge (Jul 2026); Astroport with Vermeer on autonomous construction machinery (Apr 2026). Microwave-sintered regolith cracks when cooled faster than ~16 C/min (Coatings, Feb 2026). SCALPSS imaged plume erosion on Blue Ghost Mission 1 (2025).
auton-robotic-landing-pad.why: Pads and berms matter because landing plumes eject regolith at high speed, and the hazard grows with Starship-class landers and repeated landings at one base site. Chain (S2): AI-mapped process windows and cooling-rate control 2029 -> flight unit after a 12-18 month smallsat-class lag -> landing 2031 -> pad-scale area sintered within one lunar day and plume-tested (Low). Chain (S3): process control 2028 -> landing 2030 (Low). The physics that does not compress, sintering power of kW to hundreds of kW and thermal-cycling cracking, keeps even S3 at Low, along with landing odds and the lack of a manifested flight.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.strongest_case_small: Operators can engineer around plumes with mid-body landing thrusters, throttling and standoff distance, so a pad may not be needed before the base has many landings, and the binding constraint is power, not recipes.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.signpost: A CLPS or Moon Base Phase 1 manifest that includes a construction or pad-sintering payload; a relevant-environment test in which a sintered pad survives a rocket plume.
auton-robotic-landing-pad.revision_note: B-moon-mars: New node from the advocate. It gives the dangling auton-sinter-process-control and prop-psi-models a downstream use in the skill tree. The advocate's years and bands (>2031/2031/2030, Speculative/Low/Low) are kept. Its soft input from the rejected auton-lunar-solar-grid is dropped. The test criterion allows a dedicated plume-test thruster as well as a lander plume, so the node does not need a second landing at the same site. Not a duplicate: no pad or construction outcome node exists.

science-smd-budget-restored.title: NASA science budget held near its 2026 level
science-smd-budget-restored.description: Exogenous programmatic gate: Congress again rejects the proposed cut to NASA's Science Mission Directorate (-47% in the FY2027 request) and funds HWO pre-formulation and the Explorer lines near FY2026 levels (HWO $150M). Identical across scenarios because appropriations compress 1.0x. It is not an AI capability; it sits at tier 0 because it gates tier 4-6 nodes from outside the AI chain.
science-smd-budget-restored.status_oct2026: FY2026: Congress enacted $24.4B for NASA, nearly 30% above the request (the largest gap since 1987), including $150M for HWO and $80.5M for NASA's LISA share. FY2027 request (Apr 2026): $18.8B (-23%), Science Mission Directorate -47%, HWO $5M. FY2027 appropriations are not shown as enacted on the Budget of NASA page; the LISA article says Congress 'again passed FY2027 appropriations' at a similar LISA level (unverified; conflicts with the budget page, possibly committee action).
science-smd-budget-restored.pathway: exogenous (not an AI pathway; politics and appropriations compress 1.0x)
science-smd-budget-restored.why: Load-bearing for HWO design closure and the BHEX flight (hard prerequisite) and a confounder for the portfolio shift, none of which the cognitive clock can move. Restoration has precedent: Congress rejected nearly all of the FY2026 cuts. Medium rather than High because funding must hold through FY2027-31 for HWO pre-formulation and the Explorer cadence to continue, and politics does not compress in any scenario. Identical across scenarios by construction. Bands are judgments.
science-smd-budget-restored.strongest_case_small: Congress may restore the topline but not HWO or the Explorer line; a long continuing resolution at FY2026 levels would look like restoration but block new starts such as a Small Explorer selection.
science-smd-budget-restored.signpost: Enacted FY2027 Commerce-Justice-Science appropriation: Science Mission Directorate total, HWO line and Astrophysics Explorer line versus FY2026.
science-smd-budget-restored.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the skeptic. Resolver verified the FY2026 enacted $24.4B (~30% above request), the FY2027 request (-23% NASA, -47% SMD) and HWO $150M -> $5M on Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budget_of_NASA ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_Worlds_Observatory ; LISA share from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Interferometer_Space_Antenna). Hard prerequisite of science-hwo-design-closure and science-bhex-flight. Tier 0 chosen to place an exogenous input with the roots; kind marks it as non-AI.

science-stage4-survey-data.title: Next-generation dark-energy survey data in hand
science-stage4-survey-data.description: The data supply behind the dark-energy question: DESI's final BAO analyses and Euclid's first cosmology release are public, with early Rubin and Roman survey data arriving. Makes the photon-limited clock behind science-dark-energy-verdict a visible node instead of an unstated gate.
science-stage4-survey-data.status_oct2026: DESI DR2 BAO results are out, and the preference for dynamical dark energy did not diminish from DR1 to DR2 (arXiv 2504.06118); Roman launched Aug 30 2026; Rubin's survey and Euclid's cosmology releases follow their own schedules (general).
science-stage4-survey-data.pathway: exogenous (P7 physical data supply, independent of AI mathematics)
science-stage4-survey-data.why: AI mathematics does not move survey data releases; the dark-energy verdict arrives with them. Identical across scenarios by construction. High because DESI's final analyses and Euclid's first cosmology release are both scheduled well before 2031 (general), so slips of a year leave the node inside the window. Bands are judgments.
science-stage4-survey-data.strongest_case_small: Release schedules slip, and 'in hand' is a matter of degree: full-depth Rubin and Roman cosmology comes after 2031.
science-stage4-survey-data.signpost: Euclid DR1 cosmology papers and DESI final-year BAO release dates.
science-stage4-survey-data.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the auditor: makes the data clock behind science-dark-energy-verdict visible after the skeptic's change left that node with no hard prerequisite. Hard prerequisite of science-dark-energy-verdict (2029 or later, so no ordering conflict).

science-private-observatories.title: A privately funded space telescope returns data
science-private-observatories.description: A philanthropically or commercially funded space telescope of 1 m aperture class or larger, built outside agency selection and appropriations, returns science data by 2031. The only current instance is Schmidt Sciences' 3 m Lazuli (announced Jan 2026, launch target July 2028). Smaller subscription missions (Blue Skies Space's 13 cm Mauve, 45 cm Twinkle planned) show the business model but are below the threshold. AI-run analysis, test-anomaly diagnosis and operations can trim its slips; they did not create it.
science-private-observatories.status_oct2026: Schmidt Sciences announced the 3 m Lazuli space telescope in Jan 2026 with a July 2028 launch target; its team calls two years to launch 'admittedly aggressive' and targets about four hours, or as little as 90 minutes, from command to photons (Sky & Telescope, Jan 14 2026). Blue Skies Space delivered first data to its Mauve science programme on Jul 6 2026 from a 13 cm telescope; Twinkle (45 cm) is planned (bssl.space).
science-private-observatories.pathway: P7 (P1 assists in integration, test and operations)
science-private-observatories.why: Full P7 chain: (1) capital was committed by a foundation in Jan 2026, not by appropriations; (2) design and build run 2026-28, mostly before public research-grade applied math (S2 2027), so AI's share is integration analysis, test-anomaly diagnosis (physclock-ai-mishap-analysis, S2 2027) and operations; (3) mirror and detector fabrication, thermal-vacuum testing and integration stay physical (1.05-1.3x); (4) launch is not scarce; (5) commissioning, then data. Announced schedules run 1.5-3x long (physclock slip table), so a 2.5-year plan from Jan 2026 implies launch from late 2029 to 2033 and data by 2031 at roughly even odds: Medium in every scenario (judgment). AI trims slips at the margin but does not change the earliest year, so the node is identical across scenarios. It qualifies 'no observatory flies sooner': outside agency selection and appropriations, the physical clock is the only clock. A second, AI-native private observatory started in 2028 and flying by 2031 would need an unannounced funder and is not counted.
science-private-observatories.strongest_case_small: One program carries the node; private projects slip too (Twinkle has been planned for years, general), and a 3 m space telescope built in 2.5 years has no precedent.
science-private-observatories.signpost: Lazuli design-review and launch-date updates; announcement of a second philanthropic 1 m-class space telescope.
science-private-observatories.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate, reshaped: AI-capability hard prerequisite dropped (Lazuli's funding and schedule predate public applied-math capability; AI enters as soft edges), bands set equal across scenarios at Medium (advocate had S3 High), and Mauve excluded by the 1 m threshold (resolver verified 13 cm). Facts verified on Sky & Telescope (Jan 14 2026) and bssl.space. | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): mishap-analysis year in why corrected to S2 2027 (B-certification).

science-onboard-science-inference.title: Spacecraft send answers, not raw data, with error bounds
science-onboard-science-inference.description: A science mission (smallsat, hosted payload or Explorer-class; new, or by software upload to an operating spacecraft) runs onboard inference that turns raw instrument data into science products (event detections, classifications, spectral fits, compressed fields) with certified error bounds (stated false-negative and distortion rates) that its science team accepts in place of raw data for a stated share of its downlink, and retargets observations on those products. It cannot recover information the photons never carried; the gain is selection and compression of what is recorded.
science-onboard-science-inference.status_oct2026: Onboard autonomy for science is not new: EO-1's Autonomous Sciencecraft Experiment detected events and retargeted from 2004 (general); AEGIS selects rover targets onboard Curiosity and Perseverance (general); ESA's Phi-sat-2 (launched Aug 2024) runs onboard AI applications including image compression and cloud detection (ESA). Missing are certified error bounds that let a science team discard raw data; most science instruments still downlink raw or losslessly compressed data (general).
science-onboard-science-inference.why: Two curves combine: onboard compute is becoming routine (COTS AI chips in orbit, materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops, S2 2029) and AI applied math makes instrument-specific error analysis cheap. Chain (S2): cap-applied-math 2027 -> error-bounded detection and compression for a specific instrument 2028 -> software upload to an operating mission or a rideshare smallsat (12-18 month lag ladder for derivative payloads) -> operating with a stated downlink saving in 2029. It attacks downlink, part of the domain's dominant data-supply bottleneck (research/science.json). S2 Medium because science teams are conservative about discarding raw data and certification is the novelty, not the inference; S3 High because cognition is near-free from 2029 and one mission (a university smallsat is enough) clears the bar with two years of slack; S1 Low because applied math reaches outside teams only in 2029. S3 equals S2 through 2028. Bands are judgments.
science-onboard-science-inference.strongest_case_small: Distribution-free error bounds (conformal prediction, lossy-compression bounds) already exist, so the mathematics is not the barrier; and optical downlinks may relieve the bottleneck faster than onboard inference.
science-onboard-science-inference.signpost: A science mission team publishes onboard-derived products with certified error bounds and reports the share of downlink saved.
science-onboard-science-inference.revision_note: B-science resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate, reshaped: precedent added (EO-1 ASE, AEGIS, Phi-sat-2), so the novelty is certified error bounds accepted by a science team; hard prerequisite materials-verified-fault-tolerance made soft (Phi-sat-2 flies COTS AI without proven fault bounds); S2 High -> Medium and S3 2028 -> 2029 (S3 equals S2 through 2028). | B-fix (integrator, 2026-10-07): cots-orbital-compute year in why corrected to S2 2029 (B-orbital-compute-power).
